It is not enough to show its inferiority to Christianity in this respect; it ought in fairness to be confronted with other false religions. F. von Schlegel, though by no means favourable to Mohammed or his religion, yet allows, in his Philosophy of History, that its moral code is higher than that of Buddhism. Respect for women was not unknown to the pre-Islamite Arabs, and Kadijah and Ayesha are in honourable remembrance with the followers of Mohammed. Still, however, the blight upon woman's lot, which is only removed by Christianity, presses heavily upon the weaker sex throughout all Moslem countries. Although a large proportion can only afford to keep one wife, yet polygamy, to the extent of four wives, besides concubines, being sanctioned by religion, is beyond the reach of attack. And women are certainly regarded as a subaltern class in a state of virtual servitude. Their religious education is limited to a mechanical knowledge of prayer; they are forbidden to attend the worship in the mosques; and jealousy precludes them from the visits of any religious teachers. Their paradise is supposed to be different from that of men; and a devotional life is almost unknown. There is no religious ceremony of marriage; and in this, as in her entire social status, the Mohammedan wife is probably in a position inferior to that which was enjoyed by an ancient Roman matron. Far more vast is, of course, the gulf between the women of Islam and of Christianity, of which all the chief communions can display such noble specimens of piety, heroism, and intelligence. The harems are but too often a stage for the development of bad passions, as envy, jealousy, and unnatural crimes. Abortion is so common as to have affected the population in some countries, as Turkey; nor is it punishable, if the master of the household have given his consent. Sons by different mothers are constantly rivals, and their jealousies have often rent in pieces the fabric of Mohammedan states. The most stable of Islamite governments—the Ottoman—is supposed to have owed its endurance in great measure to the circumstance that Mahomet II. made fratricide a law in the imperial family; and the Sofi in Persia used regularly to put out the eyes of princes not destined for the succession. Nor is the influence of wives able to restrain rulers, as Christian princesses have often done, from acts of cruelty. One noble but solitary exception is recorded,—that of Zobeide, wife of the celebrated Haroun Al Raschid. The extreme facility of divorce is an evil as great as that of polygamy. It is in some degree checked among the wealthy by the provision that the wife's dowry must be restored, and in Persia the feeling of the higher classes is said to be against it. Still the practice is fatally prevalent, and induces a low and degrading tone about all that concerns the matrimonial relation. Above all, the rebukes uttered by St Paul in the first chapter of his Epistle to the Romans (verses 26-28) are but too applicable to the moral condition of most Mohammedan countries, and more particularly of Turkey. Another feature in the social life of Islamism is that of slavery. Whatever difference of opinion on this head may exist among Christians, few will be found to assert that the principle of slavery is recognised by Christianity as an enduring institution; and none will deny that the abolition of slavery in Europe is attributable to the influence of the gospel. Now, Mohammedanism recognises the principle, and this is surely so far a blot upon its character. Nevertheless, when this is once admitted, the highest commendation must be bestowed on the humanity of many of the provisions for the treatment of slaves. Mohammed from the first put slaves under the protection of his creed. He taught that they were brethren, equally created by God, and that good or ill treatment of them would seriously affect an owner's prospect of paradise. A master who chastises without cause ought to let that slave go free; liberation of slaves is at all times a good work; a female slave cannot be, without her own goodwill, separated from her child; and if she have borne a son to her master, must be set free. The most recent travellers (e.g., Burton) fully confirm the reports of earlier observers. They tell us that a slave who is dissatisfied can legally compel his master to sell him. It is not merely possible, but even common, for a Mohammedan slave to rise to the highest offices. Lieutenant Burton travelled with a pacha who had been the slave of a slave, and of whom a Turkish officer remarked,—C'est un homme de bonne famille, il a été acheté. It is true that

MOHAMMERAH

Pages 322-323

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, about 40 miles from the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, is situated on the left side of that river at its point of bifurcation before entering the Persian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a>. The position of this town affords <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantages in a commercial point of view, as it communicates by means of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> channel with the Karun, and thereby with the fertile regions of Khuzistan to the N.E., while by the Euphrates it is connected with Basrah, Hillab, and Baghdad on the one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the other. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Mohammerah are intelligent and enterprising men; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon, it is probable, become one of the most important <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the Euphrates. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, however, is excessively hot, and owing to the moist and marshy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, extremely unhealthy. A colony was founded near the site of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Mohammerah by Alexander the Great, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; and the adjacent district was called by him Pellaean, after his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Pella. This town having been destroyed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, was restored by Antiochus Epiphanes, and named by him Antiochia. It was afterwards taken possession of by an Arab <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> called Spasines, from whom it obtained the name of Charax Spasinu, and the district that of Characene. It was evidently at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> much nearer to the sea than at present, a circumstance which confirms the opinions of several recent travellers in this region, that the delta of the Euphrates is encroaching on the sea with unusual rapidity. Mohammerah was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> an object of contention between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and Persia, until it was finally ruled by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, instituted by the two governments in recent years, that it should adhere to Persia. During the British-Persian <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 1857 the town was bombarded and taken by the British under Sir James Outram on the 26th of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, but shortly after evacuated by them according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between the two governments signed at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. The frontier between the two countries, according to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> watered by the Euphrates, excepting that about Mohammerah, should belong to Turkey, and that watered by the Karun to Persia. MOHILEV. See MOGHILEV.

MOHILL

Pages 323-323

a market-town and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEITRIM">Leitrim</a>, situated at the foot of a hill, 9½ miles E. by S. of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARRICK">Carrick</a>-on-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a>, and 92½ miles N.W. by W. of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. The town has a parish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, Roman Catholic and Methodist chapels, a dispensary, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and workhouse. Some trade is carried on in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and pigs, and numerous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are held. Pop. (1851) 1223.

MOIR

Pages 323-323
DAVID MACBETH, was born at Musselburgh in Mid-Lothian on the 5th of July 1798. He received his elementary education at the grammar school of his native town, and was, at the age of thirteen, apprenticed for a term of four years to Dr Stewart, a medical practitioner there. At the conclusion of his apprenticeship he completed his medical course at the University of Edinburgh, and received his diploma of surgeon in 1816. Moir had originally intended to enter the army, but the recent peace not offering much encouragement in that quarter, he returned home and spent his leisure in literary pursuits. During his laborious apprenticeship he had found time to cultivate those pursuits in which he afterwards gained a name, and had even made his first appearance as an author in some of the local magazines as early as 1812. Towards the close of the year in which he left college he put forth a small anonymous publication entitled The Bombardment of Algiers, and other Poems, which was not characterized either by originality or power. In 1817 the young surgeon joined Dr Brown as a partner in an extensive and laborious medical practice in the town of Musselburgh and its neighbourhood. While Moir entered upon the duties of his profession with great zeal, he nevertheless succeeded in snatching occasional moments to gratify his unquenchable thirst for literary studies. He had already been a frequent contributor in prose and verse to the Scots Magazine and to Constable's Edinburgh Magazine, when he made his debut in the pages of Blackwood as an occasional prose essayist, but especially as a writer of grave and comic verse. The clever effusions of The Eve of St Jerry, The Ancient Waggonere, &c., are now known to have been written by Moir, although these, as well as many others of his jocose pieces, were generally ascribed to Maginn. His serious verses bore the signature Δ, which gave origin to his literary cognomen of "Delta." This connection with Blackwood ceased only with his death. In 1823 Moir made the acquaintance of John Galt the novelist, who had come to reside in his neighbourhood; and so intimate did their friendship become, that when Galt was called suddenly off to America before completing his Lost of the Lairds, the novelist commissioned Moir to write the concluding chapters of that work. The Legend of Genevieve, with other Tales and Poems, were collected from the various magazines in which they had originally appeared, and published, with additions, in a separate volume in 1824. This work, while generally well received by the press, met with but a very limited sale. In 1824 Moir commenced to publish in the pages of Blackwood his novel of The Autobiography of Maunsie Wauch, a work which delineated with much quaint humour and quiet power some of the most subtle peculiarities of the Scotch character, and which gained for its author very considerable reputation. Moir was warmly pressed at this time by his friends in Edinburgh to remove to the Scottish metropolis, where he had at once the prospect of a more lucrative practice and a more extensive circle of literary friends. The scenes of his early days, however, had a strong hold on the poet, and he regarded the poor among whom he had laboured so long as having peculiar claims upon him. He accordingly resolved to abide by his provincial practice, which entailed so very great drudgery, that for more than ten successive years Moir never slept a single night beyond the scene of his labours. He married in 1829, and published two years afterwards his Outlines of the Ancient History of Medicine, being a view of the progress of the Healing Art among the Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, and Arabians; a work which was well received by the members of his own profession. On the visitation of the cholera in 1832, Moir put forth extraordinary exertions to check the progress of that virulent and mortal disease; and as secretary of the Board of Health at Musselburgh, gave to the public his Practical Observations on Malignant Cholera, and Proofs of the Contagion of Malignant Cholera. These pamphlets met with great success, and were recognised, even by those who differed from them, as very masterly productions. In the autumn of 1832 Delta attended the meeting of the British Association at Oxford, and afterwards visited London, where he met Coleridge and other men of literary note. On the death of his friend Dr Macnish in 1837, Moir collected together the fugitive pieces of "the Modern Pythagorean," and published them with a Life of the author. A few years later he was called to perform a similar service to the memory of his lamented friend Galt. Early in 1843 Delta circulated privately, and then published, his Domestic Verses, which contained some touching pieces full of true tenderness and beauty. In the summer of 1846 he met with a severe accident by being thrown from a carriage, which confined him for months and rendered him lame for life. Moir had always taken a special interest in antiquarian studies, and on the publication of the new edition of The Statistical Account of Scotland, he supplied an interesting paper for that work on the antiquities of his native parish of Inversesk. In 1851 he delivered a course of six lectures at the Edinburgh Philosophical Institution, which were afterwards published, On the Poetical Literature of the

MOISSAC

Pages 323-324

a town of France, department of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARN">Tarn</a>-et-Garonne, is pleasantly situated on the Tarn, here crossed by a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, in an extensive valley surrounded by hills covered with wood and vineyards, 15 miles W.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTAUBAN">Montauban</a>, and 97 miles S.E. of Bordeaux. The streets are narrow, crooked, steep, and ill paved, but the houses are well and substantially built. Moissac contains some remains of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, founded in the seventh century, consisting of cloisters, several pointed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and the old gateway, which is adorned with bold and fantastic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. The old abbey itself, however, has disappeared, and its site is occupied by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> edifice of no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> elegance. The town contains a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flour-mill, tribunals of first instance and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and a communal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. There is a considerable trade in flour, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c. Pop. (1851) 10,655.

MOITTE

Pages 324-324

Jean Guillaume, an eminent sculptor, was the son of a well-known engraver, and was born in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1747. So marked was his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that the sculptor Pigalle, who was then at the head of his profession, requested to have him for a pupil. In a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> young Moitte fully justified this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. His statue of "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> carrying the head of Goliath" gained for him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and the privilege of studying at the French Academy in Rome. Accordingly he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in 1768, and set himself with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enthusiasm to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the architectural fragments of old Rome, and the masterpieces of the great sculptors of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. His progress was rapid, and it was then that he began to evince that correctness of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of proportion, variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and happy choice of draperies, which became so conspicuous in his subsequent works. Compelled by ill <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> to return to his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1773, Moitte began to execute several great national works. Among these were the bas-reliefs of several of the barriers of Paris, the colossal figures representing the provinces of Bretagne and Normandy, the statue of Cassini, the bas-reliefs in the Louvre, of Moses, Numa, and the Historic Muse, and an equestrian statue in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> of Bonaparte. About this time he was decorated by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of the Legion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>. Moitte died in May 1810.

MOKRIN

Pages 324-324

a village of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Torontal, 42 miles W.N.W. of Temesvar. It has a Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and some trade in corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, cattle, sheep, and swine. Pop. about 5500.

MOLA

Pages 324-324
or MOLA DI BARI, a seaport-town of Naples, in the province of Bari, situated on a low point of land on the Adriatic, 13 miles S.E. of Bari. The town consists of an old and new portion; the former of which contains a castle, and is surrounded by walls and ditches, but is meanly built, with narrow and irregular streets. The new part of the town, however, which extends along the shore, is better laid out, and has three creeks for the accommodation of small vessels. The harbour is insecure; but the roadstead, though unprotected, has good anchorage. A considerable coasting trade is carried on in oil, cotton, and carrots. Pop. 8400.

MOLASSE

Pages 324-324
or Molasses, Jacques de, the last grand-master of the Templars, was born of a noble family in Burgundy, and entered his order about 1265. In a short time his bravery against the Infidels raised him to note. He succeeded William de Beaujeau as grand-master of the Templars, and was present at the recovery of Jerusalem in 1299. Subsequent reverses compelled him in 1305 to retreat to Cyprus to recruit his forces. It was then that he was recalled to France for the alleged purpose of assisting in effecting a union between his own order and that of the Knights Hospitallers; but the real object was different. Philip the Fair, with the connivance of Pope Clement V., had resolved to fill his empty exchequer with the great wealth of the Templars, even at the cost of their complete destruction. At the same time he knew that public opinion, offended at their dissoluteness and excessive pride, would easily be reconciled to their downfall. Accordingly, after soothing down all suspicion by a series of notable favours which he bestowed on Molai, he suddenly, on the 13th of October 1307, caused the whole order throughout France to be arrested, and their effects to be seized. On the same day he took up his abode in the luxurious palace of the Temple at Paris. The Templars were tried before inquisitors on the charges of heresy and immorality. On being subjected to the torture of the rack, some chose to die rather than criminate themselves unjustly, while others confessed themselves guilty of the crimes alleged. Among the latter was the grand-master Molai. However, when brought soon afterwards before the papal commissioners, he retracted his confession, and demanded the liberty of pleading his cause before the supreme pontiff himself. But the pope had already satisfied his mind on the subject, and accordingly he abolished the order of the Temple in 1312. Meanwhile Molai was lying in prison at Paris. At length, in 1314, he was tried along with three other Templars, and as he still persisted in retracting his former confession, was condemned to be burnt alive. He protested with his last breath the innocence of himself and of his order.

MOLASSES

Pages 324-325
or Melasses (in Portuguese Mel de açúcar or Melópo, from melatium, a low Latin derivative of mel, honey, signifying, according to Nonius, must concentrated to half its bulk), is the syrup or mother-water that is separated from the crystals or grains of raw sugar in the course of manufacture. It drips from those crystals like honey from the comb, a circumstance to which it no doubt owes its name, and especially to its likeness to honey in taste, consistency, general appearance, and uses. The name is sometimes given to treacle, which, as distinguished from molasses, is the syrup separated from the lowest boiling in refineries of sugar, or from the "bastard" sugar obtained in sugar-houses by boiling imported molasses. In France and elsewhere treacle and molasses bear indiscriminately the name molasse; in Germany that of syrup. Molasses varies according to the colour, strength, and treatment of the sugar which yields it. Fine bright sugar yields fine bright molasses; weak sugar, viscid or weak molasses. Muscovado or unclayed sugar yields thick or heavy molasses; clayed sugar thin, but, when kept from becoming acid, strong molasses. By strong molasses is meant molasses capable of producing a large percentage of granulated sugar. The heaviest molasses, though containing less water, and therefore a greater percentage of saccharine matter, is not generally the strongest, its thickness being often connected with the presence of much grape-sugar and impurities. The best molasses is obtained in the earlier periods of the crop season, and before rains set in. Molasses is usually of a dark-brown colour. St Croix, Molasses. Barbadoes, and Porto Rico, produce the finest, of that yellow or amber colour which is preferred. The progress of improvement in the making of sugar, for which there is still ample scope, may be expected to improve the colour, as well as reduce the proportion yielded, of this the less profitable extract from cane-juice. Molasses is shipped in tight casks (called in this country punchcans; in Cuba and America, hogheads), containing from 9 to 15 cwt. each. The bungs are left out to give free vent to the fermentation to which it, particularly if strong and fresh, is subject on the voyage. Iron tanks have been used, but only to a very limited extent. The deposit of sugar which frequently settles at the bottom of the casks during the voyage is called foot. Although molasses is produced wherever sugar is made, the only parts of the world which export it in any considerable quantity are the West India Islands, of which Cuba alone in 1856 contained 226,000 casks, mostly of large size, or two-thirds of the whole commerce in the article. Brazil, Mauritius, the British East Indies, Java, and the Philippines, which collectively supply about a third of the world's sugar, do not ship any quantity worth notice; yet they might do so profitably, notwithstanding length of voyage, if better means were devised to prevent waste and acidity. Much molasses is converted into rum on the estates. Jamaica distills all its molasses. A great deal of what is sent to the United States of America, and (when grain is dear, or inferior molasses, chiefly clayed from Cuba, is cheap) some also of what is sent to the United Kingdom, finds its way to the distilleries, producing from 6½ to 7 or 8 gallons of proof spirits per cwt., unexceptionable in quality. Sugar is supposed to yield 11 to 11½ gallons per cwt. In the city of Boston alone, the chief seat of this branch of the trade, the quantity distilled was, for the years 1854-5-6, near 50,000 casks a year. The returns for the United Kingdom show 134,682 cwts. so used in 1856. The laws of the United Kingdom prohibit the use of molasses in breweries, in order to maintain the duty on malt at its present high rate. For domestic brewing this material is allowed and is suitable, but it is not so used. There are several other ways in which it might be serviceable, but it is not used, because it is not sold here in retail; common treacle, which has a better consistency, and is also cheaper, or refiners' "golden syrup" (a finer sort of treacle), being kept by the grocers in preference. In the United States and British America molasses is largely used as an article of diet in its natural state. Molasses or treacle from beet-root sugar, an extract necessarily obtained in large quantities in the beet-sugar works of Europe, has an unpleasant vegetable flavour, and is employed for feeding cattle and for making alcohol and acetic acid. The principal consumers in the United Kingdom are the refiners of Greenock, Liverpool, London, and Leith, who, by operations not yet benefited by modern science so much as may be hoped for, obtain from it a dark, or, as the case may be, a yellow sugar, resembling West India muscovado, the residue being treacle. Of 82,000 casks imported into the United Kingdom in 1856, half came to the seaports of Clyde, 25,000 to Liverpool, and 15,000 to London. The magnitude of the molasses trade is further shown by the following figures:—The United States imported in each of the years 1854-5-6 above 25,000,000 gallons, or about 2,500,000 cwts., besides consuming its own growth, which in these years amounted to not much less. In the same years this kingdom imported an average quantity of 950,000 cwts. The remarkable progress of this trade is shown by comparing the imports into the kingdom in the years 1820-30-40, when they were only 39,991, 250,648, and 432,220 cwts. The increase is due to the greater indifference with which the planters regard the making of rum, to the enlargement of the sugar-boiling business in the chief northern ports of Britain, to the removal of the prohibitory duty, and to the vast extension of the growth of the cane, especially in the highly prosperous slave-labour Spanish colony of Cuba. It is worthy of notice that this "sweet" is used almost exclusively by the English-speaking countries of the world,—Great Britain, and the states and colonies to which she has given birth. The present duty on molasses is 5s. per cwt., and the price, exclusive of duty, has ranged for some years between 7s. and 20s. per cwt., or about half the price in bond of the lowest sorts of sugar. In this country it is sold by weight; in the United States and the colonies by measure (the old gallon). An imperial gallon weighs from 13 to 14 lb. The specific gravity of molasses from muscovado sugar is about 1·370, and from clayed sugar 1·356. A trade has lately arisen between Cuba and the United States in melado, which is cane-juice concentrated, or sugar with the molasses remaining unseparated from the crystallized portion. (See Sugar.) (R.A.M.)

MOLD

Pages 325-325

a parliamentary borough and market-town of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Flint, pleasantly situated in a fertile valley near the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Alen, 13 miles W. from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. The town is irregularly built, chiefly of brick. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are,—the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome edifice of the fifteenth century, with an embattled tower, richly carved; and the county-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which cost L3000. There are also places of worship belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, and Baptists; national and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; a market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and a savings-bank. The parish contains extensive coal pits, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, as well as some manufactories of earthenware, bricks, and cotton. Bailey Hill, a little to the N. of the town, was in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries crowned by a fortress, which was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of many sanguinary fights between the English and Welsh during the border warfare. It was captured by the latter under Owen Gwynedd in 1146, was retaken by the English, some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, but again came into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Welsh in 1201. In its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> is the humble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> of Richard Wilson, the celebrated landscape-painter. Mold combines with Caergwyll, Caerwyll, Flint, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOLYWELL">Holywell</a>, Overton, Rhuddlan, and St Asaph, in returning a member to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>. Pop. (1851) 3432.

MOLDAU

Pages 325-325

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, rising in the Bohemian Forest, on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and flowing in a S.E. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> as far as Rosenberg. It then turns to the N., and continues generally in this direction till it joins the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a> at Melnik, after a course of 230 miles. The most important tributaries of the Moldau are the Luschnitz and the Sazava on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and the Wattava and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERAUN">Beraun</a> on the left. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on its banks are Rosenberg, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUDWEIS">Budweis</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. In the lower <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its course the Moldau is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river, and contributes more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the Elbe than the Upper Elbe itself. It abounds in fish, and is navigable to Prague for vessels of 60 tons, to Budweis for barges of 10 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 15 tons, and to Rosenberg for smaller craft.

MOLDAVIA

Pages 325-327

one of the two Danubian Principalities under the sovereignty of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, is bounded on the N. and E. by the Russian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bessarabia and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, S. by the principality of Wallachia, along with the Danube and the Kilia branch of that river, which separate it from Turkey, and W. by the Austrian provinces of Transylvania and Bukowina; lying between N. Lat. 45. 15. and 48. 13., and E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25. 10. and 30. 13. It has a length of about 200 miles from N. to S., an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth of about 100, and contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of about 19,982 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The Carpathians form the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> boundary on the W., and separate it from Transylvania. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> rise to the height of from 3000 to 5000 feet above the sea, and send off numerous branches to the eastward, gradually diminishing in height as they approach the banks of Moldavia, the Sereth, which traverses the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from N. to S. The general surface of the country, excepting the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> occupied by the marsh-lands at the mouth of the Danube, slopes from W. to E., and terminates in an undulating plain of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Moldavia are the Sereth and the Pruth; the former rises among the highlands of Bukowina, flows first E. and then S., and finally falls into the Danube after a course of about 270 miles. The Pruth rises in the same region as the Sereth, flows S.S.E., and falls into the Danube at Reni after a meandering course of 360 miles. It forms the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-eastern boundary of Moldavia, and is navigable for three-fourths of its length. The other important rivers are the Bistritz, Birlat, Moldava, Tatros, and Tazjen, all of which flow southward, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Sereth. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the country is rather stony in the E., but gradually improves in fertility as it approaches the rivers; and the greater part is abundantly productive, amply rewarding the labour which is applied to it, notwithstanding the excessive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the summers, and the intense <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the winters. The corn is excellent, especially the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> hard wheat. The wine is good, and produced in abundance. Excellent cattle are fattened in the meadows; and good <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, are most abundant. The mineral resources of Moldavia are very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; but little advantage is taken of their abundance. Rock-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and bitumen, are the principal minerals, and these are found chiefly in the Carpathian Mountains and towards the N. of the principality; while small quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-dust have been obtained from some of the rivers. Great numbers of horses, cattle, sheep, goats, and hogs are reared in the meadows and forests of Moldavia; and some of the boyars or noblemen have studs of no fewer than 400 or 600 mares. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Moldavia is exposed to severe cold in winter and excessive heat during summer. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a> falls in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities in the months of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and September; but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> in October and November is very mild. The vicinity of the marshes which occupy that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the state between the Pruth and the Black Sea is, however, very unhealthy, especially during the hot season. The inhabitants live in a wretched manner in earthen huts, without windows or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>, and sometimes underground. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are few and rude in kind. But this want is fully compensated by the great advantages for importation and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> afforded by the Danube, now open to all nations. The three ports of Moldavia are Galatz, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISMAIL">Ismail</a>, and Reni, all on the Danube; but the first is by far the most important. In the year 1855, when the operations of the Russo-Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> were transferred from the Danube to the Crimea, and the trade of that river was thus enabled to resume its usual importance, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of shipping and tonnage entering and clearing at Galatz amounted to a total of 1698 vessels, with 417,584 of aggregate tonnage. The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> shows the value of the imports and exports of Galatz from and to the various countries in 1855, as well as the amount and value of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> imported and exported during the same year: | Value of Imports from— | Value of Exports to— | |------------------------|---------------------| | <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> | | £1,258,240 | £698,920 | | France | <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> | | 152,460 | 180,280 | | Turkey | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> | | 141,840 | 112,280 | | Holland | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> | | 38,480 | 78,480 | | Other countries | <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> | | 38,920 | 31,680 | | **Total** | **Other countries** | | 624,580 | 1,194,360 | The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Moldavia is almost identical in kind Moldavia, with that of the neighbouring principality of Wallachia, and seems to belong to the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Dacians, who inhabited this region from the earliest times. The Moldavians, indeed, differ very little from their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> in appearance, costume, and manner of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and they still bear the name of Roumuni or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, while their dialect is a corruption of Latin with Slavonic, Turkish, and Tartar words. There are four classes of people in Moldavia, viz.—1. The boyars or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and the clergy, who are exempted from <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a>; 2. The privileged classes, such as the academic corporation at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JASSY">Jassy</a>, but who are liable to taxation; 3. The villagers; and 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GYPSIES">gypsies</a>, who have no civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, and, till a recent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, were in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> either to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> or to private individuals. They have now, however, been released from servitude; those belonging to the government having been emancipated several years earlier than the slaves of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, who received their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> only in 1853. The established <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Moldavia is that of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, superintended by a metropolitan and a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is Jassy; and the principality is divided into Upper and Lower Moldavia, and subdivided into districts, of which the former contains six, and the latter eight, as follows: ### Upper Moldavia | Districts | Chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a> | Pop. (1856) | |-----------|-------------|------------| | 1. Dorohoi | Mihaileni | 80,222 | | 2. Botoshani | Botoshani | 146,361 | | 3. Suczava | Falichieli | 71,044 | | 4. Nyenchoo | Nitra | 90,219 | | 5. Roman | Roman | 80,877 | | 6. Jassy | Jassy | 128,566 | ### Lower Moldavia | Districts | Chief Towns | Pop. (1856) | |-----------|-------------|------------| | 1. Vasboul | Vasboul | 84,703 | | 2. Falchey | Koosh | 78,722 | | 3. Tutova | Birlat | 83,675 | | 4. Tacutel | Tacutel | 86,505 | | 5. Kowel | Kowel | 132,244 | | 6. Poohol | Poohol | 124,217 | | 7. Kovarhol | Galatz | 67,293 | | 8. Moldavian Bessarabia (ceded 1856) | Ismail | 42,600 | **Total** | **1,297,047** The principality of Moldavia occupies part of the region known in ancient times by the name of Dacia (which see). In the later times of the Byzantine Empire it was overrun by several barbarous tribes, and the inhabitants were driven across the Carpathian Mountains, where they remained until the thirteenth century, when a small colony, under a chieftain called Bogdan, re-established themselves in their country, which received from their leader the name of Bogdania, by which it is still known among the Turks and natives. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and his son gradually extended their power over the whole of Moldavia. The princes of Moldavia were at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> called voivodes, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> leaders; a name which was afterwards changed by the Turks to that of hospodars, which is still retained. In the thirteenth century Moldavia was frequently disturbed by civil war, occasioned by rival claimants for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and these dissensions rose to such a height that the country was divided into two parts, one of which acknowledged the sovereignty of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and the other that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. A union was, however, soon after effected, and Moldavia became subject to Hungary, paying at the same time a tribute to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>. In 1536 Moldavia came under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>. For a considerable time after this period it was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of constant wars between the Poles and Turks, until the claims of the former to the sovereignty of the state were finally abandoned in 1621, and peace concluded between Turkey and Poland. But notwithstanding the authority of the Sultan was now unquestioned, the boyars still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to elect their own voivodes, a proceeding which caused numerous disputes between them and the Moldavia. Porte. In 1710 Demetrius II., voivode of Moldavia, entered into negotiations with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great of Russia, by which the latter undertook to force the Turks to restore the principality to its former independence. On the failure of the Russian attempts, and the retreat of Peter, who was accompanied by Demetrius, the Sultan deprived the Moldavians altogether of the privilege of electing their princes. These were thenceforth nominated by the Porte <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, and received their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of hospodars. In 1738, during the war of Austria and Russia against Turkey, Moldavia was invaded by a Russian force under Münich, and occupied for two years, but was evacuated after the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>. In 1769 it was again occupied by the Russians, and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the victories gained by them over the Turks, became for a short time subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a>. It was, however, restored to Turkey by the peace of Kutchuk Kainaryi in 1774. Three years later, Bukowina, which had before formed a part of Moldavia, was ceded to Austria. In 1789 this unfortunate principality was again the scene of contest between Russia and Turkey, until the peace of Jassy in 1792, when the Russian frontier was fixed by the Dniester. In the war of 1807-12 Moldavia again fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Russians, who, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCHAREST">Bucharest</a>, acquired possession of Bessarabia, and thus extended their frontier to the Pruth. At the commencement of the Greek war in 1820 an insurrection broke out in the Danubian Principalities, but was suppressed by the Turks, who then occupied with an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> the two principalities until the year 1826. It was then agreed by an article in the treaty of Ackermann, that the hospodars of Moldavia should be elected by the boyars out of their own number for a period of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. In 1828 another war between Turkey and Russia broke out; and Moldavia was occupied by the Russians without opposition until peace was established by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a> in 1829. By this treaty it was stipulated that all the Turks should leave Moldavia, which was thenceforth to be under the protection of Russia. The hospodars were now to be elected for life, and their power was limited by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a>, consisting of ten boyars, and an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of deputies from the boyars, the clergy, the academic corporation, and the landowners, which was to meet annually. An annual tribute is paid to the Porte of three millions of piastres, or somewhat more than L27,000, and an additional tribute is paid at the accession of each new hospadar. The Moldavians were also bound to pay to the Porte a yearly sum as a compensation for the surrender by the latter of the fortifications N. of the Danube, and of the rights they formerly possessed. The principality was governed by the Russian general Kisseloff from 1832 to 1834, when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was approved by the Porte; and in the same year Michel Stourdza was elected hospadar. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was formed in 1840 to unite the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia into one state, but without success. In 1848 the influence of revolutionary sentiments was felt in Moldavia; the people of Jassy demanded a new constitution, and although the hospadar successfully resisted this movement, he laid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his authority in the same year. In 1849 the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALTA">Balta</a> Liman was concluded between Russia and Turkey, in accordance with which the hospodars were to be nominated by the Russian and Turkish courts for a period of seven years; and in June of that year Gregory Ghika was appointed hospadar. In 1853 a Russian army entered and seized possession of Moldavia and Wallachia, and the hospodars of the Principalities retired. After attempting in vain to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the Danube in Wallachia, the Russians, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1854 crossed that river at Galatz, and seized the fortresses in the Dobrudsha. They then proceeded to lay siege to Silistria, but this town was so vigorously defended that they were obliged to raise the siege, and the British and French troops having arrived at Varna, the Russian army evacuated the Principalities in the autumn of 1854. The hospodars then returned to their respective governments, and the Principalities were occupied by an Austrian army. At the conference of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1855 a proposal was made by Baron Boursqueny, the French plenipotentiary, to unite the two principalities under a foreign prince, subject to the sovereignty of Turkey; but the discussion of this proposal was deferred until the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the Porte was known. By the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1856, a portion of Bessarabia was reunited to Moldavia, so that the Russian territory had no longer any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the Danube. At the same time the protectorate of Russia over the Principalities was abolished, and the continuance of all their rights and immunities was guaranteed by the European powers. The future organization of the Principalities was to be decided according to the wishes of the majority of the people. The treaty of Balta Liman, in accordance with which the hospadar Gregory Ghika governed Moldavia, being annulled, and at the same time the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> of seven years for which he was appointed having expired, that prince laid down his authority, and the Sultan appointed Theodore Baltche hospadar in his stead. During his reign Ghika had granted to the Moldavians the liberty of the press, and had shown himself favourable to the union of the Principalities, which was the wish of the majority of the people; but the present hospadar, as well as the Sultan, is opposed to it, and the liberty of the press has been suppressed by the Sultan. The receipts of the principality in 1853 amounted to 13,235,230 piastres or L129,411, and the expenses to 12,456,324 piastres or L122,320, of which the tribute to the Sultan made up 715,000 piastres or L55,000. The army of Moldavia in the same year consisted of a force of 15,944 men. (For the more recent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see Wallachia.)

MOLESWORTH

Pages 327-328

Sir William, an eminent British statesman, was the lineal descendant of an old Cornish family of extensive landed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and was born in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1810. In his thirteenth year he lost his father, and succeeded to the family estate and baronetcy. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, but was rusticated there for challenging his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to mortal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. After spending some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> at the university of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, engaged in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, classics, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, he repaired to Germany. There his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was chiefly devoted to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOLOGY">philology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He then made the usual tour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and returned to England in 1831. In the same year, before he had attained his majority, he delivered an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> and elaborate speech in favour of parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> at a Cornish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> meeting. This first appearance of his in public prepossessed the local Liberals so much in his favour, that in 1832 he was returned without opposition as one of the members of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> for the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Cornwall. He was re-elected by his constituents in 1835; but in 1837 so powerful had the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> against his opinions become, that he despaired of regaining his seat. He therefore became a candidate for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, and was successful. On the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of 1841, the clouded prospects of his party deprived him of all hope of being returned by his former constituency, and induced him to retire without a contest from parliamentary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Sir William Molesworth devoted the next four years to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> study of politics and social economy. In 1845 he was again on the field as a candidate for Southwark. His bold advocacy of the Maynooth <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> excited formidable opposition; but his open and conscientious conduct at length won the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to represent this constituency during the rest of his life. Ever since his entrance into Parliament Sir William Molesworth had been gradually acquiring the reputation of a clear, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, logical, and weighty speaker. He had directed all his energies to the reformation of the colonial office, had aroused the attention of Parliament to that subject, had explained with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ability the principles of colonial self-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and had finally convinced statesmen and the public of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of his views. It was therefore with general approbation that he was appointed First <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSIONER">Commissioner</a> of Public Works in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1853, and Colonial Secretary in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1855. But this latter office he did not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy. He died of a low gastric fever in October 1855.

MOLETTA

Pages 328-328

a walled seaport town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Terra di <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, on the Adriatic, 16 miles W.N.W. of Bari. The town as approached from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> has a fine appearance, many of the houses being handsomely built of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> resembling marble, but its streets are narrow and dirty. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are,—a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, several churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and a castle. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> goods and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>. Some ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is also carried on. The harbour is formed by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> and a sandbank, which acts as a <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-BREAKWATER">breakwater</a>, and is well sheltered, except from the N. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. A considerable trade is carried on in corn, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, almonds, and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. In the neighbourhood of the town there are some curious oval caves, arranged in tiers, and hewn out of a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> rock. In all these saltpetre is found; and one of them, called the Nitre Cavern, is 1400 feet in circumference and 112 in depth. Pop. 17,000.

MOLIERE

Pages 328-332

the assumed name of Jean Baptiste Poquelin, who was born at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1622. His father, Jean Poquelin, exercised the vocation of topisier, and subsequently that of tapissier <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALET">valet</a>-de-chambre to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. Young Poquelin, who seems to have been designed for the same trade, received originally a somewhat meagre <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and remained connected with his father's shop till he was fourteen years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Nothing is known respecting the boyhood of Molière till the year 1637, when his father succeeded in securing the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of his office for his eldest son Jean Baptiste; then in his fifteenth year. It has been customary to fill up this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> blank in the early <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dramatist by an apocryphal story of a fond grandsire extorting occasional permission to take young Poquelin to witness the theatrical performances at the Hôtel de Bourgogne. Unfortunately, however, it turns out, on more accurate inquiry, that this benevolent old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> died <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> four years after his grandson's birth. Whether <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> not the slumbering genius of Molière was awakened by the indifferent specimens of the histrionic art which he beheld at the Hôtel de Bourgogne, it is at least certain that in the year 1637 he became a student at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Clermont, now known as that of Louis le <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a>. During his five years' residence at this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> he enjoyed the private instruction of Gassendi, one of the first philosophers of his age, and numbered among his fellow-students such men as Chapelle, Bernier, Cyrano de Bergerac, Hessaut, and Condé's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> de Conti, afterwards known as the liberal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of letters and the friend of Molière. His relation to Gassendi, however, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The influence exerted over the expanding genius of the future dramatist by the teaching of this illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> must have been at once powerful and abiding; and in the withering scorn and fearless satire with which Molière afterwards assailed the vices, and unmasked the hypocrisy of his age, one can detect the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a man who in his early years was a favourite pupil of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who made bold to challenge the authority of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, and to enter the lists with Descartes. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Molière distinguished himself in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at the college of Clermont, he gained a name for classical learning hardly less eminent. It was here he attained to that intimate acquaintance with the Latin dramatists which he afterwards turned to so good account in his compositions for the stage. On the completion of his collegiate course, Molière commenced the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which he prosecuted with more or less regularity during the three following years. It is difficult to say whether or not Molière had resolved upon any definite <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of life previous to this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; at all events, a circumstance occurred just when he had reached his twenty-third year which proved the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>-point in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It so happened that one Madeleine Béjart, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> actress of some celebrity, visited Paris in 1645, when "a young fellow named Molière," as old Tallemant des Réaux drily informs us, finding greater attractions in this interesting lady than he had yet discovered in the dull <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of Cujas and Trebonian, renounced his legal studies, followed the charmer to the provinces, and subsequently joined her troupe. Thus it was that Jean Baptiste Poquelin, or as he now called himself Molière, was led, whatever may have been his previous leanings, to assume a profession which from that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> became the business of his life. During the year which inaugurated his dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> Molière endeavoured to establish himself at Paris in connection with the Théâtre Illustre, which had been originated by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of young men of good family, who considered themselves possessed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a>. Failing in this attempt, Molière betook himself to the provinces, and soon found himself a member of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the previous object of his admiration, Madeleine Béjart. Little is known respecting his provincial life, which occupies a space of not less than twelve years (1646-1658), except what is exceedingly meagre and fragmentary. During the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that time Molière was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of a company of strolling players who spent their time in amusing the citizens of Nantes, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, Bordeaux, Lyons, Pézenas, Béziers, Grenoble, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>. From the outset Molière resolved to combine the profession of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> and author, and endeavour, while he built up his fame, to secure his fortune. He accordingly assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of author by converting certain Italian pieces into acting plays for his company, and which were characterized more by the faults of the Italian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> than by the genius of Molière. His first regular production was the Étourdi, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> in five acts, which was represented at Lyons in 1653, where it met with so much success that the principal performers belonging to another troupe permanently attached themselves to the fortunes of Molière. His play, although it surpassed the comedies of Scarron and Scudéri, which preceded it, was nevertheless much inferior to Molière's subsequent productions. It is made up of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of isolated incidents and intrigues, which succeed each other certainly, but display very little inherent connection. Yet, amid all these defects, it gave marked <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, in its spirited <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>, ready repartee, and felicitous flow of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, of very decided advancement in stage <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. This piece was afterwards "revised and polished" by Dryden into his Sir Martin Marall. (See Downes's Roscius Anglicanus, p. 38, 1789.) Reinforced by the recent valuable accession to his company, Molière repaired to Béziers, where his former class-fellow, the Prince de Conti, was holding the states of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. Here the rising player received the distinguished <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of his noble friend, and his company was called upon to put forth all their energies to furnish entertainment to the prince, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Dépit Amoureux was acted here for the first time in 1656. As a whole, it is inferior to the Étourdi; yet it met with decided success. So greatly was the prince delighted with the genius of the dramatist, that it is said he offered to make him his secretary,—a distinction which Molière respectfully declined, remarking, "I am a tolerable author, but I should make a very bad secretary." Fortunately for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the French drama, Molière had the courage to be faithful to his genius, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> which did as much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the player as the handsome offer did to the prince. Having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some time his strolling performances in the south of France, Molière approached the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, attracted by the hope of better fortune and greater Molière, fame. After assiduous efforts he succeeded, through the influence of De Conti, in obtaining permission to give a theatrical entertainment before their majesties and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. This was a trying position for the strolling player, but he trusted to his genius, and it proved all-sufficient. Accordingly, on the 24th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of October 1658, his company played Corneille's tragedy of *Nicomede* before this august assemblage, at a theatre erected at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of the old Louvre. Molière, who felt that his company was inferior in tragedy to the *troupe royale* of the Hôtel de Bourgogne, who were present, came forward after the performance, and adroitly observed that he and his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> were but feeble copies of those first-rate models, and hoped that his majesty, who had graciously tolerated their rustic ways, would allow them to play one of the little comic pieces which had gained their author some reputation in the provinces. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> granted the request, and the adventurous provincials represented a one-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>, now lost, called the *Docteur Amoureux*, with so much success that they were desired by royalty to remain at Paris, and received permission to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *Troupe de Monsieur*, the king's brother, and to play alternately with the Italian comedians at the Petit-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a> Theatre. So this author-actor, with his squat, ungainly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, coarse features, and melancholy countenance, finds that his reception by the fastidious public of Paris has not been inferior to that given him by the provinces. There was a fascination in Molière's person despite all its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> defects. Every limb and muscle of that awkward figure had something to say for itself; and, as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> remarked of him, "he is an actor every inch of him, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of his head to the soles of his feet." How he entertained the public at the Petit-Bourbon during the succeeding year is not known. It is certain, however, that he produced his celebrated *Précieuses Ridicules* in November 1659, which had such an extraordinary success that, though the prices of admission were trebled on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day, the piece had a run of four months. The fame of Molière and genuine French comedy began alike with this play. Its author was hailed enthusiastically from the parterre with "Courage! courage! Molière, voilà la vraie comédie." If not designed as a satire upon all the ladies or précieuses connected with the famous Hôtel de Rambouillet, a literary circle which could boast of some of the most eminent men of the age as its supporters, this play was certainly meant to heap <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> upon that class of précieuses who perverted alike good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and correct feeling by the elaborate affectation of their talk, and the mock refinement of their sentiments. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and manners of this class were portrayed with extraordinary power and boldness; and it was with no small consternation that these absurd coteries found themselves thus ruthlessly impaled before the public by this comic censor, who kept all Paris laughing at their follies for four months in succession. The public now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> what was in store for them when Molière chose, as he modestly phrased it, "étudier le monde." His next piece, *Scaramouche ou le Coq Imaginaire*, was given to the public on the 28th of May 1660, and met with a success more than equal to its merits, having been acted forty times in succession. The beginning of 1661 found Molière installed in his new theatre, the *Salle du Palais Royale*. Whether or not it was owing to the associations connected with the past history of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> that Molière felt induced to appear as a tragic author, he at all events produced a heroic comedy termed *<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Garcie de Navarre; ou le Prince Jaloux*, in 1661, imitated from the Italian, which proved an utter failure, and was the source of loud jubilation to his enemies. Molière withdrew it, and afterwards transferred some of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> to the *Misanthrope*. On the 24th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1661 he made another attempt, in his *École de Maris*, to retrieve his fallen reputation, and met with the most brilliant success. He owed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> idea of this piece to Terence in his *Adelphi*, and some of the details he borrowed from Boccaccio and Lopez de Vega. During the same year he was engaged by the unfortunate Fouquet to compose a comedy for the celebrated fête which the superintendent of finance gave to Louis XIV. at Vaux, a few days before that monarch arrested and imprisoned for life the minister who entertained him. Molière had only five days to execute his task, and at the end of that time he produced *Les Fâcheux*, a piece which introduces us to the most provoking set of "bores" that ever afflicted mortal. The materials are of the slendest, having been designed to be acted during the intervals of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BALLET">ballet</a>; but such a lecture on the follies of character and manners as it contains Molière alone could read. An event occurred on the 20th of February 1662, just two days after the appearance of *Les Fâcheux*, which was not destined to increase the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of the dramatist. He became united to Armande Béjart, a sister of that Madeleine Béjart, with whose charms the young lawyer Jean Baptiste Poquelin had been smitten some twenty years before. The envenomed tongue of slander laboured industriously to circulate the calumny that Molière's wife was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his former mistress; and the chef of the Hôtel de Bourgogne kindly improved upon the scandal by submitting to the king that Molière's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> would leave his wife at once fatherless and a widow. His majesty, however, showed his appreciation of these malicious reports by condescending, in February 1664, together with Henrietta of England, Duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, to be the sponsors of Molière's child. Much of the loathsome scandal regarding this affair has been swept away by the unequivocal testimony of certain legal documents which had escaped detection till 1821. But the worst <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of all awaited the much-wronged dramatist, in the imprudent coquetry of his wife, which served not a little to embitter the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life. He pursued his labours, however, with unmitigated ardour, although he had by this time drawn <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon himself a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOST">host</a> of assailants. The parties whose ridiculous conceits and absurd follies he had so ruthlessly exposed, too wise to express the rankling pain which the arrows of the censor had inflicted, now set themselves up as guardians of the purity of the national morals and of the national language. His next three plays aggravated the animosity of his enemies a hundred-fold.
