Lon. 36° 56', in a cognominal district, comprising the Zambesi delta, with the two stations of Senna and Tete. It stands on a mud bank on the left side of the stream, surrounded by swamps, which render the ground on which the town is situated so soft that the walls of the houses are always sinking. The climate is very unhealthy, and fevers are extremely prevalent. A large trade in slaves is carried on here surreptitiously. They are collected in the town from the interior, and remain there till the ships from Rio de Janeiro and other ports of America arrive in the river. Pop. of town, 200 Christians, 32 free blacks, and 3260 slaves.

MOLOCH

Pages 417-418
or MOLECH, or MILCHÔM, the national god of the Ammonites, who dedicated their children to him, by making them "pass through the fire." There are various opinions concerning this method of consecration. Some think that the children leaped over a fire sacred to Moloch; others are of opinion that they passed between two fires; and others conceive that they were really burned in the fire by way of sacrifice to this god. That the latter opinion is the only tenable one may be shown from such passages as Ps. cvi. 38; Jer. vii. 31; Ezek. xvi.20, xxiii.37. It cannot be precisely ascertained at what period the Israelites became acquainted with this idolatry, but it is highly probable that it was before the time of Solomon, the date usually assigned for its introduction. Moses in several places forbids the Israelites to dedicate their children to this god, as the Ammonites did, and threatens death and utter extirpation to such persons as should commit this abominable idolatry. (Lev. xx. 1-5.) There is great probability that the Hebrews were much addicted to the worship of this deity; since Amos (v. 26), and after him Stephen (Acts vii. 43), reproaches them with having carried along with them into the wilderness the tabernacle of their god Moloch. Solomon built a temple to Moloch upon Mount Olivet (1 Kings xi. 7); and Manasseh, long afterwards, imitated his impiety by making his son pass through the fire in honour of Moloch. It was chiefly in the valley of Tophet and Hinnom, to the east of Jerusalem, that the Israelites paid their idolatrous worship to this false god of the Ammonites. After the restoration all traces of this idolatry disappear. The accounts of this idol and his worship found in the Old Testament are very scanty. Münter has collected the testimonies of the classical writers on this point with great completeness, in his Religion der Karthagener. Many of these notices, however, only describe late developments of the primitive rites; the description, e.g., of the image of Moloch as a brazen statue, which was heated red hot, and in the outstretched arms of which the child was laid, so that it fell down into the flaming furnace beneath. This account, which is first found in Diodorus Siculus as referring to the Carthaginian Kpôvov, was subsequently adopted by Jarchi and others, but is not admitted by Movers, to apply to the Moloch of the Old Testament. The names of Moloch ("king") and Baal ("lord") are almost synonymous. Their connection is seen by comparing Jer. xxxiii. 35 with xix. 5; where both names are used as if they were interchangeable, and where human sacrifices are ascribed to both deities. Baal is the chief name by which the principal god of the Phoenicians is known in the Old Testament; but only the two above-cited passages ascribe to him the sacrifice of human victims. The Greek, and Latin authors, however, give abundant testimony to the human sacrifices which the Phoenicians and their colonies offered to their principal god, in whom these classical writers have almost always recognised their own Kpôvov and Saturn. Thus we are brought to the difficulty of reconciling Moloch, as Saturn, with Baal, as the sun and Jupiter. In reality, however, this difficulty is in part created by our association of classical with Semitic mythology. When regarded apart from such foreign affinities, Moloch and Baal may appear as the personifications of the two powers which give and destroy life, which early religions regarded as not incompatible phases of the same one God of nature.

MOLTON

Pages 418-418

South, an old market-town and municipal borough of England, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Devon, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>, 26 miles N.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. It has an ample market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and several well-built and cleanly-kept streets. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a Gothic edifice of the fifteenth century, containing a richly-carved <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> pulpit. It has also a guildhall and a borough jail. Moluccas. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of coarse woollen fabrics and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LACE">lace</a> are carried on here. The borough is governed by a mayor, 3 aldermen, and 12 councillors. Market on Saturday. Pop. (1851) 4482. In the neighbourhood are some rich <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is occasionally found. About 3 miles to the N.E. is a small village called <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Molton.

MOLUCCAS

Pages 418-419
or SPICE ISLANDS, a numerous group of islands in the Asiatic Archipelago, situated between Celebes on the W. and New Guinea on the E., and stretching from N. Lat. 2. to S. Lat. 9. They are believed to amount to several hundreds, though many of them are small and uninhabited. The group is formed of three smaller clusters, viz., the Gilolos or Moluccas proper, the Ceram group, and the Timor Laut group. The first of these, extending from 2. S. to 3. N. Lat., comprehends the islands of Gilolo, Morty, Mandioly, Batchian, Oooy, Mysole, Ternate, and Tidore, besides others of smaller size. The cluster of Ceram, which lies in the centre of the group, between 3. and 5. S.Lat., contains, among others, the islands of Ceram, Booroo, Amboya, and Banda. The third group lies farther to the S., situated between Australia and the W. of New Guinea, and includes the Timor Laut, the Key, and Aroo islands. The surface of the whole group is decidedly mountainous, and attains in some of the islands heights varying from 7000 to 8000 feet above sea-level. In its geological structure the group is principally volcanic, and contains several active craters, as well as a number of hot springs, which are found chiefly in the island of Amboya. The outline of the mountains, moreover, is bold and rugged, and the coasts are both steep and irregular. Violent earthquakes are of frequent occurrence. The mountains are extensively wooded, even to their summits; while in the lower regions there is a rich soil. There are numerous excellent harbours, but sand-banks are frequently thrown up on the coast by the earthquakes, which render the navigation intricate. Owing to their tropical situation, the climate of the Moluccas is at all seasons warm; but the smallness of their size, and the prevalence of the monsoons, prevent the heat from rising to an excessive degree. From October or November till April or May, when the N.W. monsoon prevails, the hot and rainy season continues; but during the other months, when the S.E. monsoon blows, the temperature is considerably lower. The moisture of the air, however, is at all times great, and even during the dry season occasional showers fall. The nature of the climate and soil prevent the cultivation of corn in the Moluccas; and the principal food of the natives is obtained from the sago palm; besides which, bread-fruit, cocoa-nuts, and many other products of tropical countries, grow in great abundance. Spices, however, as the name of the islands indicates, are the articles of produce most important to Europeans. Of these, cloves and nutmegs are the principal, and are exported in large quantities. Sandal and other kinds of wood useful for furniture are also obtained here. Small quantities of gold, coral, madreporite, and mother-of-pearl are found on the islands; and some commerce is carried on with China in edible birds' nests, seasnails, and sharks' fins. The Dutch monopolies, however, which have tramelled the trade here for so many years, are now almost completely abolished, and the good effects are rapidly becoming more apparent in an extended commerce. The inhabitants of the Moluccas are of two races,—the Papuans and the Malays. The former, believed to be the same as the inhabitants of Australia, have in many of the smaller islands been exterminated by the Malays, and in the larger ones have only retained possession of the interior and mountainous parts. The Moluccas were first visited by the Portuguese in 1510; but shortly after, their right of possession was disputed by the Spaniards under Magelhaens, at the head of a small fleet sent out by Charles V. This dispute at length terminated in favour of the latter. It was not till 1596 that the Dutch made any permanent settlements on these islands. The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1603, had obtained in 1618 the supremacy over many of the princes of the Moluccas, who were allowed to retain their authority subject to the company. This company was dissolved in 1795, and the Moluccas became immediate dependencies of Holland. During the French war of 1796, however, they were taken by the British, who held possession of them till 1800, when they were returned to Holland. The islands were again occupied by the British in 1810, but were finally restored to the Dutch in 1814, by the treaty of Paris.

MOLYN

Pages 419-419
Peter, surnamed II Tempesta and Pietro Muller or De Mulleribus, a distinguished painter, was the son of an artist of the same name, and was born at Haarlem in 1637. At an early age he was initiated in his art by his father, and is said to have been so fond of drawing, that he used to play truant from school, and to skulk by the sea-shore, sketching the ships in the distance, and the cattle that were grazing near him. His first models were the hunting pieces of Snyders; and his imitations, if continued, might in course of time have rivalled their originals. In his thirtieth year he was converted to Popery by a Carmelite monk, and shortly afterwards proceeded to Rome. There Molyn practised his art with great success. The Duke of Bracciano became his patron, and his fame rapidly increased. He was especially remarkable for the wild imaginative power with which he represented devoted ships tossing amid the confused turmoil of the elements. So striking, indeed, was his success in storm scenes, that he came to be generally known among the Italians by the name of "Tempesta." He also excelled in landscape-painting. His pictures of that description are marked by an imposing variety of scenery, consisting of woods, lakes, rocks, and romantic edifices, overhung by troubled skies, and relieved by lively and expressive figures. While Molyn was thus raising himself in the rank of his profession, he was also degrading himself in the scale of morality, and was fast becoming insensible to every virtuous emotion. At length, it is said, growing tired of his wife, an Italian lady, he left Rome on some pretence, and, after visiting Venice and Milan, settled in Genoa. From this city he was not long in despatching an accomplice to Rome with a letter to his wife charging her to come to him with the messenger. The lady, full of suspicion, at first refused, but on a second summons complied. She was murdered on the way by her companion; and her husband at the same time married a woman of Genoa, of whom he had become enamoured. Such suspicious circumstances led Molyn to be tried for murder, convicted, and condemned to perpetual imprisonment. The gloom of his dungeon, and the terrors of his guilty conscience, seem to have stimulated the peculiar powers of his imagination, for the tempests which he continued to paint were darker and more terrific than before. After Molyn had lain in prison for five years, according to some, or for sixteen years, according to others, he contrived to escape. Taking up his abode at Milan, he plied his pencil with greater success than ever, and increased both in influence and in profligacy. He lived most sumptuously, and kept a private menagerie to afford him facility for the study of animal-painting. At the same time he became so notorious a libertine that he received the additional surname of "Muller." Towards the close of his life the decaying faculties of Molyn failed to sustain him in his former style of living, and he lapsed into comparative poverty. He died of a fever in 1701. Many of his pictures may be seen among the collections in Milan and in its neighbourhood. (See Lanzi's History of Painting, and Stanley's Dutch and Flemish Painters.)

MOLYNEUX

Pages 419-419

William, a learned mathematician, was descended from a family of fortune, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> in April 1656. He entered the university of his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1671, and after graduating as B.A., he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1675 to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at the Middle Temple. The greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, was devoted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. On his return to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in 1678, his independent fortune enabled him to marry, and to devote all his time to the cultivation and advancement of his favourite studies. It was at his suggestion that the Dublin Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> was instituted in 1683. He became its first secretary; and by the zeal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> with which he discharged this office, he speedily attracted the notice of some of the most influential men in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that in 1685 he was appointed by the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to inspect the fortresses in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; and in the following year he was elected a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society of London. During the commotions that prevailed in Ireland in 1689 and 1690, Molyneux was in England engaged in completing his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>. In 1692 it was published in 4to at London, under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Dioptrica Nova, and with an appendix containing the theorem, newly discovered by Dr Halley, for finding the foci of optic glasses. Molyneux sat in the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> in 1692 for the city, and in 1695 for the university of Dublin. He was a bosom friend of Locke, and while suffering under his last illness, he undertook a journey to England to visit that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in October 1698. Molyneux also wrote a Translation of the Six Metaphysical Meditations of Descartes, together with the objections against them by Thomas Hobbes, Lond., 1680, and twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> papers on miscellaneous subjects in the Philosophical Transactions.

MOMBAS

Pages 419-420

a seaport-town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, on a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 3 miles in length by 2 in breadth, in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Zanzibar, in Lat. 4° 4' S., <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39° 38' E. The bay in which the island is situated is about 5 miles in length by 3 in breadth, and forms the harbour of Mombas, said to be one of the best in the world. The coasts of the island consist of steep cliffs of madrepore, and render the town almost impregnable; while it is still further defended by an old Portuguese fort, situated on an elevation to the S. of the town. The town, which is in a wretched and ruinous condition, consists of two parts,—one occupied by Arabs, the other by Sowhylese, a Moorish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who inhabit a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this coast. Although Mombas is very suitable both as a commercial and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> station, it seems to be less used in the former capacity than Uzi, a town which absorbs most of the trade of the neighbourhood. Mombas was first visited by the Portuguese under Vasco de Gama in 1498, and the town was then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and flourishing. In 1505 Francisco de Almeida, the Portuguese viceroy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> for some insults offered by the inhabitants, took and burned the town. It was, however, afterwards rebuilt, when the Portuguese in 1529 returned and repeated their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of destruction. From that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> to 1720 it was held by the Portuguese. In the latter year Mombas fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Imam of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSCAT">Muscat</a>, but he was soon dispossessed by a rebellion of the inhabitants. From 1824 to 1826 the town came under British protection; but it is now governed by an Arab sheikh. Pop. 3000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 4000. MOMPox, a river-port town of New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>. It is situated on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Magdalena River, about 20 miles above its confluence with the Cauca. Lat. 9° 15' N., Long. 74° 30' W. The town is regularly laid out, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets crossing each other at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. Some of the houses near the centre of the town are well built; but the greater part of them are little more than <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> sheds. Mompos has a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and a quay sufficiently elevated above the stream to be secure from the great floods, which in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> raise the waters of the river 10 or 12 feet above their usual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. This town is of considerable importance, being the great commercial emporium for the Magdalena valley. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is very warm and moist; and the neighbourhood is infested with alligators and mosquitos. Pop. (1851) 11,600.

MOMUS

Pages 420-423

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was the god of raillery, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the jester of the celestial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, who ridiculed both gods and men. He is the personification of mockery and censure. Being chosen by Vulcan, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, to give his judgment concerning their works, he blamed them all: Neptune for not making his bull with horns before his eyes, in order that he might give a surer blow; Minerva for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> which could not be removed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of bad neighbours; and Vulcan for making a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> without a window in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, that his secret thoughts might be seen. Venus he considered alone blameless. For the freedom of his reflections upon the gods, Momus was expelled from heaven. He is generally represented as raising a mask from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and holding a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. MONACHISM (from Latin monachus, a monk; Greek μοναχός, solitary) is a general name descriptive of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which has prevailed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> from almost the earliest ages, and which, during many periods of its history, has formed the most characteristic and powerful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. It sprang into settled existence during the third century, and was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> product of many influences then moving the church. Previously to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, indeed, a system of solitary and ascetic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> is found prevailing among the Jews both in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. The Essenes, on the western shores of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, and the Therapeutae, on the borders of Lake Meritis, seem to have formed regular communities of ascetics, whose existence <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> preceded the rise of Christian Monachism, and to whose example the origin of the latter may in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> be attributed. The main causes out of which Monachism arose, however, are undoubtedly to be found within the church itself,—in those hardships and persecutions which oppressed it, especially during that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the spirit which these persecutions naturally quickened and fostered. During the severities which followed the edict of Decius in the year 250, many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were driven from their homes in search of shelter from the relentless vengeance which pursued them. The comparative security of those remote wilds in which they sought refuge, the peacefulness and freedom from idolatrous intrusion in which they found themselves, combined with a growing spirit of mystical devotion which had sprung up, as in many other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, from the very extremity of the social distractions in the midst of which they had lived, seem to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> sources of the monastic idea. Such an isolation as that in which many now found themselves came to be regarded by them, under the force of such circumstances as those in which they were placed, as the only possible realization of the Christian life. In such a position alone did it appear practicable to carry out that spirit of self-denial and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from worldly enjoyments which represented the ideal of their holy calling. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> was the fruitful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in which such thoughts germinated and sprung to maturity. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their original has been shared by two names—<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> and Anthony; the former of whom may be regarded as the first in point of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> who exemplified in his own practice that Christian asceticism which developed into Monachism; but the latter of whom was really the first who drew such <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the monastic life as to spread abroad its fame and attract many to its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a>. Anthony was born on the borders of Upper Egypt, in the village of Coma, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Heracleopolis, about the year 251. A spirit of simple and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>, but somewhat unintelligent piety, animated him from his youth. Losing both his parents about his twentieth year, the care of a young sister and of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> devolved upon him. Setting aside the ordinary Christian obligations arising out of this position, he conceived himself called upon, like the rich young man in the Gospels, to dispose of his property, and submit to a life of voluntary poverty, in which he might, without impediment, give himself to his spiritual duties. In obedience to this impulse, he assigned his landed estates to the inhabitants of his native village, under condition that he should receive no trouble as to any charges to which they were liable; and having made provision for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his sister with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of pious virgins, he settled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> near his paternal mansion, and commenced a life of rigid asceticism. He supported himself by the labour of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and distributed whatever exceeded the supply of his own bare wants for the benefit of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. This solitary life, however, was not without its temptations. Those natural feelings which he strove to mortify <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to assert themselves in such a manner as to disturb the serenity of his spiritual contemplations, and grosser feelings even obtruded themselves under the guise of alluring imaginations, which rose before him with a more painful distinctness the more he laboured to subdue them. Afterwards he learned the more Christian way of resisting such temptations by cheerful activity and trust in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; but at first he thought to overcome them by a still stricter seclusion and more severe regimen. He retired to a farther distance from his native village, and took up his abode in a recess of rock, such as the Egyptians used for purposes of entombment. Here he fasted and afflicted himself till he was overtaken by illness, and carried back in a fainting and semi-deranged condition to the village. A morbid spirit of devotion, however, burned in him too ardently to be quenched. He afterwards sought a still more distant retirement, where he remained for twenty years, maturing a saintly renown which spread abroad his name, and brought many to seek his advice and to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> under his encouragement to the same mode of life. The deserts of Egypt began to swarm with devotees, who courted his presence and example, and naturally acknowledged him as their leader. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of seclusion prevailed over his love of power; and the numbers who intruded upon his solitude drove him to a still more inaccessible retreat among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. But even here he did not escape molestation. Followers gathered around him in spite of all his efforts to maintain his privacy; and the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> grew up in this remote wild. Anthony did not indeed aim at any complete organization of his followers; this task remained for another; but he taught them to labour for their support, and directed to some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> their religious duties. The life of Anthony was prolonged to upwards of a hundred years, and his saintly fame, as may be easily conceived, grew with his years, till a peculiar sacredness and a miraculous virtue were supposed to attach to his person. On two occasions on which he made his appearance in Alexandria the religious enthusiasm which he excited was intense and universal; and especially on the latter occasion, in the year 352, when he was more than a hundred years old, it reached such a height that even pagans are said to have pressed forward to touch his garment, in the hope of being healed of their diseases. He distinguished himself at such times of public activity as the warm friend of Athanasius in his contest with Ariusian; and it is to this circumstance that we probably owe the record of his life from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Trinitarian—a record to which the historian is indebted for such facts as we have now related. The system thus begun by Anthony speedily spread into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Palestine, favoured by the congenial circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and the prevalence of a similar ascetic spirit to that which existed in Egypt. Hilarion, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Anthony, was chiefly instrumental in the promotion of Monachism in Palestine; while the great Basil of Cesarea, the fellow-student and friend of Gregory Nazianzen, warmly embraced its spirit, and more than any other contributed to its progress throughout Syria and to the shores of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Sea. It is interesting to contemplate in such men as Basil and Gregory, particularly in the latter, the struggles of the monastic with the higher and more comprehensive Christian spirit, and the manner in which this spirit at length succumbed to the perverted tendency of their age, always gathering fresh strength from the increase of social confusion and disorder. Gregory, indeed, never virtually assumed, like Basil, the monastic vows; but the triumph of the ascetical bent was in the end scarcely less complete in him than in his friend. It is deserving of notice that the single monastic order which has subsisted in the Greek church derives its name from St Basil. While the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of Monachism thus extended itself, from the example of Anthony, not only in Egypt, but throughout the East, its more complete organization is associated with the name of Pachomius, another Egyptian ascetic, who, independently of Anthony, had entered on a similar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. To him is attributed the foundation of the cloister life, or the collection of the monks in several classes, according to a regular system, and in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> connected building. This was properly the first establishment of the monastery or cenobium. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of monks thus formed was placed under a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> (from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> or Syriac word for father), from whom descended an organized gradation of offices and ranks, fitted to preserve the integrity of the society and to secure its order. In the natural course of things, this organized form of Monachism soon came to usurp an exclusive character as the only valid expression of the ascetic spirit. The earlier Anachoretes—who lived in single cells, with only a casual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, and without submitting to any definite rule—were gradually absorbed into the more regular establishments, although in the East they long continued to survive, and to assert their independence in all shapes of ungoverned fanaticism. One class of these independent ascetics, who are known to us under the name of Sarabaites, seem to have been peculiarly obnoxious to the regular monks in the vigour with which they maintained their separate position, and refused to own any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> or superior. Cassian, a monk of Palestine, who travelled into Egypt towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fourth century, with the view of inquiring into the various orders of ascetics there, attributes to the Sarabaites all sorts of excesses and disorders; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is to be received with suspicion, as that of a partisan who resented their independence as insubordination, and blackened their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> because they opposed his system. The most various results, as may be imagined, sprang from an institution like eastern Monachism. In some cases there was formed a comparatively pure spirit of devotion, such as that which, upon the whole, with all his earlier excesses, animated its great founder Anthony. Nor can it be disputed, that social consequences of a useful and benevolent kind followed the establishment of monasteries throughout the deserts of Egypt and along the bleak shores of the Pontus. A ready and generous hospitality distinguished the cloisters. The traveller received with an ungrudging spirit maintenance and lodgings. The Cenobites of Egypt, especially, were productive corn-growers, and sent ships laden with food and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of clothing to be distributed among the poor of Alexandria. The wildest and most ridiculous excesses at the same time grew out of the system. Bands of roving devotees, historically known under different names, as Euchites (εὐχεῖς), from their notion about constant inward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, as Choreutes (χορευταί) from their mystic dances, and as Enthusiasts (ἐνθουσιάσται) from their pretended spiritual communications, infested whole districts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and spread themselves from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> to the Black Sea. These fanatics abandoned all useful employment, and even any regular practices of devotion, and professed to give themselves up to spiritual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>; not unfrequently degenerating, by that necessary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> inherent in all extremes, into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> licentiousness. Individual fanaticism, moreover, took the most <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and incredible shapes; as in the case of the famous Simeon Stylites, who is reported to have passed thirty years on the top of a pillar 60 feet from the ground. "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABIT">Habit</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>," writes Gibbon in his characteristic manner, "instructed him to maintain his dangerous position without fear or giddiness, and successively to assume the different postures of devotion. He sometimes prayed in an erect attitude, with his outstretched arms in the figure of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>; but his most familiar practice was that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> his meagre skeleton from the forehead to the feet; and a curious spectator, after numbering twelve hundred and forty-four repetitions, at length desisted from the endless account. The progress of an ulcer in the thigh might shorten, but it could not disturb, this celestial life; and the patient hermit expired without descending from his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>." (Milman's Gibbon, vol. vi., pp. 251-2.) Athanasius has obtained the reputation of extending Monachism into the West. During his compulsory sojourn in Rome in 341 he is said to have carried certain Egyptian monks in his train, whose austerities and devotion, though at first disgusting to the polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, gradually attracted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and at length admiration. His Life of Anthony, moreover, which was speedily translated into Latin, gave a great impulse to the monastic spirit. It could not fail, indeed, that this spirit, so soon as it became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a> in the East, should spread to Rome, and, in such a centre of mingling superstitions, receive a ready support. All the most illustrious of the western teachers contributed by their countenance to this result. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, Martin of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, and even Augustine, were drawn within its influence, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LENT">lent</a> it their encouragement. The restless activity of Jerome during his residence in Rome was exerted in its behalf, and under his influence rich and noble ladies were led to retire from the world and consecrate themselves, amid the solitudes of Palestine, to a life of devotion.1 The labours of Martin of Tours, and of Cassian at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, were especially successful in transferring Monachism westwards, until, in the course of the fifth century, thousands of devotees spread themselves through the south and middle of France into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, carrying with them, it cannot be doubted, many influences of civilization, and forming in their settlement rallying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of Christian enlightenment and education, under the repeated incursions and devastations of barbarian tribes. It may be readily conceived that such a fanatical spirit, in its growth and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, had a constant tendency to degenerate from its primitive strictness, and to end in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> indolence and license. A yet more thorough system of organization was accordingly necessary to strengthen its widely-branching relations, and to consolidate it in its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a>. And such a system was not long wanting. There arose among the monks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> one who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the dangers to which Monachism was exposed, and who resolved to encounter them by a more systematic and efficient control. Benedict of Nursia was prepared for this great task by a self-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the strictest character. Secluding himself --- 1 The case of Paula and her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Eustochium, alluded to by Gibbon, vol. vi., p. 238, is well known. from all companionship, he spent three years of solitary devotion, unrelied by a single visit, and his retreat unknown to any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> monk, who provided him with what he could spare of his own daily allowance of food, by dropping it by a rope to the foot of a steep rock near the grotto in which Benedict lived. Some shepherds at length discovered his retreat, and spread abroad the fame of the holy hermit. His influence was thus at once secured; he was invited to the rule of a neighbouring convent, and accepted it, although under protestation that the severity of the government which he would feel bound to establish would prove intolerable to those who gave him the invitation. It turned out as he supposed; the refractory monks even sought his life; and, leaving them in disgust, he retired once more to his solitude. This event only contributed the more to his fame; wealthy citizens of Rome reverentially sought him out, and entrusted their sons to him for education. He was gradually enabled to found and regulate, according to his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, twelve cloisters in the neighbourhood of his original seclusion; and subsequently, on retiring from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his labours to a mountain at some distance, he laid the foundation of a monastic institution, which, under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a> of Monte Casino, was destined to play an illustrious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the annals of the Papacy. Rigorous as were the personal austerities of St Benedict, he was convinced by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that an undue severity of fasting and mortification was incompatible with a western climate and western habits. His rule, accordingly, in the ultimate form in which it obtained ascendancy throughout all the monasteries of the West, was characterized rather by its simplicity and order than by any particular severity. He aimed at subordination and discipline by a regular system of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> labour and devotion, so that no period of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> remained unoccupied. Two hours after midnight the monks were aroused to vigils, and the time between this and daybreak was consumed in learning the psalms by heart, or some other similar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. At daybreak matins were performed, somewhat in the same manner as vigils, by chanting psalms and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> from Scripture. The duty of private and mental prayer was also enjoined under certain restrictions. These early services were followed throughout the day by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour and reading. During <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the day was so divided that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hours were given to the former occupation and at least two to the latter; during winter more time was given to study, but no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> appears to have been made in the hours of labour. The Sabbath was entirely given to reading and prayer. A system of rigid <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> was of course enjoined, but of such a reasonable character that even the moderate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wine was not forbidden. The rule thus established by Benedict extended itself, as we have said, throughout the West, and for many years was instrumental in preserving the integrity and simplicity of devotion in its cloisters. With the gradual increase of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, however, the Benedictine monasteries lost their primitive character, and became the seats of indolence and vice rather than of cheerful industry and piety. Many attempts were made to revive the first vigour of the rule, and still more successfully to apply it in new forms, each of which in their turn achieved a great reputation, and powerfully helped the cause of the Papacy in the different countries into which they spread. In this manner arose the Order of St Cluni, and the Cistercian and Carthusian Orders—all branches, as it has been said, from the stem of St Benedict. (Waddington's Church History, vol. ii., p. 377.) One and all of these orders, it is remarkable, sprung from the teeming soil of France, in the south and east; and they follow one another, in their full prosperity, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of about a century, beginning with the commencement of the tenth. As a monk of Cluni it was that Hildebrand nursed those ambitious schemes which he afterwards carried out as Gregory VII. The immortal name of St Bernard is associated with the Cistercian Order, of which the Abbey of Clairvaux was a dependent; and the simple purity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>, maintained for many years in the midst of surrounding license, acquired for them a great reputation and a strong settlement in almost every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, from the south of Italy to the northern shores of Scotland. In the meantime other forms of monastic order had sprung up, the most notable and distinguished of which, dating from an early period, was the Order of St Augustine, which was destined to play so prominent a part in the advance of the Reformation. This order, at least in its origin—which, although claiming the sanction of the great teacher of the West, cannot be carried back so far—was chiefly composed of those who were looking forward to, or ordained to, the clerical profession—who were <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, in short; while in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> generally, according to their original <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, there were but a few eligible or devoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> life. In the course of time, however, and from the increase of wealth, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those exclusively given to spiritual or ecclesiastical offices multiplied in all the convents—a change which was greatly fostered by the institution of what were called Lay Brethren, upon whom the routine of manual labour and the discharge of all servile duties devolved. There are still two further developments of the monastic system that claim notice, although our space <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely enable us to do more than mention them. These are the rise and establishment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> and the Mendicant or Preaching orders. The former sprang up out of the close union subsisting between the ecclesiastical and the military <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> in the middle ages, and especially out of the crusading spirit of the twelfth century, and the necessities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> which it created. They are well known under the historical names of The Knights of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, The Knights Templar, and The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> Order. They one and all took their rise in Palestine, and are associated with some of the most brilliant, and at the same time tragic, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the history of the church. They gradually disappeared about the time of the Reformation—the Knights Templar, especially, having been, two centuries previously, subjected to a fierce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, instigated and chiefly carried out by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> IV. of France, who cherished towards them the most deadly and unrelenting hatred. While the Military orders arose out of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> necessities of the church, and the warlike spirit kindled by the advance of Mohammedanism; the Mendicant orders originated in the internal dangers of the church from the encroaching spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> and of free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. St Dominic (1191) acquired his fame as a preacher against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> of the Albigenzes; and, recognizing the effects following such eloquence in his own case, he framed the bold idea of establishing an order of Mendicant preachers, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOW">vow</a> should especially bind them to the interests of the Holy See, and the extirpation of heresy. Innocent III. at first looked coldly on the project, but its obvious policy soon commended it to papal recognition; and St Dominic found himself at the head of one of the most devoted and illustrious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> which ever sought its own aggrandizement in the gratification of papal ambition and of orthodox vengeance. For it was under the shadow of the Dominican Order—although not, as it has been sometimes maintained, under the sanction of St Dominic himself—that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a> inaugurated its bloody career. St Francis of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSISI">Assisi</a> was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of St Dominic, and pursued, independently of him, a similar course of fanatical activity. Enthusiastic almost to insanity, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> capable of sustaining the most intense and prolonged raptures of devotion, and covetous of the most abject and degrading austerities, he burned to realize, in a definite social form, the pictures of evangelical purity and of self-renunciation which his imagination had conjured up. The story of his interview with Innocent III., when he first appeared before him with his plan, is well known. Hurried away from the holy presence as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> madman—a convenient dream aroused the Pontiff to his mistake, and led him to lend all his countenance to a scheme which at first he repelled. While preaching was the characteristic feature of the Dominican rule, poverty was intended to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> distinction of that of St. Francis; but the two orders gradually merged their distinctive peculiarities, and the members of each gave themselves equally to mendicancy and preaching. The history of these orders, as well as that of Jesuitism—which may be said to be a development of the monastic spirit, but in such a distinct shape as to require separate notice—is inseparably bound up with that of the Papacy. Their labours and rivalries form one of the most stirring chapters of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> interest, of ecclesiastical ambition, and, we should add, so far at least as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> are concerned, of philosophical and theological activity. Since the Reformation Monachism cannot be said to have manifested any inherent vitality or power. With the advance of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> civilization, its highest meaning and only conservative use are gone; and, so far as it still maintains itself in Europe, it must be held to be an opponent at once of genuine religious life and the advance of an elevated rational cultivation. (For the more particular history of Monachism, the general reader may be referred to the Church Histories of Neander, Waddington, and Milman; and for a special account of its earlier phases, to Burgham's Antiquities, and the learned reader to Helyot's Histoire des Ordres Monastiques, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1714 and 1792.)

MONACO

Pages 423-423

a small principality of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the S. by the Mediterranean, and on all other sides by the Sardinian States, under whose protection it is. It has a length of about 10 miles from N. to S., a breadth of 6, and an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 52 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile, and its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> mild, as it is sheltered towards the north by the lofty range of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. Oranges, lemons, citrons, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are produced in abundance, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> herds of cattle are fed on the excellent pastures. Since the tenth century Monaco has been in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Grimaldi family, to whom it still nominally belongs; but it is now governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, and garrisoned by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The town of Monaco is situated on a lofty promontory 9 miles E.N.E. of Nice. It was called in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times Are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> Monocci, from which its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name is derived. The town is walled and fortified, but is completely commanded by the higher elevations towards the north. It has a good harbour, which is secure and well sheltered. Pop. about 1500. Mentone is a larger town than the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and contains about 4000 inhabitants. The entire <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the principality is about 7000.

MONAGHAN

Pages 423-429

an inland <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, bounded N. by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a>, E. by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a>, S. by Louth and Cavan, and W. by Cavan and Fermanagh. It comprises an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 500 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 319,757 acres, of which 285,885 are arable, 21,585 uncultivated, 5816 in plantations, 304 in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 6167 are under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; of the 21,000 acres of uncultivated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> 14,500 are situated at elevations exceeding 800 feet, the remainder consisting chiefly of small detached bogs and marshy lands on the margins of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. About 7000 acres are capable of improvement by cultivation, 8000 acres might be improved by draining, and 6000 acres may be considered as incapable of improvement. The general appearance of the surface is hilly, yet not rising into heights of considerable elevation. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mountain range is that of Slievebeagh, a rugged and barren tract, extending south-westward along the Tyrone boundary into Fermanagh, and nowhere exceeding 1050 feet in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> of Castleblayney, on the confines of Armagh, the Mallyash Mountain rises to the height of 1030 feet. There are no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The Finn, which rises near the centre of the county, scarcely merits the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of river until after its entrance into Fermanagh; and the Blackwater, forming <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the northeastern boundary towards Tyrone, is the receptacle of many of the smaller rivulets which take their rise in Monaghan. Although deficient, however, in rivers of magnitude, it is amply furnished with streams of running water, well suited to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and of manufacturing industry. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lakes in this county is 184, thirty of which are considerable sheets of water, but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> majority are of very small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. The most remarkable are Lough Egish, on Criev Mountain, which supplies water for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> succession of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>-greens; Lakes Damby, Camm, and Oona. Others are celebrated for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> which they impart to the scenery; more particularly the chain of lakes between Cooliehill and Ballybay, which ornament the demesnes of Dawson <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROVE">Grove</a> and Bellamont Forest, and the beautiful Lough Muckno, which contains several islets, and forms part of the demesne of Castleblayney. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of various kinds. In the central and more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> part of the county it consists of a rich <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. The southern districts are partly of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and partly a deep clay, capable of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cultivation under judicious management. The north consists mostly of a stiff retentive clay, marshy in winter, and hardening quickly by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, yet interspersed in many parts with tracts of valuable calcareous soil. Whilst the limestone formation predominates in the level districts, the more elevated portions exhibit traces of sandstone and basalt. Coal has been found between Moynalty and Carrickmacross, in more than one portion of a small basin which rests on a patch of the carboniferous limestone insulated within the slate district; but in beds so <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and scanty as not in any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> to exceed 14 inches in thickness, which, in addition to the very difficult working caused by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> at a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, renders this coal district valueless in an economical point of view. Slates of good quality are quarried in Criev Mountain. A <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> mine was also worked there, but has long since been relinquished. Ochre, potters' clay, brick-clay, manganese, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and fullers' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> are also found. There is a chalybeate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> at Drumtubberbuy, on Cairnmore, the water of which casts up a thick scum of ochre. A well near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLONES">Clones</a> is much celebrated for its efficacy in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, whence it has acquired its name of Granabuymore, or "the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> cure." This county has a large proportion of bog, which, together with its great number of lakes, and its exposure to the N.W. winds, renders the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> damp, though not unwholesome. The state of agriculture has much improved during the present century. Descriptions given shortly after the year 1800 speak of the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> of clumsy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, the slide-car without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, the conveyance of manure and field produce on horses' or asses' backs, and of spadehusbandry, as being generally prevalent. At present many of the improvements introduced by scientific agriculturists are to be seen in practice here, as far as they have been found consistent with the peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soil and climate. Ploughs on the most improved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, Scotch carts, and implements of various kinds to supersede the improvident exertion of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour, are universal; yet in some parts, where the nature of the ground forbids the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the plough, considerable tracts of land are still cultivated by the spade. The old, stunted, and ill-conditioned breeds of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and hogs, have given way to Monaghan, the most esteemed British or foreign stocks, the character of which has not unfrequently been made more suitable to the agricultural localities by judicious crossings with the native breeds. The extent of land under each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of crop in 1850, 1855, and 1857 was: | Crop | 1850 Acres | 1855 Acres | 1857 Acres | |-----------------------|------------|------------|------------| | Wheat | 5,961 | 3,468 | 5,045 | | Oats | 80,946 | 83,662 | 75,402 | | Barley, bere, rye, beans, and peas | 16,767 | 15,411 | 4,605 | | Potatoes | 22,105 | 25,329 | 23,915 | | Turnips | 7,190 | 7,061 | 6,963 | | Other green crops | 2,543 | 2,129 | 2,162 | | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a> | 10,157 | 11,858 | 11,337 | | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">Meadow</a> and clover | 11,899 | 15,377 | 17,659 | Total: 147,668 acres Oats and potatoes are the principal crops, together with flax; for the growth of which the soil is peculiarly favourable. Clover is much encouraged, and few farmers are without a patch of it, however small. It is cut for green food, and found extremely economical. The tops of furze or gorse are also used, when pounded, as food for horses. The manure is formed of composts, of which lime and burned turf-mould are generally component parts; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>, though abundant, is little used; and the coal strata of the county afford a large deposit of gypsum, which, from its moderate solubility in water supplies lime for the growth of clover, &c., better than any other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. The fences in some parts are of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, interspersed with sallows; in others a slight mound of earth serves rather to determine the boundary than to prevent trespassing. The county, which is now very bare of trees, was once almost a continuous forest, excepting the higher lands, which appear to be of a nature ungenial to the growth of trees. The numerous demesnes of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry, however, are richly embellished by plantations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> growth. Ash and sycamore are much encouraged, the wood of the latter being in great repute for some parts of mill-machinery. Osieries are frequently to be found in the marshy bottoms at the foot of hills, and prove highly profitable. The estates in land are of every value, from £20,000 per annum to £20, being partly held under grants of the escheated lands in Ulster in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of James I., and partly arising out of the forfeitures in the time of Cromwell. The total number of farms or holdings exceeding one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> in extent, which in 1847 amounted to 23,255, has diminished to 19,000. Of this number about 3000 are between 1 and 5 acres in extent, 9000 between 5 and 15 acres, and 5000 between 15 and 30 acres; the remaining 2000 exceed 30 acres. The mansions of the landed proprietors are numerous and elegant; the houses of the wealthier farmers, and more particularly of those who combine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> with agriculture, exhibit every indication of comfort; but the dwellings of the cotters and labourers are miserable in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">Flesh</a>-meat seldom forms a part of their diet; and those living in districts remote from towns are seldom able to procure any food but potatoes and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUEL">Fuel</a> is cheap and abundant in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bog. The principal manufacture is that of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, which has long been carried on with great spirit. The woollen manufacture is chiefly employed in supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> consumption. The sand or gritstone of Cairnmore has given rise to a manufacture of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a> there, which are in considerable demand. Coarse earthenware is manufactured at Glasslough; and a small ironwork at Smithborough, near Clones, supplies many of the agricultural implements used in the county. The Ulster Canal, which intersects the county, passing the towns of Monaghan and Clones, affords water <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Lough Erne and Lough Neagh; and the Dundalk and Enniskillen and other <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> shortly furnish Monaghan the means of transit to the ports of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DROGHEDA">Drogheda</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SLIGO">Sligo</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the county is chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the national <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. In 1851 there was a total of 242 schools in Monaghan, with an aggregate of 9372 scholars. Of the schools in that year, 114 were national, 58 private, and 45 connected with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> bodies. The number of persons, five years old and upwards, who could neither read nor write, in 1841 and 1851, was ascertained by the census commissioners to be— | Year | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">Male</a> | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> | Total | Rate | |------|------|--------|-------|------| | 1841 | 37,431 | 53,666 | 90,437 | 51 | | 1851 | 22,270 | 31,859 | 54,129 | 42 | The use of the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in this county, as elsewhere, is on the decline. Monaghan has few remains of antiquity. The most remarkable are two round towers,—one near the county of Fermanagh, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-ground adjoining an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Clones; the other at Inniskeen, on the borders of Louth. The former, which is a very rude specimen of these singular monuments of antiquity, consisted of five storeys, the traces of which are still visible in the walls, its door being about 4 feet above the level of the ground. Near it is a large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, above ground, with a cover of the same material shaped like the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The tower at Inniskeen, which is in a very inferior state of preservation, is unique, as having its door upon a level with the surrounding country, although this is supposed by some to be the effect of a modern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. Near Clones are two large raths, one in good preservation, exhibiting distinct traces of its fosses and ramparts; the other smaller and much decayed. Danish forts are numerous; but the county is singularly deficient in those ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> remains which abound in the neighbouring counties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, Louth, Armagh, and Fermanagh. The only monastic structure of which any vestiges remain is that of Clones, which was a foundation of regular canons. It was destroyed by Hugh de Lacy shortly after the arrival of the English; but was rebuilt soon afterwards, and protected by the erection of a castle in its neighbourhood. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Conventual Franciscans was founded at Monaghan by one of the McMahons, but was afterwards totally destroyed, and a castle erected on its site, which also was in a ruinous state in the reign of James I. The ruins of the castle of Mannan are to be seen at Donaghmoyne near Carrickmacross. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the county has been ascertained at the following periods:—In 1821 it amounted to 174,697; in 1831 to 195,536; in 1841 to 200,442; and in 1851 to 141,813. In 1841 Monaghan was one of the most densely peopled counties in Ireland, having no less than 401 inhabitants to each square <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; in 1851, however, this number had diminished to 287,—a decrease in ten years of 114 persons for each square mile, being the greatest decline of population exhibited by any Irish county during that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. This county was represented in the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> by four members,—two for the county at large, and two for the borough of Monaghan. The latter were struck off at the Union, and no alteration has since been made. The district now forming the county of Monaghan is supposed to have been occupied by a tribe of the Scotti in the time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. Subsequently it formed part of the territory of Uriel and Orgial, and was long known as "MacMahon's Country," after a sept who for some time maintained their authority here. In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> it was reduced into shire-ground, and divided into the five baronies which still exist,—viz., Cremorne, Dartrey, Farney, Monaghan, and Trough. The whole of the county, which contains twenty-one parishes, is comprised within the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Clogher. Monaghan, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above county, is situated near its centre, a short distance north of the Blackwater, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable thoroughfare and business in the linen trade and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of agricultural produce. Its ancient name was Muinechán (The Town of Monks), given to it from the religious establishment formerly existing there. The principal buildings are a market-house, erected by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Rossmore in 1792, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-house, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church. In the immediate vicinity of the town is a Roman Catholic chapel, a Presbyterian meeting-house in the New Market, the county infirmary, the diocesan school-house, the barrack for cavalry at the northern entrance of the town, an extensive county prison, and the union workhouse. Its population in 1851 amounted to 3484. The other towns in the county whose population exceeds 2000 are as follows:—Carrickmacross, 2534; Clones, 2333; and Castleblayney, 2084. (II. 8—II.) <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">MONARCHY</a>. Literally translated, this imposing word signifies single power, implying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> placed in the hands of one individual, that individual being the sole ruler of his people. Originally, the difficulty of obeying the wills of many different persons possessing authority, and not agreed as to the method of administration, led, in all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, to the establishment of a monarchy. The corruption of the proto-republic thus gave birth to kings. A French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> has said, that when commonwealths become rotten they degenerate into monarchies; and a French <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> has given it as his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that old monarchies can never be successfully converted into young republics. A third Frenchman has asserted that there exists no example of a people voluntarily destroying their own republic, and surrendering themselves and their laws to the irresponsible rule of a despotic monarch. The latter may, by force or cajolery, have imposed himself upon a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and, it may be added, that when the nation has been unfit for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, a salutary despotism may be for the country's good.
