There is but one real basis for the stability of a monarchy,—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The hatred of subjects denaturalizes the kingly system. According to Montesquieu, the true principle of monarchy is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>,—of a republic, virtue; which is very like many other of the distinctions drawn by Montesquieu, having in them very little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> indeed. It has been objected against what may be called the legality of monarchy, that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had been of Divine origin, it would have rendered those subjected to it happy. Here again is a fallacy; for the monarchy of heaven itself was assailed by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> who could not be happy under that Divine system. The wellbeing of a people is perhaps never so perfectly secured as under a constitutional monarchy, which is, in fact, a republic with safeguards against revolution; or rather a commonwealth under which the people do not learn the "sacred <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of insurrection," but accomplish all necessary revolutions quietly, surely, and according to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. When the accomplished <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> was treating of despotic monarchs and turbulent republics in his Character of a Trimmer, he said:—"We take from the one the too great power of doing hurt, and yet leave enough to govern and protect us. We take from the other the confusion, the parity, the animosities, and the license, and yet reserve a due care of such a liberty as may consist with men's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; but it being hard, if not impossible, to be exactly even, our government has much the stronger bias towards monarchy, which, by the general consent and practice of mankind, seems to have the advantage in dispute against a commonwealth." This advantage was acknowledged so long ago as the era of the Macedonian monarchy. The system was of course despotic; yet, if we may believe Quintus Curtius, the Macedonians had an innate affection for their kings:—"Ingentiam illi genti erga reges suos venerationem." But this is always advanced by interested rulers or writers in favour of despotism. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> followed another system, which they considered the best,—Monarchy, namely, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> system. It was a miserable failure; and yet the people, by which must be understood the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> only, were wont to boast of it in these terms,—"In other kingdoms the monarch holds the people, but we hold the monarch." The elective system is still followed in the case of that ecclesiastical monarch, the Pope, the electors of whom are supposed to be influenced by the Holy Ghost, in answer to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, "Veni Creator Spiritus." According to Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JEWEL">Jewel</a>, the prayer was once replied to by the appearance of an owl in the conclave; and, according to Beranger, the reply to the invocation was, "Non," dit le Saint Esprit, "je ne descends pas!" The state papers recently published having reference to the candidature of Wolsey for the papal throne, best show the system by which this elective monarchy was perpetuated. The third form is constitutional monarchy, according to which the sovereign is the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of a free people, with regard to whom there are laws in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and duties peculiar to each. And this constitutional monarchy may be in its origin elective, as that of England, when the nation, through Parliament, disinherited one family, elected a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and then declared that the sceptre should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in such family, under certain stipulations. It may, however, be considered as a general rule, that all monarchies are the consequences of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> on the part of the people. Except where a conqueror has chosen to rest on his right of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, there has seldom existed even an usurper who has snatched the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> without going through some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> by which he seemed to acknowledge, or the people were made to imagine, that the result was the effect of a cause traced to the love, veneration, free-will, and unshackled choice of the nation. To a constitutional monarch laws are not manacles, but garlands. They adorn rather than oppress him. "There is a wantonness," says the noble statesman whom we have already quoted, "in great power, which men are generally too apt to be corrupted with, and for that reason a wise <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, to prevent the temptation arising from common frailty, would choose to govern by rules, for his own sake as well as for his people's, since it only secures him from errors, and does not lessen the real authority that a good magistrate would care to be possessed of. For, if the will of a prince is contrary either to reason itself or to the universal opinion of his subjects, the law, by a kind restraint, rescues him from a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that would undo him. If his will, on the other side, is reasonable or well-directed, that will immediately becomes a law, and he is arbitrary by an easy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> consequence, without taking pains or overturning the world for it." For a monarch under such restraint there is no doubt a far greater degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> than was ever enjoyed by despots, who feared their own guards next to dreading their own people, and that, too, when the acknowledged system of government was comprised in the talismanic words, "Quod principi placuit, lex esto!" It was in those days when monarchy was supposed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and to be, simply the will, more or less idle, of the monarch, that men were slaves whose very breath could scarcely be drawn in freedom, even when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> slept. The old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> by M. Bret illustrates this sentiment exactly; and, "done into English," they run thus:— Upon his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> couch a tyrant dread, In seeming tranquil <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, reclined his head: 'Is slumber made,' said one, 'for wretch so rare? Does <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> nod, and Heaven its victim spare?' 'Hush!' said a fakir, 'lest the noise you make, E'en by a whisper, should the monster wake. 'Tis God who thus allows him to be blest, That Innocence may have a moment's rest.' In classifying the great monarchies which have held the world in awe, St Augustine names but two,—the Baby- Monarchy, Iranian and the Roman. The more usual method is to reckon the four great monarchies,—the Assyrian, the Persian, the Grecian, and the Roman. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a>, however, notices a monarchy older than the oldest of these,—namely, the Chaldean. This dynasty, which, like that of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, is wanting in records, is said to have commenced 460 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and under ten kings to have lasted half a million of years! The name of the first <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of this wonderful dynasty was Alorus,—in other words, "Shepherd of his People,"—a significant title to commence with; it must be allowed. We are accompanied by the wonderful even when we have the traditionary. Thus of Nimrod (or Belus, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORION">Orion</a> of the skies), the first king named by Moses, we are told in a pretty story, doubtless suggestive of the Divine origin of his kingship, that as he was one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> abroad hunting, he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in the heavens the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a starry crown. Taking the appearance to have special reference to himself, he engaged a craftsman to copy the sparkling pattern; and when this was fashioned into a sparkling <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> crown, Nimrod wore the same as a symbol of the authority and the favour conferred on him by Heaven. The Assyrian empire properly commences with Nimus, the son of Belus, who reigned in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, built <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, and captured <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. This took place about 2060 years B.C. About 1200 years elapsed before <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JONAH">Jonah</a> told of the disastrous end, in the streets of Nineveh; and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> gave way to the conquering Arbaces 820 years before that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REDEMPTION">Redemption</a>. The empire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to exist, however, with narrower limits, till 621 B.C., when the second Sardanapalus perished like the first, and Assyria was divided among the conquerors. The Persian monarchy, which may be said to have annexed, or to have been included in, that of Assyria, dates from Zoroaster, 2115 B.C. Its early annals present only inextricable confusion; but we find <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, King of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> in the sixth century B.C.; and the Persian empire stood, under alternations of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and disaster, till the conquering Alexander subjected the country, and laid the foundation of the Greek empire, 331 B.C. The Greek or Macedonian empire had, in Alexander, for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> the twenty-first king of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. Such part of that wide empire as, after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Alexander, was comprised in Macedonia, fell before the Roman Emilius Paulus, who pronounced Macedon a Roman province, and (167 B.C.) took its last king, Perseus, and his sons to Rome, where they walked in chains before the chariot of the conqueror. The Roman monarchy, if it is to be dated from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, commenced 752 B.C. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> kings had reigned when, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of Tarquinius Superbus, the first consuls Brutus and Collatinus were appointed 509 B.C. The republic existed till the foundation of the imperial monarchy in the person of Julius Caesar, 48 B.C. In the year of our Lord 363 the Roman empire was split into two divisions on the death of Jovian. The Western empire expired on the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, by Odoacer, King of the Heruli, A.D. 476. The Eastern empire, with Byzantium for its capital, existed nearly a thousand years later, its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dating with the extinction of the imperial families of the Comneni and the Palaeologi, A.D. 1453. It would be impossible to name here all the other monarchies under which government has been administered; for of some, like that of Achaia, the names of the kings have been forgotten, and of others, like the Davids of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, their acts are scarcely worth recording. In a tabular and alphabetical form, however, we give below some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of the existence of the principal monarchical systems which have won or exacted the obedience of mankind. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>.—Founded by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a>, 1152 B.C.; annexed to Rome by Tullus Hostilius, 665 B.C. Algiers.—Founded as an independent monarchy in 1505 Monarchy, by Harush Barbarossa, a Sicilian renegade. Houssan, the thirty-second and last of the "Dey's," was dethroned and expelled by the French in 1830. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>.—Founded by Pelasgus, 1521 B.C. The last king, Aristocrates II., was stoned to death, and Arcadia made a republic, 681 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>.—Founded by Inachus, 1856 B.C. It existed as a monarchy upwards of seven centuries, but it subsequently became a republic. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>.—The kings of Armenia were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> over their own subjects, but the country itself was successively subject to the three great monarchies; and the Roman power became paramount in Armenia after the dethronement of Tiridates, A.D. 62. Assyria.—(See above). <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>.—Cecrops founded a monarchy here 1556 B.C. After a period of nearly 500 years, occupied by seventeen kings, royalty was abolished, on the singular ground that it would be impossible to find such another king as Codrus, the last of the line. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>.—(See below, Germany). Babylon.—(See above, Assyria). <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>.—This monarchy was established in 1805, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, Maximilian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, was declared king. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELGIUM">Belgium</a> was formed into a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in 1831. Bithynia.—The first independent king was Dydalsus, 383 B.C. The last sovereign, Nicomedes, bequeathed the kingdom to the Roman republic, 75 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>.—This monarchy, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, 1493 B.C., was abolished by the Thesians, 1215 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> was originally governed by dukes. The regal title was conferred by the Emperor of Germany on Vratislaus in 1061. The crown was ultimately secured to the Austrian family by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of 1648. Bosphorus (Cimmerian).—A line of kings ruled here for about five centuries and a half. The last was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> II., at whose deposition the Emperor Claudius made of the kingdom a province of the empire. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>.—Erected into an empire, A.D. 1825. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> had its kings at the period of the Roman invasion. The first Christian king was Lucius, A.D. 179. Constantine added Britain to the Roman empire, A.D. 306. In the year 446 the Saxons were invited over by King Vortigern. The Saxon heptarchy was converted into a monarchy by Egbert, King of the West Saxons, A.D. 827. During the heptarchy, however, the most powerful king was called Rex Gentis Anglorum. From the establishment of the Norman line, A.D. 1066, the following are the dates and names of the successive dynasties that have possessed the English throne:—House of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, 1399; <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>, 1461; Tudor, 1485; Stuart, 1603; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, 1714. Burmese Empire.—Founded by Alompra, from whom the reigning monarch is descended, in the middle of the last century. Caliphate (The).—The first caliph was Abu Bekir ("Father of the Girl"), A.D. 632. After a succession of fifty-seven caliphs, the capture of Baghdad by Holagon Khan, A.D. 1258, put an end to the line in the person of Al Mostasim Billah. The Egyptian caliphate, which was the consequence of a schism, A.D. 908, flourished vigorously till the overthrow of the Eastern caliphate. When Selim I. annexed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in 1517, and received from the last of the Abbassides the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> became the representative of the caliphs, and the "Father of the Faithful." <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a> has been governed by twenty-two dynasties since the establishment of the first dynasty, 2207 B.C. The last monarch of the Chinese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, Whyt-tsong, of the House of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-MING">Ming</a>, hung himself, 1628. Since his death the Mogul race of Tsing has reigned in China. Corinth.—The monarchy was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a> 1376 B.C. The glory of Corinth dates from the establishment of the republic 582 B.C. It fell under the dominion of Rome 146 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>.—In the Danish annals there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of fifty-six kings previous to the period when Margaret united the three crowns of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, Denmark, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>. The present king is the twenty-first sovereign of Denmark since the last-named era. Egypt.—Vulcan, or "Elementary Fire," is fabulously said to have been the first king of this ancient monarchy. There is nothing that is said of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> records that can be relied on till the period of the foundation of the dynasty of the Pharaohs in the person of Mizarim, 2188 B.C. This dynasty disappeared before the conquering Cambyses 525 B.C. The Persian dynasty held Egypt till its conquest by Alexander, at whose death commenced the line of Ptolemies, beginning 304 B.C. with Ptolemy Soter, and terminating 27 B.C. with Cleopatra, the thirteenth sovereign of that line. Since that period it has never been, in the strict <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, an independent monarchy. England.—See Britain. Epirus.—The annals of this monarchy are obscure. Neoptolemus, son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>, is said to have been the first king, 1170 B.C. It was annexed to Macedon, 220 B.C., about fifty years after the death of its last king, the great Pyrrhus. Etruria.—The monarchical system observed in this ancient kingdom deserves a word of notice in this place. The country anciently comprised twelve different nations, each of which had its respective monarch, under the title of Lucumon. France.—This monarchy popularly dates from Pharamond, the Frank invader of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, A.D. 418; his second successor, Merovaeus, or Merovig, gave name to the line Merovingian. The Carolingians began with Pepin, the father of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, A.D. 751; the House of Capet with Hugh Capet, A.D. 987; House of Valois, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> VI., 1328; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOURBON">Bourbon</a>, Henri IV., 1589; the empire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> I., 1804; Bourbons restored, 1814; House of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, 1830 to 1848; second empire, 1852. Germany.—The "Holy Roman Empire" in the west was restored by the Pope, A.D. 800, in the person of Charlemagne. His line has been thus followed:—By the Saxon line, A.D. 911; the Franconian line, 1024; the Sbissian line, 1138 to 1212. The imperial throne was occupied by sovereigns of various houses, but chiefly of Austria, from the latter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> till the year 1438, when Albert II., a descendant of Rudolph of Hapsburg, commenced the uninterrupted line of Austria. In 1804 the elective German empire was abolished; but its last emperor, Francis II., became Francis I., hereditary emperor of Austria. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>.—The modern kingdom of Greece was founded in 1832 in the person of the Bavarian Otto, the reigning monarch. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a> was erected into a kingdom in 1814, George III. of England being its first king. The succession being in the male line only, Ernest, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, succeeded to the throne on the death of William IV., King of England and Hanover, in 1837. Hagti has been a hybrid sort of monarchy from the time Dessalines was crowned emperor in 1804. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.—This commonwealth became a kingdom in 1806, under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> Bonaparte. After the fall of the French empire, William Frederick, Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, assumed the style of King of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, 1815. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, having become free of the German empire in 997, Stephen, Duke of Hungary, was named by the Pope "Apostolic King" of that country. After a line of thirty-two monarchs, it became permanently annexed to Austria (1527) by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of Hungary with Ferdinand of Austria. Ilium.—This kingdom was founded by Dardanus 1480 B.C.; and at the overthrow of Priam, its sixth king, had lasted about three centuries. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>.—The Ghizian dynasty, the first of which we have authentic records, was founded by the invader Mahmoud Ghizai about the year 1000 of our era. After a succession of thirteen kings, Mahmoud Ghour established the short-lived dynasty of two kings, named after him, in 1186. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PATAN">Patan</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> line, commenced in 1210 with the Kutub-ul-Deen. The Mogul race of Timour commenced in 1526 in the person of the famous Zebir-ul-Deen Mahomed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BABER">Baber</a>, or the "Tiger." This once glorious race sank into insignificance in the middle of the last century, since which time the Mogul monarchs ceased to have any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> importance until the temporary restoration of a Mogul chief, consequent on the outbreak of 1857. Ireland.—The monarchical annals of Ireland contain lists of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of kings, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> downwards. The first sole monarch, however, was Brian Boru, by election of the people, A.D. 1027. Nearly a century and a half later Henry II. of England became "Lord of Ireland." <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.—After the deposition of Romulas Augustus, A.D. 493, Odoacer, chief of the Heruli, assumed the title of "King of Italy"; the line existed about three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a century, disappearing before the Lombard kings. In modern times the first and only crowned "King of Italy" was Napoleon I., A.D. 1805. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> has had an hereditary succession of ecclesiastical emperors from the year 660 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>.—When the Crusaders captured the city, A.D. 1099, they established a kingdom which lasted eighty-eight years,—that is, till the recapture by Saladin, A.D. 1187. The first Christian king was the renowned Godfrey de Bouillon; its ninth and last was Guy de Lusignan. The monarchy was elective. Jews.—The kingdoms of the Jews commence, it is almost superfluous to say, with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, chosen by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>; but it was not until the death of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> that the kingdoms divided into Judah and Israel, about 975 B.C. That of Israel lasted till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a> was captured, and the ten tribes were carried into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> by the Assyrians, 721 B.C. The kingdom of Judah existed till the year 587 B.C., when the temple and city were burned by the invading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>, who razed the walls of Jerusalem to the ground. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>.—The kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, a people from North Germany, existed from the year 570, when the Lombard <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> proclaimed their chief Alboin king, till the year 772, when Charlemagne took possession of the country, and deposed the last king, Desiderius. Lydia.—This kingdom boasted of a long line of monarchs, namely, from Argon, a descendant of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, 1223 B.C., to Croesus, after whose deposition the "kingdom of the richest king among kings" was annexed to Persia by Cyrus, 548 B.C. Macedon.—Named above. Media, although at different times annexed to Assyria and Persia, claims mention as an independent monarchy from the period of its revolt against Arbaces, 820 B.C., till its conquest by Cyrus, 537 B.C. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, when discovered in 1518, had long been under the rule of a line of monarchs. After it threw off the yoke of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, Iturbide was made emperor in 1822, but was deposed, and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> for attempting to restore the empire in 1824. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>.—A line of kings in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> was commenced as early as the end of the eleventh century; the line did not expire till the opening of the thirteenth. About two centuries later the foundations of the empire of Morocco were laid by Hascen, of the race of Sheerefs, at a time when there were still chiefs in Fez styling themselves kings. The empire, as comprising Morocco, Fez, Susiana, Tophilet, &c., was not, however, consolidated and established till the Monarchy, seventeenth century, under Muley Abdel Melech, whose descendant is now on the throne. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, or the Two Sicilies.—Goth, Lombard, Saracen, Norman, Gaul, and Spanish, alternately occupied this locality. The treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> (1713) made Victor Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, King of the Two Sicilies, a title known as early as 1442. Subsequently the Savoyed king exchanged his crown for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, with a kingly title. The Two Sicilies belonged to the German empire till 1734, when Spain conquered them, and established there a line of Bourbon princes, of whom the present monarch is a descendant. Netherlands.—See Holland, and Belgium. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>.—The monarchy here lasted from the period of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARSACES">Arsaces</a>, 250 B.C., to that of Artabanus V., A.D. 229, when it was annexed to the new kingdom of Persia. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>.—This kingdom was founded by Philoletus, 283 B.C. The last king, Attalus Philomater, bequeathed his kingdom to Rome, 133 B.C. Persia was reconstructed by Ardaheer Babegan (<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> I.) Between the death of Alexander and this last period, Persia had seen the Syro-Macedonian dynasty of Seleucus and that of the Parthian Ash, or Arsaces. Artaxerxes I. was the founder of the Sassanian dynasty, which, amid triumphs and defeats, existed upwards of four centuries. Persia was subsequently possessed by the Caliphs and by the Tartars; afterwards by Timour Leng, at the beginning of the fifteenth century. A century later the disorganized monarchy was seized by Hussoon Uzun, chief of the tribe of "White Sheep," whose son Shah Ismael (1502) was the first of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shahs of the Safaviean dynasty. The Afghan line commenced with Mahmoud, A.D. 1722, and ended with the eighth and last monarch, Shah Rohk, 1750. After a few years of anarchy, the Zund dynasty succeeded in the person of Kureem Khan Zund. His last descendant, Lootf <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Khan, was slain in 1794 by Aga Mahomed Khan, the founder of the Kujur dynasty, of which the reigning shah, Nasr-ul-Din, is the fourth sovereign. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, at first governed by dukes, was raised to a sovereignty by papal authority under Boleslaus I., A.D. 999. The Piast kings of Poland were native sovereigns, and not a regular dynasty. The Jagellon line commenced at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fourteenth century, and continued till the middle of the sixteenth. The monarchy existed in its elective form till 1795, when Stanislaus Poniatowski was deposed by Russia. Pontus.—This kingdom was an offshoot from that of Persia. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes, named "Artaebazus," was the first sovereign of Pontus, 487 B.C. After the death of Mithridates VII., A.D. 40, the kingdom became a province of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Subsequently a new and Christian monarchy was established within a portion of the limits of the old kingdom of Pharmaces, Tigranes, and Mithridates. When the Crusaders, or "Latins," established their temporary empire at Constantinople, a dynasty of five successive sovereigns carried on the old succession from 1204 to 1261, under the name of the Greek empire of Nicaea. In the last-named year Michael Paleologus recovered Constantinople from Baldwin II. Popes of Rome, as elected monarchs with temporal power, claim a word of notice in this record. Stephen II., the ninety-ninth pope, who was elected in 752, was the first who united the sovereign temporal and ecclesiastical dignities, in which he has been followed by 169 orthodox successors, one only of whom was an Englishman (Nicholas Breakspeare of St Albans), Adrian IV., 1154-1159. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>.—The monarchy here dates from A.D. 1139, when Alphonso, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of Portugal, was proclaimed king by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, after defeating the Moors at Ourique. With the exception of the period 1580-1640, when Portugal was a province of Spain, and that of the French occupation in the present century, the independent monarchical system Monarchy, has been uninterrupted in Portugal. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, after being governed since 1134 by margraves, electors, or dukes, was raised to a kingdom in 1701. It has had six kings of whom the present, Frederick William IV., began to reign in 1840. Rome.—See above. Russia.—From the period of Ruric, 862, to the commencement of the sixteenth century, the Russians were governed by sovereign dukes, called of Kiev, Vladimir, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>. In 1533 Ivan Vasilievitch assumed the title of "<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a>," and that title <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great exchanged in 1708 for that of Emperor. Sardinia or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>.—See also Naples. The first king of Sardinia was Victor Amadeus, 1713. The present monarch, Victor Emanuel II., is the eighth of the line, four sovereigns of which have abdicated. Scotland.—The Scottish annals name kings of Scotland as far back as the period of Alexander the Great; but it will suffice to state here, that Kenneth MacAlpine, by uniting Scots and Picts, became the first sole monarch of Scotland, A.D. 843. From that period till the accession of James VI. to the throne of England, A.D. 1667, the government was administered, more or less independently, by above forty kings. Spain.—Few nations have seen so many different monarchical systems as Spain. At length the various crowns of the kingdoms of Oviedo, Navarre, Cordova, Castille, Leon, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, and (Moorish) <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, were united on the head of Ferdinand V., in 1512, since which period fourteen sovereigns have successively occupied the throne. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> (Lacedaemon).—This celebrated republic under kings, some of whom were puppets and many were "absolute," enjoyed a long but a chequered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. The rule of kings begins with Lelex, 1516 B.C., and nearly thirteen hundred years elapsed before royalty was totally abolished. Sweden.—Between the year 1001, when Olif Schoet Konung was elected first king of Sweden, to the year 1389, when the tyranny of Albert of Mecklenburg was followed by revolt, and that by anarchy, Sweden reckons twenty-one monarchs. In 1397 the three northern kingdoms were governed by one sovereign, but this union was repealed in 1523, when the patriotic Gustavus Vasa ascended the throne. The reigning monarch, Oscar, is the son of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> John Bernadotte, originally a private soldier in the army of Louis XVI. of France. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>.—See Assyria and Persia. Thrace.—The government here was originally monarchical, but divided among independent princes. It was annexed to the Macedonian empire about 335 B.C. Turkey.—This monarchy established itself in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by the capture of Constantinople under Mahomed II. in 1453. That sultan was the ninth of a line founded in Asia by Othman, A.D. 1299. Abdul Medjid is the twenty-fifth sultan since the fall of the great Christian capital in the east of Europe. Vandals and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>.—The Italian monarchy of the latter has been already noticed. About the end of the fourth century they founded a kingdom in Spain, which expired in the eighth century with Roderick, their last king. In the year 428 Genseric crossed from Spain, and established the dynasty of Vandal kings in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The line consisted of six monarchs, with the last of whom fell modern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, Arianism, and the royal Vandal line, before the conquering sword of orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a>, A.D. 534. Württemberg, formerly a ducal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>, became a kingdom at the close of 1805, of which the reigning king, William I., is the second sovereign, having succeeded his father Frederick in 1816. By the above list the reader may learn in what period the strongest empires have fallen into decay, and may safely predict that the mightiest which have followed them will, like them, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away, and all earthly distinctions shrink to nothing. When all crowns <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> shivered, as one day they must, then will be applicable to the entire roll of once living monarchs the noble lines which Beaumont penned on the royal tombs in Westminster: "Mortality, behold and fear! What a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of flesh is here! Think how many royal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> Sleep within these heaps of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>! Here they lie, had realms and lands, Who now want strength to move their hands; There, from their pullets, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>'d with dust, They preach. In greatness is no trust! Here an acre, somnolent, With the richest, royallest seed That the earth did ever suck in Since the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> died for sin. Here the bones of birth have cried, Though gods they were, as men they died. Here are wands, ignoble things, Dropt from the ruin'd state of kings. Here's a world of pomp and state Buried in dust, once dead by fate." (J. D-R-N.)

MONASTEER

Pages 429-429

a seaport-town of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, on the Mediterranean, 85 miles S.E. of the town of Tunis; Lat. 35.45. N., <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10.49. E. It has a citadel, a harbour, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of woollen stuffs, and a considerable trade. Pop. 12,000.

MONASTIR

Pages 429-429
or BITOLLA, a town of European Turkey, capital of a department of the same name, in the province of Macedonia, is situated on the Vestrizza, at the edge of a large plain, 90 miles W.N.W. of Salonika. Most of the commercial intercourse between Albania and the Aegean is carried on through it; and it is the centre of all military operations in Albania, Macedonia, Thessaly, and Bosnia. Pop. 15,000.

MONCEY

Pages 429-429

BON-ADRIEN JEANNOT, Duc de Conégliano, was the son of an advocate, and was born in 1754 at Moncey, the village near Besançon of which he afterwards assumed the name. In 1774 his relations, yielding to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for a soldier's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, allowed him to enrol in the gendarmerie of Lunéville. After passing into the volunteers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Siegen, and then into the "Classeurs Cantabres," he became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in 1791; and in 1794 we find him, as general-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, defeating the Spaniards at Villa Nova. Chancing to be in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> at the revolution of the 18th brumaire, he zealously supported <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>, and thus opened a path to future preferment. He was appointed by the First <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSUL">Consul</a> inspector-general of the gendarmerie, and in 1804 was rewarded with a marshal's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Duc de Conégliano, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> officer of the Legion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>. In 1808 he commanded in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Catalonia, but was recalled by Bonaparte to the command of the gendarmerie. In 1813 he received the additional appointment of commander-in-chief of the Parisian National <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">Guard</a>, and was entrusted with the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> during the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of Napoleon. No one was more <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> in 1814 than Marshal Moncey. He organized the National Guard of Paris, and was among the last to lay <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his arms after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> of the city. At the beginning of the Hundred Days his submission was tendered to the Bourbons, but was withdrawn as soon as Napoleon landed from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>. He was nominated <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of Marshal Ney in 1815; yet, rather than accept this nomination, he chose to be deprived of all his titles and to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for three months in the prison of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HAM">Ham</a>. In 1816 he was restored to his dignities, and was received into the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>. On the outbreak of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> in 1823 Moncey was far advanced in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; he accepted, however, the command of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, and served in Catalonia with all the fire and Moncelier vigour of his prime. He died in April 1842.

MONCOLIERI

Pages 429-429

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, is pleasantly situated on the slope of a hill, near the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Po, 5 miles S. of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. The town is entered by two gates. It possesses an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, two handsome churches, several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of earthenware, tiles, cabinet-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, are carried on; and the town has a considerable trade in cattle, for which there is a fair in October. Pop. 9129.

MONCREIFF

Pages 429-430

SIR HENRY WELLWOOD, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONET">Baronet</a>, D.D., an eminent Scottish divine, was the son of the Rev. Sir William Moncreiff and Catherine Wellwood, and was born on the 7th February 1750, at Blackford, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a>, of which his father was minister. After completing his elementary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the parochial school of Blackford, he repaired to the university of Glasgow in 1768, with the view of pursuing his studies for the Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the midst of a brilliant collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> he had the misfortune to lose his father. The patrons of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> thus left vacant at once resolved to reserve the living for young Sir Harry, who had already given such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of future eminence. He removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1768 to prosecute his theological studies; and on the 16th August 1771 was ordained minister of his native parish. The superior talents of the young preacher early attracted the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>; and in October 1775 he was appointed minister of St Cuthbert's parish in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Edinburgh. Here he commenced the arduous duties of his office with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> zeal, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to labour with remarkable energy, at once for the spiritual advancement of his parish and for the general good of the Scottish church. He was possessed of talents which might have won for him a bright reputation in any of the higher walks of public distinction, but he preferred the more exalted, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> less ambitious career of fulfilling the pious duties of the Christian pastor, and of freeing his church from what he conceived to be serious barriers to her spiritual progress. "Had he not preferred his church to every other object," says <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cockburn, "there is no public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to which he might not have fought his way." (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Lord Jeffrey, vol. i., p. 188). When Sir Harry entered upon public life the moderate party was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a> in the Scottish church, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> independence was seldom to be met with. Worldly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> might have inclined him to the majority, but he at once took a decided position with the liberal and evangelical party. He soon became their leader and oracle; and among the people his "<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> name," says Cockburn, "was a tower of strength." He was unanimously chosen moderator of the General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> of his church in 1785, and during his subsequent career had the same honour repeatedly conferred upon him. He possessed great power and energy as a debater, and was distinguished for soundness of judgment and unflinching integrity. The writer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> quoted, who knew Sir Harry well, remarks in his Memorials of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">Time</a>, p. 234.—"In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with him every other churchman who has appeared since I knew the world must withdraw. Nothing that I could say would express one-half of my affectionate and reverential admiration of this great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>." He shone more on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> than in the pulpit; and public speaking, rather than literary labour, seemed to be his peculiar sphere. As a writer he was comparatively feeble. His Life of Dr John Erskine is in no way remarkable; and his three volumes of sermons do not possess very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> merits. They were published in 1829 and 1831, with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> memoir by his son, Lord Moncreiff. His opinions were uniformly liberal and charitable, and he was characterized by very great benevolence. He took a deep interest in whatever was calculated to relieve suffering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> encourage merit. Among his personal friends he numbered the most distinguished names in Scotland during his time. He died in August 1827, leaving his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to his son James Wellwood Moncreiff, who had been chosen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a> during the previous year. Sir James was born in 1776, and was educated at Edinburgh, Glasgow, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He devoted himself entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, but inherited much of his father's zeal for the evangelical cause of the Presbyterian Church and for the politics of the Scottish Whigs. He was a man of an energetic mind, and was distinguished for great zeal and purity. So exceedingly conscientious was he, that Lord Jeffrey, who had the greatest regard for him, used to call him "the whole duty of man." He was raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> under the title of Lord Moncreiff in 1829. He died on the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1851.

MONDONEDO

Pages 430-430

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, 30 miles N.N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUGO">Lugo</a>. The streets are paved and clean, and the houses generally commodious. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, commenced in 1221, has an image of wonderful remedial power, said to have been conveyed from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> at the Reformation. MONDOVI

Pages 430-430

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a cognominal department in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONI">Coni</a>, and see of a bishop, stands on a hill near the Ellero, 53 miles W. of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. The town proper, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIAZZA">Piazza</a>, is situated on the summit; and the three suburbs of Carazzione, Brea, and Piano, on the sides and at the foot of the hill. The upper town is walled, and contains a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piazza of a hexagonal shape, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, four other churches, an episcopal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> consist of woollen and cotton stuffs, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, earthenware, &c.; and the trade is considerable. Mondovi was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of a victory gained by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> in 1796 over the Sardinian troops under Colli; and three years later was taken and pillaged by General Moreau. Pop. (1851) 17,370.

MONEY

Pages 446-465

money really is, and how coins may be best divided, we proceed briefly to inquire into the effects produced by the depreciation of the latter. This is a very important inquiry, both in a practical and historical point of view. Directly to alter the terms of the contracts between individuals, would be too barefaced and tyrannical an interference with the rights of property, to be tolerated. Those, therefore, who endeavour to enrich one part of society at the expense of another, find it necessary to act with caution and reserve. Instead of changing the stipulations in contracts, they have resorted to the ingenious device of changing the standard by which these stipulations are adjusted. They have not said, in so many words, that ten or twenty per cent. should be added to, or deducted from, the debts and obligations of society, but they have, nevertheless, effected this by making a proportional change in the value of

MONEY

Pages 464-483

money. The stoppage of a bank which had deposited securities would have to be officially ascertained before any steps could be taken for their sale; and after this had been done, some considerable time would have to elapse before they could be disposed of, and their produce made available for the liquidation of the notes. Most securities, too, are of fluctuating and uncertain value, and might not, even under the most favourable circumstances, realise the sums for which they were pledged. And in the event of the occurrence of a panic, or disturbed state of credit, it might be impossible immediately to convert the securities into cash, or possibly only at a heavy loss. This plan is, therefore, very far from giving that effectual security for the conversion of notes into coin, which, on the first blush of the matter, it appears to afford. Latterly, it has been extensively acted upon in some parts of the United States; and there, when a bank stops payment, its notes are always sold at a discount, which, of course, varies according to the peculiar circumstances affecting each case.—(See post.) 2. But supposing that this plan were effectual, which it is not, to ensure the immediate convertibility of notes into coin, it is defective from its not preventing their over-issue. A paper currency is not in a sound or wholesome state, unless—1st, Each particular note or parcel of such currency be paid immediately on demand; and 2d, Unless the whole currency vary in amount and value exactly as a metallic currency would do were the paper currency withdrawn and coins substituted in its stead. The last condition is quite as indispensable to the existence of a well established currency as the former; and it is one that cannot be realised otherwise than by confining the supply of paper to a single source. The issues of paper
