One feels, as he listens to this strange blending of simple gossip and deep wisdom, told in an easy, rambling, picturesque style, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he occupied a seat in that small round study of Montaigne's, with its "three noble and free prospects," from "the third storey of a tower" of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, windy Montaigne Castle, and enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and familiar friendship of this robust, indolent, thoughtful old Gascon. As to his personal appearance, he was of low stature, he informs us: "I am, as to the rest, strong and well-knit; my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> is not puffed, but full; my <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, betwixt jovial and melancholic, moderately sanguine and hot." He deplores his incorrigible awkwardness and want of personal dexterity. "My <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are so clumsy that I cannot so much as write so as to read it myself." He consoles himself, however, for these physical defects by the reflection, that "my bodily qualities are very well suited to those of my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; there is nothing sprightly, only a full and firm vigour. I am patient enough of labour and pains; but it is only when I go voluntarily to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and only so <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> as my own desire prompts me." (Essais, t. ii., c. 17.) He dwells now upon his want of memory and his perfect truthfulness,—upon his occasional absence of mind,—upon his dislike of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>,—and upon his disbelief in omens and ghosts. Again, he has a profound <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the sad instability of all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs, becomes gravely thoughtful, and shows symptoms of a real though passing melancholy as he meditates on death. He wore for his device a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, with the characteristic motto, "Que say je?" was vain of his cordon of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and was fond of showing his coat of arms. He was strongly averse to all cruelty and malignity of feeling; and never fails to denounce injustice, inhumanity, and uncharitableness. His reputation as a writer is founded solely on his Essais, which were at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> extremely popular, and which are still read by a numerous class. As a writer, he imparted to the French language an energy which it did not before possess, and which but few of his successors have equalled. As a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, his object was to describe man as he is, without reserve and without exaggeration; he studied himself, and recorded his observations with surprising acuteness and fidelity. He united in a high <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the powers of observation and reflection, without which the study of man can never be successfully prosecuted; and although there is no doubt much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> in the acute but severe strictures on his character by the Port-Royalists, who freely expose his vanity, his self-love, and the indulgent manner in which he speaks of his vices; yet, as Mr Stewart observes, "this consideration, so far from diminishing the value of his Essais, is one of the most instructive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> they afford to those who, after the example of the author, may undertake the salutary but humiliating task of self-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>." In the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Dissertation (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> i., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> ii.), to which the reader is referred, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found an exposition and criticism of Montaigne's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. Montaigne's Life was first written by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Bouhier, and prefixed to a supplementary volume of his works in 1740. In 1774 the Academy of Bordeaux awarded a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> to Talbert for an éloge de Montaigne; and the French Academy bestowed a similar honour on Villemain in 1812. This masterly éloge Montalvan is attached to the 8-vol. edition of Montaigne's Essais, Paris, 1825. The best English translation of the Essais is that of Cotton, first published in 1700, but revised and corrected in 1759. Since the above was written a new Life of Montaigne has been published by Bayle St John, Lond. 1857. (For valuable papers on Montaigne, see <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>'s Essays and Tales, Emerson's Representative Men, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> Essays for 1857.)

MONTALEMBERT

Pages 521-521

MARQ.-RÈSE, MARQUIS DE, a distinguished French engineer, was descended from a noble and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and was born in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1714, at Angoulême. After receiving an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> suitable to his birth, he entered the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of eighteen, and was present at the sieges of Kehl and Philippsburg. He was next engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. On the conclusion of peace he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the cultivation of those sciences upon which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art is founded. He became a member of the Academy of Sciences in 1747, and contributed to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> several papers on fortification. He also established forges at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a> and Périgord, for the purpose of supplying the French <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> with cannons and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. During the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Years' War the important <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the Russian and Swedish armies was entrusted to him. In 1776 he began to publish at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> his La Fortification Perpendiculaire, ou l'Art Défensif supérieur à l'Offensif, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which was completed in eleven volumes in 1796. Meanwhile he had been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> in 1779 with the task of fortifying the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> against the attacks of the English. The wooden fort, which he constructed on a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, proved efficient in spite of the prognostications of his fellow-engineers. By these efforts for the promotion of military art Montalembert brought himself into debt, and was compelled to sell his foundries to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But the price of them could not be obtained even after frequent applications. It is no wonder, therefore, that, aristocrat though he was, he became a supporter of the principles and practices of the French revolution. A pension, awarded to him for the loss of an eye during his services to the government, was resigned for the behoof of the state; and, like a true democrat, he divorced his wife to make room for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of an apothecary. In return for such conduct he was allowed to recover his sequestered estate, and to sell it for the supply of his wants. The assignats, however, which he received as the price, fell immediately in value, and left him as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> as ever. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> Montalembert recommended himself to the notice of the Committee of Public Safety; and was frequently consulted by Carnot on the subject of military operations. He died of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1800. Besides his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> work, already mentioned, Montalembert wrote Correspondance pendant la Guerre de 1757, 3 vols., 8vo, 1777; L'Ami de l'Art Défensif, 4to, 1796; and Relation du Siège de Saint-Jean-d'<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>, 8vo, 1798.

MONTALVAN

Pages 521-522

JUAN PEREZ DE, an eminent Spanish dramatist, was the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>'s bookseller, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in 1602. His youthful genius was stimulated by the example, and guided by the advice and assistance, of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dramatic writer Lope de Vega. So strong, indeed, was the mutual esteem between the two poets, that the elder treated the younger as a son, and the younger adopted the elder as his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> in almost everything. Like his admired <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, Montalvan entered the Montanaro priesthood, and accepted an office in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>. He was also a most voluminous writer. By his thirteenth year he had produced thirty-six dramas; and in 1636 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> had increased to about sixty. In their success, as well as in their flimsy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and careless execution, he likewise resembled Lope de Vega. One of the last works of Montalvan was an extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on his great friend, published in 1636. By this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> his intense and incessant labours had begun to derange his brain. Not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> afterwards he fell into a state of imbecility, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1638. Montalvan's collected dramatic works appeared in 1638–39, and were reprinted in 1652.

MONTANARO

Pages 522-522

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, is situated near the Orco, 14 miles N.N.E. of Turin. It is well built, and has two squares, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a castle, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Some trade is carried on here in cattle and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>. Pop. 4400.

MONTANCHES

Pages 522-522

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Cáceres, is situated in a hilly region, 20 miles S.E. of the town of Cáceres. The streets are steep and well paved; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are a town-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, prison, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, nunnery, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. The town has many flour and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; but it is chiefly noted for the excellence of its hams. Pop. 5587.

MONTANUS

Pages 522-522

the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Montanists, appeared as a teacher of new doctrine at the village of Ardahan, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, about the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century. At that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was suffering under bloody persecutions from without and distracting heresies from within. In his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> desire to cheer and enlighten her, Montanus began to imagine himself to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of God for dispensing new revelations. He foretold the near approach of those judgments that would <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> all persecutors from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, of the second advent of Christ, and of the commencement of the blessed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLENNIUM">millennium</a>. With such a prospect at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> he admonished all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to live soberly and righteously, and more especially to risk all for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. At such startling announcements many scoffed; but others, including two females of fortune, Maximilla and Priscilla, became converts, and fell immediately into ecstasies of exhortation and prophesying. Stimulated by this success, the delirious imagination of Montanus began to create more portentous delusions. He fancied himself to be an inspired prophet sent to the entire church to complete the code of moral duties, to extinguish all heresies by new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and to prepare the church for the coming of her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. He even pointed out a paltry Phrygian village, called Pepuza, as the future site of the New <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Such presumptuous ravings, in order to merit the name even of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, required a systematic arrangement which the crazed brain of Montanus was too weak to execute. This arrangement was afterwards effected by Tertullian, the greatest of the Montanists, and may be represented in the following outline:—Christianity, like all the other works of God, undergoes a gradual development, and is constantly approaching perfection. This developing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> may be distinctly seen running through the successive ages of the patriarchs, the prophets, and the teachers of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. But in the last of these periods it had not attained perfection; for Christ explicitly foretold the coming of a Comforter who should elucidate all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and even after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the apostles there remained pagan practices to be condemned, heresies to be refuted, and obscure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Scripture to be explained. It therefore stands to reason that the Spirit of God, the same in all ages, should descend with restless influence in these latter times, as in the days of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> prophets and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>, and should fill certain chosen vessels with that supernatural illumination which is to light the church on to perfection. Accordingly Montanus, like the Apostles, became the passive recipient of the Holy Ghost. Nor was the supernatural gift restricted to the priests, who claimed to be successors of the Apostles. Christians of every grade fell into divine rhapsodies, and even women, as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOEL">Joel</a> had foretold, began to prophesy. The precepts with which these enthusiastic teachers checked out the moral code were, as might have been anticipated, full of severe asceticism and a stoical contempt of pain. The old fasts were prolonged, and new fasts were added. Those who were guilty of the more deadly crimes were excluded from the church for ever. Martyrdom was held up as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> object of ambition, and to attempt to shun this kind of death, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> to wish for any other, was denounced as a sin. Those <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> who wished to become superior channels for the stream of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> passing from heaven to earth, were required to remain in celibacy. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> was defined to be a bond, not merely bodily and temporal, but also spiritual and eternal; and therefore they who married a second time were treated as adulterers. A denunciation also fell upon all usages and all arts and sciences that arose during the reign of heathenism. The followers of Montanus, in the midst of much controversy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase under the several names of Montanists, Catachrygians, and Perpetuans; they were found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. They still existed in the time of Augustine and Jerome. (See Neander's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Church.)

MONTARGIS

Pages 522-522

a town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the arrondissement of the same name, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRET">Loiret</a>, is situated on the Loing, 40 miles E.N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. The town, which is partly walled, is well but irregularly built, and formerly contained a castle, which was entirely destroyed in 1809. Montargis has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> are carried on here; and the town has a considerable trade in cattle, corn, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, leather, &c. Pop. 7757.

MONTAUBAN

Pages 522-522

a town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARN">Tarn</a>-et-Garonne, is situated on an elevated plain on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tarn, which is here crossed by a brick <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, 342 miles S. by W. of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It is small and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, and the houses ill built; but on the other side of the river stands a suburb called Ville Bourdon, which is regularly and well built. The town itself has three squares, one of which, called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> Royale, is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and surrounded by handsome houses. There is a fine promenade called Les Terrasses, which commands an extensive view of the surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as far as the Pyrenees and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Montauban was formerly strongly fortified; but the only remains of its defences at present are its gates. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are,—the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUCIFORM">cruciform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in the Italian style, with two turrets; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St James; the prefecture; the town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> building with four turrets; and the bishop's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Montauban has also a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> and several other educational institutions. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are extensive, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, and cotton stuffs, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, earthenware, brandy, &c.; and some trade is carried on in these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> and the produce of the neighbourhood. Montauban has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, a tribunal of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a chamber of manufactures, a public library, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, science, and literature. Five <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are held here annually. Montauban was founded in 1144 by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Alphonse of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>. At the Reformation the people embraced the Protestant cause; and the town was inefficaciously besieged by the adverse party in 1580. Afterwards, in 1621, resisted for three months the assaults of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., and did not yield till after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in 1629. The fortifications were soon after destroyed. The Ville Bourdon was founded by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> expelled from Montauban in 1562. Pop. (1851) 23,314.

MONTBELLARD

Pages 522-523
or Montréal (German Münster), a town of France, capital of an arrondissement of the same name, in the department of Doubs, is situated at the confluence of the Allan and the Luzino, 48 miles N.E. of Besançon. The town is well built, and adorned by several fountains. The principal buildings are—the castle, now used as a prison, situated on an eminence; the town-hall; and the churches of St George and St Martin. The manufactures consist of silk, cotton, and woollen fabrics; leather, clocks, watches; scythes, and other implements of husbandry. There is also an active trade carried on in timber, corn, cheese, &c., with Switzerland and the south. Montbéliard was in former times a place of some strength, and the capital of a county that originally formed part of the kingdom of Burgundy, but was transferred to the Wurtemberg family in 1395. Although twice taken by the French in the seventeenth century, it was not finally ceded to them till 1796. Pop. (1851) 5605.

MONTBLANCH

Pages 523-523

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARRAGONA">Tarragona</a>, and 19 miles N.W. of the town of that name. It has a town-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, several churches and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a prison. There are distilleries, tanneries, cotton factories, flour and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; and some trade is carried on in wine, brandy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. Pop. 4200.

MONTBRISON

Pages 523-523

a town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, is situated at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep rock, on the Vizézy, 37 miles W.S.W. of Lyons. The streets are narrow and crooked, and the houses <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and ill built. The town was formerly fortified; but the walls are now replaced by fine boulevards. It has a Gothic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of the thirteenth century, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> and trade are carried on to a very trifling <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Pop. (1851) 6435.

MONTE CHIARO

Pages 523-525

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIESE">Chiese</a>, 12 miles S.E. of Brescia. It is walled, and was formerly defended by a castle, of which one tower is all that now remains. There are two churches, and Montecuculi, several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> are carried on; and there is a considerable trade. Near this town the French gained a victory over the Austrians in 1796. Pop. 6700. Montecuculi, Raimondo, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Melli, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENERALISSIMO">generalissimo</a> of the imperial armies of Germany, was descended from a noble family, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in 1608. He entered the imperial forces as a volunteer, was engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Swedes, and quickly rose through the several grades of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> until he was placed in command of 2000 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. At the head of these, in 1639 he surprised an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 10,000 before Numslau in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, cut them to pieces, and took their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and baggage. But he was speedily overtaken and captured by General Bannier near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. After a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of two years, spent in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, he returned with renewed eagerness to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of war. His reputation as a general was retrieved by the defeat of Wrangel at Triebel in 1647. On the peace of Westphalia in 1648, he visited his native <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>; but being so unfortunate as to kill one of his dearest friends, Count Manzani, in a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNAMENT">tournament</a> held in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Francesco I., he hastened his return to Germany. His next expedition was against Prince Ragotski and the Swedes, who, in 1657, were threatening to drive John Casimir, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, from his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. No sooner had he forced these to conclude a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, than he was despatched to relieve the King of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> from the Swedish force that was besieging his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. In this enterprise he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> his usual success until peace was re-established in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Gustavus, King of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. He was then sent to check the advance of the Turks into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. At the head of a very inferior force, he continued, by the rapidity of his movements, to baffle all the projects of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vizier, until, receiving reinforcements from the French, he came forth boldly into a fair field of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and finished the war in 1664 by the brilliant victory of St Gotthard. Montecuculi was reserved for achievements still greater. On the outbreak of the war with France in 1673, he was placed at the head of the imperial troops, and contrived to effect a junction with the Prince of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, in spite of the manoeuvres of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> general Turenne. In the following year the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> was chosen to supersede him. But it was soon manifest that none but Montecuculi could cope with Turenne; he was therefore reinstalled in the supreme command in 1675. Then began a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of manoeuvres and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-maneuvres more glorious than an equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of victories. For four months these two generals continued to follow each other, to watch every movement, and to be ever on the alert to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the slightest advantage. Yet endurance, rapidity, and stratagem were all tried in vain, and could not affect the equality of the contest. Each divined the purposes of the other by supposing what he himself would have done in his position; and no sooner had the one begun to execute any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> than he found that he had been anticipated and thwarted by his opponent. At length the scarcity of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> rendered it necessary for both parties that a battle should be risked. Turenne was already reconnoitring the ground, when a random <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BALL">ball</a> from a cannon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him dead, to the deep regret of the magnanimous general whom he had been ready to attack. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was taken by the Prince of Condé. But not even that great commander could out-maneuvre Montecuculi; and the war was closed without any decisive <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Montecuculi had now finished his last and most glorious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. He spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the enjoyment of the distinction and honours which his great deeds had won, and in promoting the cause of learning and science. He died at Lintz in October 1681. The military <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> which he wrote show how profoundly skilled he was in his profession. They were published in Italian at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1704, and in Latin at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> in 1718. A French translation, with a Life of the author, appeared at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1752. Montecuculi, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEBASTIANO">Sebastiano</a> di, the alleged poisoner of the eldest son of Francis I., was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and was originally in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Charles V. He came to France in the suite of Catherine de Medici, and was appointed cup-bearer to the Dauphin. It was in this capacity that he accompanied the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> prince on a journey up the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> in the midsummer of 1536. While halting at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURNUS">Tournus</a>, the Dauphin, in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENNIS">tennis</a>, became over-heated, and commanded his cup-bearer to give him a draught of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. He drank it off with great avidity, dropped <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> sick, and expired in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Montecuculi was immediately suspected of having poisoned him. His knowledge of medicine, and the fact that a treatise on poisons was found in his possession, confirmed the suspicion. He was therefore examined at Lyons in the usual manner of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and a wavering confession was wrung from him by torture. At one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> he affirmed that he had been employed to perpetrate the crime by two of the generals of Charles V.; at another time he shifted the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> on Catherine de Medici. But as he could adduce no facts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of either of these charges, he was dragged on a huritle to the scaffold and executed. The infuriated populace tore his still quivering <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> into a thousand pieces, and threw them into the Rhone. Yet since that time historians have generally agreed in thinking that the Dauphin died of pleurisy, and that Montecuculi was innocent. Montefiascone, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Papal States, situated on a hill, 9 miles N.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VITERBO">Viterbo</a>, and 54 N.W. of Rome. The only public buildings are a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> and a few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>. Some remains have been found here of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Etruscan <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the place of which is occupied by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> town. The wine of the vicinity is reckoned of fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Pop. 4800. Monteforte, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Principato Ultra, 5 miles W.S.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVELLINO">Avellino</a>. It is situated at the foot of a hill, on which stand the remains of a castle formerly the residence of the family of De <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, who thence derived their name. The ruins are very picturesque; and from them a fine view of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> may be obtained. Pop. 4000. Montego, a town of Jamaica, capital of Cornwall <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, is situated on a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, on the N. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 17 miles W. of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>. The town is defended by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>; and the harbour is protected by a <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-BREAKWATER">breakwater</a>, but is exposed towards the N. There is a considerable trade carried on here. Pop. 4000. Monteleone, a town of Naples, in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Ultra II., in a lofty position, 15 miles N.E. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NICOTERA">Nicotera</a>. Its imposing appearance is heightened by its castle, which overlooks the town. The town itself is irregularly and meanly built, chiefly of wood, and is badly paved. There are four churches, with some fine paintings; a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The inhabitants are chiefly engaged in the tunny fishery; but there are also some silk-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; and a considerable trade is carried on. N. of the town, and on the coast, stands the village of S.Pietro di Vivona, where there are some remains of the harbour of Hipponium <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Vibo, a city of considerable importance in ancient times. It was originally a colony from the Epizephyrian Locrians, on the other side of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Bruttium; but was taken n.c. 389 by Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, who transported the people to that town. Ten years later they were restored by the Carthaginians; but soon afterwards the town fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Bruttians, in whose possession it remained till conquered by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. A colony was established here by the latter in 192 B.C., and the city became one of the most flourishing in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Italy. It had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> dockyards for ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and was conveniently situated for trade both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> and by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The ancient town probably stood on the same site as the modern, which is not older than the thirteenth century; but there are no ancient remains to be seen. Pop. 6630.

MONTE SAN GIULIANO

Pages 526-526

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Trapani, is situated on a mountain 2184 feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, 5 miles E.N.E. of Trapani. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. The mountain was in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times called <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ERYX">Eryx</a>, and had a temple of Venus on the top, founded, according to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, by Æneas. This is now replaced by a Saracen castle. The town of Eryx belonged to a Sicilian tribe called Elymi, but afterwards fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Carthaginians. Though taken by Pyrrhus in 378, it was regained by the Carthaginians, who abandoned it in the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It does not seem to have been restored by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Pop. 6600.

MONTE-VIDEO

Pages 529-530
or San Felipe de Monte-Video, the capital of Uruguay in South America, is situated on the northern shore of the estuary of the La Plata, 130 miles E.S.E. of Buenos Ayres, S. Lat. 34° 53', W. Long. 56° 16'. It stands on a gentle eminence at the extremity of a small promontory which forms the east side of the harbour, a bay 4 miles in length by 2 in breadth. The houses are well built, and floored with unbaked bricks. They are for the most part only one storey high, and have flat roofs. The streets are broad, regular, and well paved. There are no great public buildings, except the cathedral, a handsome stone edifice, and the town-hall. Monte-Video is surrounded by walls, which are mounted with guns; and there is also a citadel. The climate is healthy, and the soil of the surrounding country rich and productive; but water is very scarce, and can only be obtained by wells dug on the seashore, or by collecting the rain-water in cisterns. The harbour is shallow, varying from 14 to 19 feet in depth; but the bottom is soft, and does not injure the vessels that may run aground. The winds from the S.S.W. blow into the harbour and cause a considerable swell. The number of vessels that entered the harbour in 1863, including the coasting trade, was 1220, and their tonnage 149,567; while those that cleared were 978, and their tonnage 141,131. The trade of Monte-Video is very considerable; the exports, consisting of wool, hides, tallow, salt beef, &c.; and the imports of cotton and woollen fabrics, hardware, wine, provisions, &c. A line of steamers was established in 1856 between Monte-Video and Genoa; and there is also another, supported by the government of Brazil, between this place and Rio Janeiro. Pop. about 12,000.

MONTELIMART

Pages 525-525

a town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an arrondissement of the same name, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DROME">Drome</a>, is situated at the confluence of the Roubion and the Jabron, 26 miles S. of Valence. The town is defended by Gothic walls, is entered by four gates, and has a castle standing on an eminence in the centre. The houses are well built, and the streets <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and paved with basalt. It derives its name, Montel d'Adhemar (Mons Adhemari), from an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> noble family who had possessions here as early as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. Montelimart was one of the first <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France to adopt the Reformed doctrines; and is noted in the civil wars of the Reformation. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of primary instance, and a communal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, hosiery, tiles, &c., are carried on; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is famed for a sort of cake made of almonds and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Some trade is carried on in these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, as well as in cattle, corn, &c. Pop. (1851) 8632.

MONTEN

Pages 525-526

DIETRICH, an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-painter, was born at Düsseldorf in 1799. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his art seems to have been strong from his earliest boyhood. The descriptions of warlike encounters in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Tasso, and Ariosto were the favourite readings of his school-days, and furnished subjects for his first attempts in sketching. That he might become thoroughly intimate with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> scenes, he volunteered into the Prussian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in 1828, and served for a year. The next two years were devoted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in the Academy of Arts in his native town. He then placed himself under the tuition of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Hess at Munich, and with the aid of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> battle-painter began to develop his own peculiar style of art. His pictures were executed with a rapidity that left no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> for faithful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and elaborate finish. Yet they were full of spirited figures, boldly drawn, and strikingly coloured. In 1827 they had obtained for him the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the painter Cornelius, and of Ludwig I, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. By the former he was employed to execute on the arcade of the Hofgarten three frescoes, representing the scenes from Bavarian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of "The Storming of the Turkish Entrenchment at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a> in 1717," "The Battle of Arcis-sur-Aube," and "The Granting of the Bavarian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a> by Maximilian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> I in 1818." For the latter he painted "The Battle of Saarbrück," and "The Departure of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a> from their Fatherland." Among his other important historical pieces are "The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a> of Gustavus Adolphus," and "The Great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a> in 1838 at Augsburg." Monten died in 1843. (See Bryan's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Painters and Engravers.) MONTENEGRO (called by the natives Zernagora, and by the Turks Karadagh, all which names are derived from the dark forests with which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are covered) is a small state in European <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, tributary to the Porte, but virtually independent. It extends from 42° 10' to 42° 56', N. Lat.; and from 18° 41' to 20° 22', E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>.; and is bounded on the N. by Herzegovina, E. and S. by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, and W. by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">Area</a> about 1450 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> consists for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mountains, forming a part of the Dinarian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. The slope towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is very steep; so that there are no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of any size on that side, and very little vegetation is found on the rocky acclivities. The lowest parts of this mountainous district are probably more than 2000 feet in elevation, and many of the higher summits rise upwards of 5000 feet above the sea. The interior is intersected with numerous ridges, forming valleys, which, however, are of no great size. Towards the E. the mountains diminish in height, till they are lost in the plain of the Moratsha; and the access to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands from this side lies through several narrow gorges. The Moratsha is the only river of any importance in Montenegro; it flows southward, and falls into the Lake of Skutari, which is situated in Albania, on the confines of Montenegro. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is healthy, but <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, owing to the elevated position of the country. The winter is long, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn are often very severe. Owing to the configuration of the country, there are few streams <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> rivers, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> do not occur in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> numbers; so that the inhabitants are obliged to collect the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> in cisterns to supply their wants. Except in a few well-watered spots, the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is not very great; and the ground is not largely cultivated. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, potatoes, cabbages, and other vegetables are raised; but the inhabitants depend for support chiefly on the live stock which they rear. Sheep, goats, and pigs are numerous, but there are few horses or cattle. Most of the mountains are covered with forests, chiefly consisting of oak and beech, which, though they do not attain their full height on the higher elevations, are often of great size in the lower regions. The Venetian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUMACH">sumach</a>, a shrub, the wood of which is largely used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, is found here in great abundance, and forms an important article of trade. The Montenegrins, from fear of invasion, have made no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in their country; and internal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> is carried on by means of footpaths impassable for beasts of burden. A good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of trade is carried on with the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CATTARO">Cattaro</a> in Dalmatia; but the Montenegrins are not allowed to carry on any intercourse with the neighbouring Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. They export live stock, smoked mutton, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BACON">bacon</a>, cheese, tallow, sheepskins, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c., as well as the sumach wood and firewood; while they import wine, spirits, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, fire-arms, and other manufactured <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> value of the annual exports to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> is L1,392, and that of the imports from that country L434. Montenegro proper consists of four nahias or cantons—Katunska, Rietskha, Zermnitshka, and Lieshanska; but besides these there are some other tribes which belong to the confederation. These also are divided into four cantons, called berdas, distinguished by the names of Bielopovitskha, Piperska, Kutschka, and Moratshka; and the inhabitants are called Berdiani, to distinguish them from the Montenegrins proper, or Zernagorzi. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a vladika or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, residing at Zetlinie; and the office is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> line. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the people is that of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; of which the vladika was formerly a bishop, uniting the supreme civil and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authority in his own person; but since 1851 these offices have been separated. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of elders, consisting of 12 members, to assist the prince. The people are tall, hardy, and athletic. They have great hospitality and a strong feeling of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>; but their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of warfare is barbarous and unsparing, and they are constantly making plundering forays into the neighbouring districts. Their system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, when their country is invaded, consists of posting sharpshooters in various positions in the mountains, and enticing the invaders into these fastnesses, where they are gradually <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the unerring aim of the Montenegrin riflemen. When out of their own country, however, these mountaineers cannot stand against regular troops. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken in Montenegro is a dialect of the Slavonic, the same as that spoken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a> is in a very low state, and it is thought a great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> to be able to read and write. There are only two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, one at Zetlinie and one at Dobroskoselo, both of which have been founded since 1841. The Montenegrins were reduced under the dominion of the Turkish empire in the reign of Soliman the Magnificent, and they remained in this condition till the year 1700, when, at the instigation of the Vladika Daniel, all the Mohammedans were put to death, and the country declared independent. In 1712 the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Katunska took up arms in Monte Rosa, a mountain of the Pennine Alps, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, is a union of several mountain chains rather than a single summit. Four mountain chains radiate from a centre point, N., S., E., and W., respectively. A ridge of inaccessible mountains extends E. and W., from the Cime de la Pisse on the E., to the Col du Mont Cervin on the W.; and this is intersected at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> by another chain, extending northwards as far as the Cima di Jazy, and southwards as far as the Col d'Olen. The centre where these branches unite, called the Signal Kuppe, is not the most elevated point, there being three of greater height on the northern range. The first of these is called the Zumsteinspitze, and is the only one of the three which has been ascended; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the Höchste Spitze, or highest of all, which is connected with the former by a narrow and sharp ridge, descending steeply on one side into a tremendous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>; and the third is the "<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORD">Nord</a>-End," which, like the highest, has not yet been Monte Rosa ascended. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the height of these four peaks is not, however, more than 200 feet between the highest and the lowest. The height of the highest is 15,158 feet above the sea. The four branches of Monte Rosa inclose between them four glaciers,—viz., that of Macugnana on the N.E., that of Gorner on the N.W., that of Lys on the S.W., and several of less size in the valley of Sesia on the S.E. The geological formation of Monte Rosa is gneiss and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a>-slate; and it separates the waters flowing to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> from those which join the Po. (See Alps.)

MONTESQUIEU

Pages 526-529
CHARLES DE SECONDAT, Baron de la Brède et de, was descended from an ancient and noble family of Guienne, and was born on the 18th of January 1689, at the castle of La Brède, near Bordeaux, where he passed his early days, and composed those works which have acquired for their author an imperishable reputation. His father having early discovered in him indications of genius, and a promise of future eminence, bestowed the utmost pains on his education, which appears to have been conducted with equal judgment and success; and being destined for the magistracy, he employed the energies of his active mind in studying the immense collection of the different codes, and in endeavouring to detect the motives, and unravel the complicated relations, of the obscure or contradictory laws contained in them. His taste for this study was insatiable; and if it proved the source of his future glory, it was also that of his greatest happiness. He himself stated, that he never had to reproach himself with an hour of reading wasted or misspent. When exhausted with his arid labours upon jurisprudence, he recruited his mind with books of history and travels, and with the productions of the classical ages of Greece and Rome. Enchanted, as he says, with antiquity, he at the age of twenty composed a work, in the form of letters, wherein he sought to prove that the idolatry of the pagans did not appear to deserve eternal damnation; but this first production of his genius he wisely abstained from giving to the world. On the 24th of February 1714 he was received as counsellor to the Parliament of Bordeaux; and on the 13th of July 1716 he was, through the influence of his paternal uncle, named president à mortier. The same year he was admitted into the Academy of Bordeaux, which had been recently founded by a number of persons possessing a common taste for music and works of entertainment. Conceiving, however, that its object was too limited, and desirous to extend the sphere of its utility, he undertook to convert this coterie of wits into a learned society; and his views in this respect were warmly seconded by the Duke of La Force, who founded a prize, and held out several other inducements to the cultivation of science. As a member of this learned association, he contributed his contingent of memoirs or communications, chiefly on subjects connected with href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, a species of study for which he had a particular taste. But his physical constitution disqualified him for that minute observation which is essential to the successful prosecution of this particular science. He was not only short-sighted, but his vision was weak; and this infirmity increased so much with time, that towards the close of his life he became almost blind. It may also be observed that, at the period when Montesquieu applied himself to natural history, the fundamental principles of that science had not yet been established. In 1719 he circulated, by means of the journals, an *Histoire Physique de la Terre ancienne et moderne*; and he read successively to the Academy of Bordeaux a dissertation *Sur la Politique des Romains dans la Religion*, an *Eloge du Due de la Force*, and a *Vie du Maréchal de Berwick*, a production which in several points recalls the manner of Tacitus. Montesquieu, however, was by no means in haste to appear before the public in the character of author. He preferred waiting until his faculties were ripened by time and matured by reflection; nor was it until the year 1721 that he entered upon his literary career, by the publication of the *Lettres Persanes*, the first idea of which seems to have been borrowed from the *Siamois* of the *Amusements Sérieux et Comiques* of Dufresnoy, though, in works of genius, the primary conception is of little moment compared with the execution. The success of the *Lettres Persanes*, and the influence which they exercised, were unparalleled. This is to be ascribed to two causes; the circumstances of the period at which the book appeared, and the form into which it was cast. On the death of Louis XIV., libertinism succeeded to devotion, effrontery to hypocrisy, familiarity to respect, and audacity to submission. The liberty of saying or writing anything with impunity led men to examine and to combat all that had been agreed to without opposition, or even assented to with enthusiasm. In the midst of this general effervescence appeared the book of the *Lettres Persanes*. From the shape into which it was cast, it had all the attractions of a romance; it abounded in voluptuous details, which flattered the taste of the age for pleasure, and in irreligious sarcasms, which gratified its tendency to infidelity; and it treated with contempt Louis XIV., and his reign, which people now sought to depreciate. But it must nevertheless be admitted, that, with all these faults, the book displays an ardent love for the welfare of mankind; a courageous zeal for the triumph of reason and virtue; luminous views upon commerce, public law, criminal jurisprudence, and the dearest interests of nations; a penetrating insight into the vices of society, as well as those of governments; and, generally, strong evidence of profound reflection, which takes the reader the more by surprise that it seems to be the constant object of the author to disguise it under the mask of frivolity. Its principal attraction, however, and that which won the suffrages of all, consisted in the keen, animated, sprightly satire of French manners and caprices, and in a style always lively, sparkling, full of happy inundation and unexpected contrasts, the pointed irony of which sometimes rose to the most energetic eloquence. Four years after the publication of the *Lettres Persanes*, Montesquieu caused to be printed separately, in 1725, the *Temple de Guilde*, an ingenious trifle, though cold and without interest, being equally devoid of easy wit or natural grace, and which Madame du Deffand happily called the "Apocalypse of Gallantry." The same year, at the opening of the Parliament of Bordeaux, he delivered a discourse on the duties of magistrates, advocates, attorneys, and all those connected with the administration of law, which, though but little noticed, is written in a fluent, impassioned style, different from the ordinary manner of Montesquieu, and in that vein of eloquence which addresses itself more to the sentiments than to the reason of men. In 1726 he sold his office and withdrew from the magistracy, the duties of which he had so well described. The desire to regain his freedom, and apply himself entirely to philosophy and letters, was no doubt one of his motives; but the principal cause of this determination seems to have been a sense of inadequacy to fill the situation in which he was placed. He informs us, indeed, that his whole merit as president consisted in rectitude of purpose and understanding sufficiently the questions themselves; but that he had never been able to master the forms of procedure, although he had applied himself to the subject. Being now at liberty to devote himself exclusively to philosophy and letters, he presented himself as a candidate for the place in the French Academy vacant by the death of M. de Sacy; but Cardinal Fleury wrote to the Academy that the King had declared he would not give his approbation to the author of a work containing impious sarcasms against religion. Montesquieu, however, though at once amazed and offended by the refusal of the King and his minister, contrived, by a device more dexterous than candid, to propitiate the cardinal. He asserted his claim with firmness, yet disavowed those letters of the book which formed a legitimate ground of objection against him. The King was appeased by the intervention of the minister, and on the 24th of January 1728 he was received into the Academy, on which occasion he delivered an inaugural discourse, which appears amongst his printed works. Montesquieu having accomplished this object, resolved to travel, and in the course of his peregrinations visited almost all the countries of Europe. He proceeded first to Vienna, where he often saw Prince Eugene; he then passed into Hungary, whence he journeyed to Italy, and at Venice became acquainted with John Law of Lauriston, who, from the height of grandeur, wealth, and celebrity, had fallen into obscurity, neglect, and poverty; and also with the Comte de Bonnevol, who had as yet only gone through part of the cycle of his romantic adventures. From Venice he proceeded to Rome, where he became acquainted with Cardinal Corsini, afterwards Clement XII., and with Cardinal Polignac, author of the *Anti-Lucrèce*. He next visited Genoa, but having met with a cold reception there, he soothed his ill-humour by writing some satirical stanzas, which, however, he did not think fit to print. From Italy he passed into Switzerland, and traversing the different countries watered by the Rhine, stopped some time in Holland, where he met Lord Chesterfield, with whom he had become acquainted at Venice. He then visited England, where he resided about two years, was admitted a member of the Royal Society, and treated with marked distinction by Queen Caroline. On his return to his own country, he retired to his castle at La Brède, where he resumed his favourite pursuits. He had either before or during his travels caused to be printed in Holland a little work entitled *Réflexions sur la Monarchie universelle*, which is now but little known, and extremely rare, though it is referred to by the author himself in a passage of the *Esprit des Lois* (I. xxi., c. 22). The object of this piece was to prove that, in the actual state of the modern nations of Europe, it is impossible even for the ablest and most ambitious of sovereigns to establish a universal monarchy. After two years spent in his retreat at La Brède, Montesquieu published in 1734 his *Considerations sur les Causes de la Grandeur et de la Décadence des Romains*; a work which, if not the most remarkable, is perhaps the most finished of all his productions, and in which he had to enter into competition with several eminent men, both amongst the ancients and the moderns, particularly Polybius, Machiavelli, Saint-Evremond, and Bossuet. But Montesquieu was the first writer who grappled with this great subject in all its details, and who compared all the facts with laborious sagacity. He overlooked none which could afford matter for reflection, or warrant any inference of importance, and yet he managed to compress the whole into a volume of moderate size. The *Dialogue de Sylla et d'Eurate*, which is subjoined to this work, and may be considered as forming part of it, is one of those productions in which Montesquieu has displayed the greatest eloquence; and with this may be classed another piece not less remarkable, namely, *Lysimaque*, in which he has delineated, in a manner altogether sublime, that system of stoicism which raised man above the ordinary weaknesses of his nature, and enabled him to brave with joy, and even with pride, the cruelties of tyrants and the iniquities of fortune. The *Considerations on the Grandeur and Decline of the Romans* make us acquainted with the history of a single people; but Montesquieu had long been engaged in studying that of all other nations, in discovering the causes of those revolutions which had successively changed the face of the world, and in investigating those laws and customs which had contributed to their prosperity or decline. The success of the treatise on the Roman people, which in some sort formed only a detached portion of the vast plan he had conceived, served to increase his ardour in the execution of so great an undertaking, to the completion of which fourteen more years of incessant labour were devoted. Sometimes he thought that he advanced rapidly, and would speedily accomplish his design; at other times he appeared to recede, and to become perplexed by the immensity and complication of the subject. At length, after twenty years of unremitting application, he had the satisfaction to put the last hand to a production upon which he had expended so much anxious labour and meditation, and which he entitled *L'Esprit des Lois*. But before sending this work to the press, he judged it prudent to consult one of his intimate friends, whose talents and knowledge he respected; and with this view he sent his manuscript to Helvetius. The latter, however, was so little satisfied with the production after perusal, and so much alarmed for the danger to which the reputation of Montesquieu would be exposed by the publication of a work which he considered as so defective, that at first he did not venture to express what he thought of it, and solicited the author's permission to communicate the manuscript to a common friend, Saurin, the author of *Spartacus*. The latter coincided in opinion with Helvetius, and both agreed that, by the publication of this book, the celebrated author of the *Lettres Persanes* would injure his reputation, and lower himself in the estimation of the world. After some hesitation, this extraordinary judgment was communicated to Montesquieu, accompanied with an earnest entreaty on the part of both that he would subject the whole to careful revision, and upon no account publish the work in the crude and imperfect state in which it then appeared. The strange counsels of these friends, however, had so little influence on Montesquieu, that he sent the manuscript to the press without altering a word, prefixing this epigraph, "*Prolem sine matre creatum*," to indicate that his work had no model; and, as if to mark still more strongly how little he was moved by their unfavourable judgment, he congratulated himself in his preface on having produced a work which was not altogether destitute of genius. Nor did the result disappoint the just expectations he had formed. Its success was in fact so great, than in little more than a year and a half after its publication, it had gone through twenty-two editions, and been translated into almost every language of Europe. The *Esprit des Lois* appeared about the middle of the year 1748, and before the end of the year 1750 its reputation was universal. If the *Spirit of Laws*, however, was much read, much admired, and much praised, the work, like all those which have produced a great impression, was also much criticised. Madame du Deffand said of it, that it was not *l'esprit des loix*, but de l'esprit sur les loix*, a saying which had just that degree of truth which gives currency to an epigram. But the work was not of a kind likely to interest the epigrammatic mind at all. It was written with quite a different aim, and has had quite a different reputation now that men have had time to judge of its merits. Its author addressed himself to men of reason and experience, to statesmen and thinkers in general. Those political problems which had hitherto shaded by uncertainty, or obscured by ignorance, and with which the world had been occupied previous to his time, Montesquieu either solved or placed in a clear light for subsequent investigators. And although not a few of the hostile criticisms with which his work was assailed appeared to be well founded, the reputation of Montesquieu was greatly enhanced by the publication of the *Spirit of Laws*; and it may be said with truth, that this work alone would have been sufficient to insure him lasting renown, and to constitute a noble monument of his genius, sagacity, and wisdom. For an estimate of the relative merit and true historical position of the *Esprit des Loix*, in establishing just ideas of jurisprudence, see the First Preliminary Dissertation (part i., sect. iii.) Montesquieu had resolved not to reply to any of the criticisms which might be made on the *Esprit des Loix*; but the attacks of an anonymous author, who, in a journal called Nouvelles Ecclésiastiques, had, amongst other things, represented him as an atheist, induced him to deviate from this resolution. In the *Lettres Persanes* he had treated the Christian religion with too much levity; but afterwards, when his mind was fully matured by age, study, and reflection, he had seen cause to alter his views; and hence in the *Esprit des Loix*, he recommends Christianity in expressive terms, not only as the most perfect of all religious systems, but also as the most powerful support of the whole social system. He therefore deemed it of importance to repel the calumnious insinuations of the ecclesiastical journalist, and at the same time he wished to refute by anticipation the theologians of the Sorbonne, who, being dissatisfied with some passages in the *Esprit des Loix*, were proceeding to condemn the work. It was with this double purpose that he wrote his *Défense*, which may be considered as a model of solid discussion, light pleasantry, and contemptuous moderation. "What pleases me in my *Défense*," said he, "is not seeing the venerable theologians grappled; it is seeing them laid gently upon their backs." But he took no notice whatever of a crowd of brochures, filled with absurd criticisms or gross abuse, which appeared against the *Spirit of Laws*. "The public," said he, "avenge me on the one by their contempt, and on the other by their indignation."
