Muttra, the capital of the district, is described by Bishop Heber as a striking town, much resembling Benares, its houses being lofty, with the same sort of ornaments as in that city. The place is regarded as sacred in Hindu mythology, from being the birthplace of the divinity Krishna. Towards the close of the last century the town of Muttra was seized by Scindia, the Mahratta chief, who conferred it on the French adventurer Perron, on condition of military service. In October 1803 it was, without resistance, occupied by the British troops, and in the same year permanently ceded to the East India Company by Scindia, under the treaty of Serje Arjengau. Muttra is in N. Lat. 27. 30., and E. Long. 77. 45. MUZIANO, GIROLAMO, an eminent Italian painter, was born at Acquafredda, near Brescia, in 1528. Under Romano, an imitator of Titian, he studied his art, and became an adept in designing and colouring according to the principles of the Venetian school. But it was not until he had left his native place, and had repaired to Rome about 1550, that he came into notice. There his pictures soon gained for him the surname of Il Giovane de' Paesi ("the young man of the landscapes"). Stimulated by success, he tried the more elevated style of historical painting. He imitated Michael Angelo in giving great prominence to the anatomy of his figures, and became fond of painting persons emaciated by abstinence or disease. His great picture of the "Resurrection of Lazarus" at once established his fame as an historical painter. Michael Angelo praised it, and pronounced its author one of the first artists of that age. It was placed in the church of Santa Maria Maggiore, but was afterwards transferred to the Quirinal Palace. Muziano, with dauged perseverance, continued to proceed in the path on which he had so successfully entered. He grew excellent in depicting foreign and military dresses, and in introducing landscapes into his historical pieces after the manner of Titian. Mosaic working also occupied his attention; and from being a crude art of inlaying coloured stones, it became under his hands a perfect imitation of painting. His ability and industry soon gained for him a handsome fortune. Part of this he expended in assisting to found the Academy of St Luke at Rome. He died in 1590, or, according to another authority, in 1592, and was buried in the church of Santa Maria Maggiore, where his great masterpiece was placed. Many of Muziano's works are in the churches and palaces of Rome. There is his group of "Anchors listening to a saint," in the church of the Carthusians; his "Circumcision," in the church of Gesù; his "Ascension," in the church of Ara Coeli; and his "St Francis receiving the Stigmata," in the church of the Conception. A picture by him, representing Christ washing the feet of his disciples, is in the cathedral of Rheims. (Lanzi's Storia Pittorica.) MYCENÆ or MYCENE, an ancient city of Greece, stood about 7½ miles N.E. from Argos, on a rocky height in a recess of the mountains that border the Argelian plain. Its name is said to have been derived from Mycene, daughter of Inachus, or from the Greek word ἀπέξ. It was founded by Persians; and, according to a favourite legend, its massive walls were reared by the strong hands of the Cyclopes. After the death of Perseus it was ruled in succession by Sthenelus and Eurystheus; then coming into the power of the Pelopidae, it gradually rose into importance until, under the sway of Agamemnon, it became the first city of Greece. But no sooner had that powerful prince died, than Argos began to assume a supremacy over the other towns of the plain. The Mycenaean were soon fain to trust to their strong walls, and to an alliance with Sparta for protection against their aggressive neighbours. At length, in 463 B.C., the Argives, summoning to their aid the inhabitants of Tegea and Cleonae, sat down before Mycenæ. After a blockade, the city was forced to capitulate, and was ever afterwards abandoned to desolation. In the second century A.D., its ruins were visited by Pausanias. They are still very extensive, and are the most ancient in Greece, next to those of Tiryns. The walls of the Acropolis exist, in a greater or less degree of preservation, round almost the entire circuit. They consist in some places of huge misshapen blocks piled up irregularly, and in other places of stones, skilfully hewn and regularly placed. At their N.W. angle is a gate, formed of three long massive stones, surmounted by two enormous lions in bas-relief, and called on that account the Gate of Lions. On the S.W. of the Acropolis the site of the lower town is indicated by the remains of a wall extending from N. to S. In this part of the ruins there are four subterraneous erections in which, according to Pausanias, the treasures of the Atridae were deposited. One of these, called the Treasury of Atreus, consists of two apartments, the outer of which is large, and the inner comparatively small. (Leake's Morea, and Mure's Tour in Greece.) MYCONE, or MICONI, a small island in the Ægean Sea, situated in N. Lat. 37° 29', E. Long. 25° 21'. It is of a triangular form, and in length is 8½ miles from E. to W.; in breadth from N. to S., 6 miles. The surface is rugged, but does not rise to a very great height, and the soil is dry but fertile. Wine and fruit are the principal products of the island, and it also contains abundance of game. There is very little water here, and the wants of the inhabitants are for the most part supplied by rain water. The town of Mycone stands on the N.W. coast, and is chiefly inhabited by sailors, who are reckoned among the best in these seas. The roadstead is exposed to all winds except those from the N.N.E. Pop. of the town about 5000; of the island, about 6000. MYHERE, in Hindustan, a petty native state in the territory of Saugor and Nerhudda, containing an area of 1026 square miles, and a population of 100,000. The present chief is a minor, and arrangements have been made for his education at Agra, under the direction of the British government. Myhere, the principal town, is in N. Lat. 24° 16', E. Long. 80° 49'. MYLAÈ (Milazzo), an ancient town of Sicily, was situated about 30 miles W. from Cape Pelorus, on the isthmus of a peninsula of 5 miles in length. It assisted, according to Strabo, in 648 B.C., in colonizing Himera. It was for many centuries a dependency of the Greek colony of Messana. Laches took it in 427 B.C.; and the Reginans, in 394 B.C., attempted to make it the seat of an opposition to Messana. It enjoyed separate municipal privileges in the time of Pliny; and its importance as a military station is still great. MYLASA, or MYLASA (Melasso), a noble city of Caria in Asia Minor, situated about three leagues from the Sinus Ceramicus, in a beautiful plain at the foot of a steep mountain, containing fine white marble, of which its buildings were composed. It was the capital of Hecatomnus, King of Caria and father of Mausolus, and the birthplace and residence of the Carian kings before Halicarnassus became the capital. The chief citizens of Mylasa were made priests of Zeus for life; and the splendour of its temples was the wonder of all who visited it. Caria was taken by Mithridates, and afterwards by Labienus, whose father had been one of Caesar's generals. Hybriss, whose eloquence and valour entitled him to a distinguished rank amongst his countrymen, in vain encouraged them to make an obstinate defence. He himself was obliged to yield to necessity, and to take refuge at Rhodes; but scarcely had the conqueror quitted the city, when Hybriss returned and restored liberty to his country. Pliny calls it Mylasa libera; and Strabo informs us that it was one of the most magnificent cities of antiquity, and that its temples, porticoes, and other public monuments were highly admired. When Pococke visited this place it was comparatively perfect, but at present few traces of it remain. (See Leake's Asia Minor, and Fellows' Journal and Discoveries.) MYLINE, ROBERT, the architect of Blackfriars Bridge, London, was the descendant of a family of architects, and was born in Edinburgh in 1734. Having adopted at an early age his hereditary profession, he was sent to the Continent to complete his studies. His enthusiastic prosecution of his art soon brought him into notice. He became a most distinguished pupil, and ultimately a member of the Academy of St Luke at Rome. Returning to England, he executed a design for Blackfriars Bridge, which was chosen from among twenty others. The bridge was begun in 1760, was finished in 1769, and established the fame of its architect. He was employed to erect or improve many edifices throughout the kingdom. The office of engineer to the New River Water-works Company, and the surveyorship of St Paul's Cathedral, were conferred upon him. While holding this latter appointment he suggested the famous inscription to the memory of Wren in St Paul's, "Si monumentum requiras, circumspice." He died in 1821. MYMUNSING, a district of Hindustan, in the province of Bengal, situated between the 24th and 26th degrees of north latitude. The boundaries of this territory are the Garrow Mountains and the district of Goalpara on the N., Dacca Jelalpoor on the S., Silhet on the E., and Bogra and Rungpoor on the W. The country is intersected by the

His great picture of the "Resurrection of Lazarus" at once established his fame as an historical painter. Michael Angelo praised it, and pronounced its author one of the first artists of that age. It was placed in the church of Santa Maria Maggiore, but was afterwards transferred to the Quirinal Palace. Muziano, with dauged perseverance, continued to proceed in the path on which he had so successfully entered. He grew excellent in depicting foreign and military dresses, and in introducing landscapes into his historical pieces after the manner of Titian. Mosaic working also occupied his attention; and from being a crude art of inlaying coloured stones, it became under his hands a perfect imitation of painting. His ability and industry soon gained for him a handsome fortune. Part of this he expended in assisting to found the Academy of St Luke at Rome. He died in 1590, or, according to another authority, in 1592, and was buried in the church of Santa Maria Maggiore, where his great masterpiece was placed. Many of Muziano's works are in the churches and palaces of Rome. There is his group of "Anchors listening to a saint," in the church of the Carthusians; his "Circumcision," in the church of Gesù; his "Ascension," in the church of Ara Coeli; and his "St Francis receiving the Stigmata," in the church of the Conception. A picture by him, representing Christ washing the feet of his disciples, is in the cathedral of Rheims. (Lanzi's Storia Pittorica.) MYCENÆ or MYCENE, an ancient city of Greece, stood about 7½ miles N.E. from Argos, on a rocky height in a recess of the mountains that border the Argelian plain. Its name is said to have been derived from Mycene, daughter of Inachus, or from the Greek word ἀπέξ. It was founded by Persians; and, according to a favourite legend, its massive walls were reared by the strong hands of the Cyclopes. After the death of Perseus it was ruled in succession by Sthenelus and Eurystheus; then coming into the power of the Pelopidae, it gradually rose into importance until, under the sway of Agamemnon, it became the first city of Greece. But no sooner had that powerful prince died, than Argos began to assume a supremacy over the other towns of the plain. The Mycenaean were soon fain to trust to their strong walls, and to an alliance with Sparta for protection against their aggressive neighbours. At length, in 463 B.C., the Argives, summoning to their aid the inhabitants of Tegea and Cleonae, sat down before Mycenæ. After a blockade, the city was forced to capitulate, and was ever afterwards abandoned to desolation. In the second century A.D., its ruins were visited by Pausanias. They are still very extensive, and are the most ancient in Greece, next to those of Tiryns. The walls of the Acropolis exist, in a greater or less degree of preservation, round almost the entire circuit. They consist in some places of huge misshapen blocks piled up irregularly, and in other places of stones, skilfully hewn and regularly placed. At their N.W. angle is a gate, formed of three long massive stones, surmounted by two enormous lions in bas-relief, and called on that account the Gate of Lions. On the S.W. of the Acropolis the site of the lower town is indicated by the remains of a wall extending from N. to S. In this part of the ruins there are four subterraneous erections in which, according to Pausanias, the treasures of the Atridae were deposited. One of these, called the Treasury of Atreus, consists of two apartments, the outer of which is large, and the inner comparatively small. (Leake's Morea, and Mure's Tour in Greece.) MYCONE, or MICONI, a small island in the Ægean Sea, situated in N. Lat. 37° 29', E. Long. 25° 21'. It is of a triangular form, and in length is 8½ miles from E. to W.; in breadth from N. to S., 6 miles. The surface is rugged, but does not rise to a very great height, and the soil is dry but fertile. Wine and fruit are the principal products of the island, and it also contains abundance of game. There is very little water here, and the wants of the inhabitants are for the most part supplied by rain water. The town of Mycone stands on the N.W. coast, and is chiefly inhabited by sailors, who are reckoned among the best in these seas. The roadstead is exposed to all winds except those from the N.N.E. Pop. of the town about 5000; of the island, about 6000. MYHERE, in Hindustan, a petty native state in the territory of Saugor and Nerhudda, containing an area of 1026 square miles, and a population of 100,000. The present chief is a minor, and arrangements have been made for his education at Agra, under the direction of the British government. Myhere, the principal town, is in N. Lat. 24° 16', E. Long. 80° 49'. MYLAÈ (Milazzo), an ancient town of Sicily, was situated about 30 miles W. from Cape Pelorus, on the isthmus of a peninsula of 5 miles in length. It assisted, according to Strabo, in 648 B.C., in colonizing Himera. It was for many centuries a dependency of the Greek colony of Messana. Laches took it in 427 B.C.; and the Reginans, in 394 B.C., attempted to make it the seat of an opposition to Messana. It enjoyed separate municipal privileges in the time of Pliny; and its importance as a military station is still great. MYLASA, or MYLASA (Melasso), a noble city of Caria in Asia Minor, situated about three leagues from the Sinus Ceramicus, in a beautiful plain at the foot of a steep mountain, containing fine white marble, of which its buildings were composed. It was the capital of Hecatomnus, King of Caria and father of Mausolus, and the birthplace and residence of the Carian kings before Halicarnassus became the capital. The chief citizens of Mylasa were made priests of Zeus for life; and the splendour of its temples was the wonder of all who visited it. Caria was taken by Mithridates, and afterwards by Labienus, whose father had been one of Caesar's generals. Hybriss, whose eloquence and valour entitled him to a distinguished rank amongst his countrymen, in vain encouraged them to make an obstinate defence. He himself was obliged to yield to necessity, and to take refuge at Rhodes; but scarcely had the conqueror quitted the city, when Hybriss returned and restored liberty to his country. Pliny calls it Mylasa libera; and Strabo informs us that it was one of the most magnificent cities of antiquity, and that its temples, porticoes, and other public monuments were highly admired. When Pococke visited this place it was comparatively perfect, but at present few traces of it remain. (See Leake's Asia Minor, and Fellows' Journal and Discoveries.) MYLINE, ROBERT, the architect of Blackfriars Bridge, London, was the descendant of a family of architects, and was born in Edinburgh in 1734. Having adopted at an early age his hereditary profession, he was sent to the Continent to complete his studies. His enthusiastic prosecution of his art soon brought him into notice. He became a most distinguished pupil, and ultimately a member of the Academy of St Luke at Rome. Returning to England, he executed a design for Blackfriars Bridge, which was chosen from among twenty others. The bridge was begun in 1760, was finished in 1769, and established the fame of its architect. He was employed to erect or improve many edifices throughout the kingdom. The office of engineer to the New River Water-works Company, and the surveyorship of St Paul's Cathedral, were conferred upon him. While holding this latter appointment he suggested the famous inscription to the memory of Wren in St Paul's, "Si monumentum requiras, circumspice." He died in 1821. MYMUNSING, a district of Hindustan, in the province of Bengal, situated between the 24th and 26th degrees of north latitude. The boundaries of this territory are the Garrow Mountains and the district of Goalpara on the N., Dacca Jelalpoor on the S., Silhet on the E., and Bogra and Rungpoor on the W. The country is intersected by the

The surface is rugged, but does not rise to a very great height, and the soil is dry but fertile. Wine and fruit are the principal products of the island, and it also contains abundance of game. There is very little water here, and the wants of the inhabitants are for the most part supplied by rain water. The town of Mycone stands on the N.W. coast, and is chiefly inhabited by sailors, who are reckoned among the best in these seas. The roadstead is exposed to all winds except those from the N.N.E. ROBERT, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was the descendant of a family of architects, and was born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1734. Having adopted at an early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> profession, he was sent to the Continent to complete his studies. a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, situated between the 24th and 26th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The boundaries of this territory are the Garrow <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> and the district of Goalpara on the N., Dacca Jelalpoor on the S., Silhet on the E., and Bogra and Rungpoor on the W. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is intersected by the

MYRIAPODA

Pages 760-764

A wingless tribe of insects, formerly so called, of which centipedes (the genus Scolopendra of Linnaeus) form the most characteristic example, are now regarded as a separate class of the articulated tribes, in conformity with the views of Dr Leach and other writers who have studied their structure and economy. Under this <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, therefore, as formerly intimated, we shall present the reader with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> notice of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> genera, of which the prevailing forms have been already exhibited (in connection with our representations of insects) on Plate CCLII. of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. We owe the establishment of the class to Dr Leach, M. Lamarck having viewed the Myriapoda as arachnides, while M. Latreille, except in a single work, regarded them as true insects. As such they were likewise included by Linnaeus, and the older systematic writers, in the order APTERA. The Myriapoda are distinguished from true insects by their greater amount of feet (twenty-four and upwards), by the want of any precise <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> appreciable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into thorax and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and by the numerous segments into which their bodies are divided. Each segment, with the exception of the first, is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of legs, terminated for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by a single hook. The stigmata, or openings for respiration, are placed on each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> segment, a circumstance which has induced some observers to regard the latter as only semi-segments, in as far as in true insects each <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> has its pair of stigmata. But we see no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for the establishment of any strict <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of form between the subjects of two distinct classes of articulated beings; and indeed, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we do so in regard to the character in question, we produce a greater discordance by the necessity, in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, of assigning to each so-called (<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>) segment, a couple of pair of legs. The mandibles are bi-articulate, and are followed by a piece in the form of a labium, quadrid, with articulated divisions resembling little feet, and corresponding in position to the languette of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">Crustacea</a>. Then succeed two pair of small feet, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, sometimes hook-shaped, seem to replace the four maxillae of the last-named order, or the two maxillae and the lower lip of insects. They may be regarded as maxillary feet. The antennae are two in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Their form cannot be easily generalised, because, although they may often be, as Latreille says, "courtes, un peu plus grosses vers le bout, ou presque filiformes;" yet in some (genus Scutigera) they are very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and become much more slender towards the extremity. The number of the articulations also varies greatly. The organs of vision are usually formed by a union of smooth or simple eyes; but in some these parts are analogous to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> eyes of insects, the facettes, however, being proportionally larger, rounder, and more distinct. All Myriapodes are apterous. The subjects of our present notice differ likewise from insects in this remarkable peculiarity, that the number of their segments, and consequently of the stigmata and legs, increases with the size of the individual. It would even appear, from the observations of Savi the younger, that the genus Julus is born without feet; from which it has been observed, that those Myriapodes are subject, at some early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their lives, to a regular metamorphosis. Degeer had long before observed, that the number of their parts increased with the general growth of the body. The organs of respiration consist of two principal tracheae extending <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> along the body, and receiving <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> from the lateral spiracles. Myriapodes are generally supposed to be longer lived, and of more continuous growth, than insects; and, according to Savi the younger, two years elapse (at least in the genus Julus) before the development of the generative system; but it must be borne in mind, that many insects exist for a length of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the larva state (to which the early condition of the Myriapodes so closely corresponds), and are thus of equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> with the many-footed subjects of our present inquiry. The Myriapodes in general shun the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. They conceal themselves under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, beneath the bark of trees, among old <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and in various other localities. Some inhabit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and others are destructive to culinary vegetables. Many are carnivorous, seizing upon animal substances, both dead and living, with their curved jaws. They are said to infuse a poisonous juice into their wounded victims. In our subdivision of the class, as in the preceding generalities, we shall follow the system of Latreille, by whom the Myriapodes are partitioned into two primary groups, which differ from each other both in habits and structure. ORDER I.—CHILOGNATHA. This primary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> corresponds to the genus Julus of Linnaeus. The body is for the most part cylindrical, and of a crustaceous consistence. The antennae are composed of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, of nearly equal size. The mandibles are thick, without palpi, distinctly divided into two portions by a median articulation, and with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> implanted in a concavity of their upper extremity. Beneath is a kind of labium or lower lip, divided at its exterior surface, by notches and longitudinal sections, into four principal areas, tuberculated on the upper margin, and of which the two intermediate are short and narrow, and placed at the upper extremity of another <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, which serves them as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> base. The feet are very short, and always terminate in a single hook; four anterior feet placed immediately beneath the labium, resemble the others in form, but are more approximate at their base, with the radical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> proportionally longer. Most of the other legs are attached by double pairs to a single segment of the body. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs are placed beneath the seventh pair of legs, those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> behind the second pair. The stigmata, as usually described, are very small, and placed on alternate segments outside the origin of the legs. The Myriapodes of this division are slow of movement, and advance, as it were, by a gliding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. They assume in defense a round or spiral form. The first segment of the body, in some the second, is larger than the others, and presents the form of a corselet or buckler. The double pairs of legs do not occur until we reach the fourth, fifth, or sixth pair; the first three or four pair being free from their origin, or adhering to their respective segments only by a median or sternal line. The two or three terminal segments of the body are usually without feet. On each side of the body there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of pores, formerly regarded as stigmata, but which, according to M. Savi, merely emit an acid liquor of disagreeable odour, and probably intended as a means of defense; the true stigmata, or respiratory openings, as described by the Italian naturalist, being placed on the sternal piece of each segment, and communicating internally with a double series of pneumatic pouches, disposed in chapelet along the body, and giving out tracheal branches, which ramify over the other organs. These pouches or vesicular trachea, according to M. Straus, are not connected with each other, as among ordinary insects, by a principal trachea. The form of the newly-hatched bodies of the Iulusidae, as observed by M. Savi in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, was somewhat kidney-shaped, quite plain, and without appendages. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of eighteen days they underwent their first moult, and only then assumed the form of the adults; but they were still composed of only twenty-two segments, and the total number of their legs amounted to twenty-six pair. These observations are in some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> inconsistent with the assertion of Degeer, who in the young state of these creatures counted only three pair of legs and eight segments; but is it certain, asks M. Latreille, that the moult described by M. Savi was actually the first; or ought we not rather to presume that they do not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> suddenly from an apodal state to the possession of twenty-six pair of legs; in other words, that they are subject to certain intermediate changes, which may have escaped the observation of M. Savi? After the second moult, however, the last-named naturalist informs us, the genus Iulus exhibits thirty-six pair of legs, and after the third, forty-three, and the body then consists of thirty segments. In the adult state the number is considerably increased. Two years afterwards another moult takes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and it is only then that the generative system is developed. From the period of birth, which takes place in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the renewals of the skin were observed by M. Savi to take place almost monthly till November, and the exuviae were seen to contain even the membrane which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the interior of the alimentary canal and trachea. The organs of the mouth were the only parts not there observed by M. Savi. The food of these Myriapodes consists both of animal and vegetable substances, generally dead and decomposed. They deposit a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of eggs. The generic groups are as follows. We shall enter into few details, as we have illustrated so many of the prevailing forms by means of accurate figures. Genus Glomeris, L. Body convex above, concave below, with a range of small scales along the lower sides. It is composed of twelve segments, exclusive of the head. The male has thirty-two legs, the female thirty-four. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are not numerous. Although G. ovatus inhabits the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, the greater proportion are terrestrial, occurring under stones, particularly in mountainous countries. G. marginata (Plate CCLII, fig. 1) is common in most European countries. Genus Iulus, L. Body cylindrical and extended, without any projecting <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> margins. The larger species are terrestrial, and live in woods; the smaller attack fruits, roots, and various <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> produce, to some of which they are very destructive. They all assume a spiral position in repose or when alarmed; the head being placed in the centre. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> to the time of Latreille, this entire division was included under the genus Iulus, Linn. But the French naturalist restricted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> to the cylindrical species, and formed of the others his genera Glomeris, Polydesmus, Polyzenus. Various species are described by Dr Leach, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which stands in need of revision. We have here figured I. sabulosus, a common European species, Plate CCLII, fig. 3. A monstrous Myriapod is mentioned by Ulloa as inhabiting the district of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. He describes it (if his terms have not been mistranslated) as sometimes extending a yard in length, and measuring five inches across. Here there is no doubt some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> exaggeration. He adds that its bite is mortal, if a timely remedy be not applied. From its cylindrical form it has been regarded as an Iulus. Genus Polydesmus, L. Body linear, the segments compressed on the under surface, with projecting ridges on the upper, somewhat in the form of transverse <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> scales. The species of this genus, of which our Iulus complanatus, Linn., may be regarded as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> (Plate CCLII, fig. 2), dwell under stones in dampish places. They assume the spiral form when touched, and feed both on animal and vegetable matters in a state of decomposition. Certain other species, of which the eyes are obvious, form the genus Craspedosoma of Dr Leach. Genus Polyzenus, L. Body soft, membranous, terminated by a tuft of lengthened scales. The only species of which we have any knowledge is the Pol. lagurus, L. (Plate CCLII, fig. 5), regarded as a scolopendra by the generality of systematic authors, and described by Degeer under the name of Iule à <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUEUE">queue</a> en pincone. It is a very small creature, of rather singular aspect. Our magnified representation <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> referred <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the necessity of descriptive details. Its early organization is less complicated than that of the adult state; that is, the young consist of fewer segments and a less number of legs. We know little of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> habits. It occurs in the clefts of walls, and beneath the bark of old trees. Order II.—CHILOPODA. Lat. This division of the Myriapoda bears nearly the same relation to the unrestricted genus Scolopendra of Linnæus, --- 1 Règne Animal, iv. 332. 2 See Observazione per servire <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALLA">alla</a> storia di una specie di Iulus complanatus, reprinted in Memorie Scientifiche, Pisa, 1829. 3 Linn. Trans. xi. 377. 4 Voyage, vol. i. p. 61. 5 Kirby and Spence's Introduction to Entomology, vol. i. p. 128. 6 Mémoires, t. vii. pl. 36. as the preceding does to the genus *Julus* of the Swedish naturalist. The antennae become slender towards the extremity, and are composed of fourteen articulations and upwards. The mouth is composed of two mandibles, each furnished with a small palpitiform appendage, and exhibiting in their centre the appearance of a jointing, and ending in a spoon-shaped termination, with toothed edges. The labium is quadrifid, with the two lateral divisions larger than the others, transversely ringed, and resembling the membranous feet of caterpillars. This labium is analogous to the lower lip of the chilognathous kinds, which represents in Latreille's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> the tongue of the crustaceous tribes, but possesses also the functions of maxillae. It is what Savigny names the first auxiliary lip. Besides these parts, there are two palpi or minute feet, united at the base, and unguiculated at the point; a second labium (*seconda lèvre auxiliaire* of Savigny), formed by a second pair of feet dilated and joined at their origin, and terminated by a strong hook, moveable, and pierced at the extremity, for the transmission of a venomous or acrid liquid. The body of these unseemly creatures is depressed and membranous. Each ring or segment is covered by a coenocytic plate, and usually bears only a single pair of legs; and the terminal segment is generally thrown backwards, and elongated into a kind of tail. The organs of respiration are composed, either in whole or in part, of tubular tracheae. The sexual parts are interior, and placed at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> extremity of the body, as in the generality of insects properly so called. The stigmata are more obvious than in the preceding family, and are either lateral or dorsal. The species of this division are of much more nimble habits than those of the preceding; and the peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> produces an undulating lateral motion. They are of carnivorous habits, and, avoiding strong light, usually conceal themselves under stones or old timber, beneath the bark of trees, &c. They are held in some dread by the inhabitants of tropical countries, where they attain a great size, and are consequently capable of inflicting dangerous wounds. But the majority of travelers seem agreed that, although the bite is more painful than that of a scorpion, it is never attended by fatal consequences. In more northern countries they are quite harmless, though disliked in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their repulsive aspect. Our common centipede (*Scolopendra forticata* of Linn.) so frequent in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> under stones, may be mentioned as a familiar example. Leeuwenhoeck, the great Dutch microscopical observer, has described the perforation of the hooks, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POISON">poison</a> is supposed to flow. This order (which corresponds to the *Syngnatha* of Latreille's earlier works, the title adhered to by Dr Leach) is divided into the following genera. The first two have only fifteen pair of legs; and their bodies, when viewed from above, seem to present fewer segments than when examined from below. **Genus Scutigera**, Lamarck. Body covered by eight plates or shields, beneath each of which are two pneumatic pouches or vesicular tracheae, which receive the air, and communicate with lateral and inferior tracheae of a tubular form. The under surface is divided into fifteen semi-segments, each <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a pair of feet terminated by an extremely long, slender, and minutely articulated <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARSUS">tarsus</a>. The terminal legs are long, and seem to increase in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from the foremost to the hindmost pair. The eyes are comparatively <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and reticulated. The antennae are very long and slender, and the palpi projecting and spinous. The species keep themselves concealed during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in barns, or the unfrequented parts of houses, lying between old planks, or sometimes under stones. They are seen at night running on the outside walls with great velocity, feeding on onisci, and various insects. They seem to pierce their prey with their mouth-hooks, and infuse into them a poisonous fluid, which immediately deprives them of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. These Myriapodes make their appearance in great numbers, chiefly in rainy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. According to Illiger, they are greatly dreaded by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. The best known European species is the *S. araneoides* (Plate CCLII., fig. 4). It is the *Scolopendra coleopterata* of Linn. and Fab. Pallas asserts that it was taken by a friend of his among some fuci in the sea; but as all analogy is against its natural occurrence in such a locality, we may infer that it had fallen accidentally from the timbers of a vessel. **Genus Lithobius**, Leach. Body divided into an equal number of segments both above and below, each bearing a pair of legs. The dorsal plates are alternately long and short. The stigmatic openings are lateral. We have figured our most common species, *L. forficata* (Plate CCLII., fig. 6), a familiarly-known Linncean scolopendra, as an example of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> genus. It occurs almost everywhere, throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, under stones. The anatomical structure of the genus has been described by M. Leon Dufour. The remaining generic groups of this order have at least twenty-one pair of legs, and the segments of the body are of nearly equal size, and of similar number, both above and below. In the genus *Scolopendra*, properly so called, there are eight distinct eyes, four on each side, and the basal joint of the terminal legs is armed with small spines. We have no British species, but the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> produces *Scol. cingulata*, which presents almost as formidable an aspect as some of the exotic kinds. The great foreign species (one of which sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> above a foot in length) have been as yet but ill defined, several kinds being no doubt described under the name of *Scol. morstans*, a native of South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> (Plate CCLII., fig. 9). A monstrous species, called *Scol. Plumieri*, is figured in Lister's Journey to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and appears to be also represented in Seba's Thesaurus, under the name of *Millepeda <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> ex Nova Hispana*. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and the great eastern <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, produce some very large species; and scolopendras of alarming size likewise occur on the African continent. The bite of these creatures is said to be dangerous; but it seems that the poison of the wound is allayed by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a>. M. Amoreux is of opinion that no poisonous power is possessed by any of the European species. The whole are carnivorous and voracious, and, all things considered, they may be regarded as among the ugliest of creeping things. Nevertheless they are not without their advantage to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "I have seen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> chil- --- 1 This piece is not attached to the head, but to the anterior extremity of the first semi-segment. The two hooked feet form by the union and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of their first article a plate in the form of a labium or mentum, and the same semi-segment bears the two first ordinary feet. (*Regne Animal*, iv. 356.) 2 Latreille and others have adopted Lamarck's designation, although the title of *Ceratiota* had at a prior period been assigned to this generic group by Illiger. See Reuss's *Fauna Etrusca*, t. ii. p. 299. 3 *Spicilegia Zoologica*, fascic. 9, tab. 4, fig. 16. 4 *Bulletins de la Soc. Phil. Januar*, 1824, p. 24. 5 *Annales des Sciences Nat.* ii. 81. 6 *Insect. Venim.* p. 277. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MYROBALANS">MYROBALANS</a> are the unripe drupe-like fruits of a tree found in the East Indies, growing from 40 to 50 feet in height. It is the Terminalia Chebula, Roxburgh, of the natural order Combretaceae. (See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.) The myrobalan of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is about an inch and a half in length, oval in shape, dry, hard, and wrinkled, and of a brownish-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It was first imported in 1842 as a substitute for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and was for some time supposed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALL">gall</a>, and returned as such in the revenue accounts. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> imported during the first three years only amounted to about 8 tons; but so greatly has the demand increased in consequence of the valuable properties of the myrobalan, that in 1856 the importation had reached 3150 tons. The myrobalan is gathered unripe, and then dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and packed into pockets containing about half a cwt., and bags holding about one and a half cwt. Of these bags, the number imported in 1856 was 41,250, and of the pockets 2300, nearly all of which are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>. The value is, according to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, from 6s. to 12s. per cwt. With the salts of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> the myrobalan yields nearly as fine a black as the Turkish oak-gall; and from the fact that it contains a large quantity of tannic acid it has been extensively used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a> when more than ordinarily cheap. Besides black, they yield various shades of yellow and yellowish-green, with proper mordants. There are numerous species of myrobalan, some of which are very useful. They are,—the Terminalia citrina, Rox., used as a gentle aperient in Indian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>; the Terminalia belerica, Rox., the seeds of which are eaten, and are likewise used in tanning and dyeing; the Terminalia catappa, Linn., yielding the edible kernels called Indian almonds; the Terminalia glabrata, Forskål, eaten in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> and Friendly Islands; the Terminalia angustifolia, Jacquin, formerly celebrated for its richly odorous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUM">gum</a>; and the Terminalia alata, used in tanning operations in India. The emblic myrobalan, the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica, Linn., is used for similar purposes in the East Indies. (t.c.A.)

MYRON

Pages 764-764

one of the most famous of Greek statuaries, was born at Eleutheræ in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> about 480 B.C. He studied along with Polycletus under Ageladas of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, and flourished at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> about the commencement of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Some of his works were executed in marble, but he wrought most successfully in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a> of Delos. The range of his subjects was not confined to the varied attitudes of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It also comprised the forms of other animals; and this fact distinguished him from the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> statuaries of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Another characteristic of Myron was the want of all idealization in his works. "He was," says Pliny, "curious in all corporeal detail, but paid little regard to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>." There was an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ease in his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> which indicated the admirable spontaneity of his genius. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> that first raised him to celebrity was a brazen cow, in the attitude of lowing, and, according to some, of suckling a calf. It was set up in a public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Athens, and there it stood till at least the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Cicero, attracting more notice by its simple truthfulness than all the highly-idealized statues of men and gods that abounded in the thoroughfares and streets of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Many authors mentioned it both in prose and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and no less than thirty-six of the epigrams in the Greek anthology were written in its praise. The last writer who alludes to its existence is Procopius, in the sixth century. It was then standing in the temple of Peace at Rome. The next most famous work of Myron was the "Discobolus," <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> quoit-thrower. This <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> is described by Lucian as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> one knee in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of preparing to play, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> his head slightly to one side, and extending his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> behind his back to take the quoit from his left. Of this bronze statue many marble imitations were probably taken, in accordance with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Some of these are supposed to have been discovered. One found in the Villa Palombra, on the Esquiline, in 1782, and now seen in the Villa Massimi at Rome, closely agrees with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the original given by Lucian. Not so faithful is another that was discovered in the grounds of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>'s villa near <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a> in 1791, and is now exhibited in the Townley gallery of the British <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>. It has both <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> bent, instead of one only, and the head inclining forwards, instead of turning round. The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of some of Myron's other works is given by Pliny.—A dog; Perseus; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-monsters; a satyr admiring a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; Delphic pentathletes; pancratists; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. There are also mentioned in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors, a colossal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, Juno, and Hercules at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>; four oxen, which were placed by Augustus in the portico of Apollo's temple on the Palatine; a statue of Apollo, with the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> in small silver letters on the thigh; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; several athletes; and a drunken old woman, in marble, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>. Myron was also a carver in wood and an engraver in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. He is said to have died in great poverty, leaving a son, named Lycius, who inherited a considerable portion of his father's talents. (English Cyclopaedia of Biography.)

MYRRH

Pages 764-765

a resinous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUM">gum</a> which exudes from the bark of the myrrh tree (Balsamodendron myrrha, nat. ord. Terebinthaceæ), found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. (See the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.) As a balsam, myrrh has been highly prized from the most remote times. We find the earliest mention of it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> xxxvii. 25. The Egyptians used it extensively for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> their dead, and its sweet odour is easily recognisable in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bituminous material which is now found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities in mummies. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> employed it in medicine; and Pliny speaks of it as an important article of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and as selling at a price so <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to provoke extensive and ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a>. (See Pliny's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, Bohn's edition.) Myrrh is now imported from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and the East Indies. That from the former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is considered superior in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and is easily known from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> sort by its paler <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and purer fragrance. It is a true gum-resin, partially soluble in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and partially in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>. It is, however, more soluble in water than in alcohol. Brande gives the following <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>:—Volatile <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, 2·60; resin (soft), 22·24; resin (hard), 5·56; gum (soluble), 54·38; gum (insoluble), 9·32; salts, 1·36; impurities, 1·60; loss, 2·94. It is used in medicine, and enters largely into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of tooth-powders; it is also used in incense and other fumigations. Myrrh is packed in chests containing from 1½ to 2 cwt. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> imported into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in 1856 was 310 cwt. In that year the most inferior East Indian myrrh sold for L.2, 10s. per cwt., whilst the best Turkey brought L.8.

MYSIA

Pages 765-765

an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the N.W. of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, was bounded on the S. by Lydia, on the E. by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> and Bithynia, on the N. by the Propontis and the Hellespont, and on the W. by the Ægean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. The name Mysia, however, was often applied to particular parts of this district. The province was divided into five parts,—Mysia Minor, Mysia <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, Troas, Æolis, and Teuthrania. To the first of these the Mysians were originally confined. They had come thither from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Lydians, as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> asserts, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> from Thrace, as Strabo maintains, and as their alleged identity with the Mosians implies. Gradually they spread themselves southward, encroaching upon the Trojans, Æolians, and Phrygian settlers, until they had attained sufficient importance to communicate their name to the entire province. Little is known about their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. They are mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> among the allies of Priam. This country was subject at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the Lydian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. It then formed in succession a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the third satrapy under the Persians, and a part of the Syrian empire that was formed after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. On the defeat of Antiochus, the last <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in 65 B.C., it was given by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a>, King of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>. It was afterwards incorporated in the Roman province of Asia. Mysia was rendered rugged by Mount Temnus, Mount Ida, Olympus, and other offshoots of Mount Taurus. There were many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> were Caicus (Ak-sou) in the S., and Æsepus in the N. Pergamum (Bergama), Cyzicus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a>, and Adramyttium (Adramytti), were the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>.

MYSORE

Pages 765-772

MAHESURA, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> MAHISOUR, a raj or native principality in the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, under the protection and administration of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. It is situated principally between N. Lat. 11. and 15., and is completely surrounded by the British territories subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> presidencies. Its length is estimated at 210 miles, and its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth at 140. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, inclosed between the Eastern and the Western Ghauts, and elevated 3000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from which rise numerous lofty hills, containing the sources of many streams. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which intersect the country are,—the Cauvery, Tumbrudda, Vedawati, and the Northern and Southern Penna. The elevation of this inland plain varies at different places. The highest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Mysore, namely, those of Babubulin, near Bednore, rise to the height of 6000 feet; the elevation of Sivaganga is 4600 feet; at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">Pass</a> of Peddanaik Durgum the height is 1907 feet, according to barometrical observations; at Baitaman-galam, 2435; at Bangalore, 2807; at Hurryhur, 1831. The seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is mitigated by the height of the ground, and the climate throughout the whole of this extensive tract is remarkably temperate and healthy. This country has another peculiar advantage, namely, that it is sheltered by the Ghaut Mountains from the violence of the monsoons, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> along the lower plains, and deluge with torrents of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> the coasts of Coromandel and Malabar. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> which are driven on the land from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean by the south-west monsoons are opposed by the mountain-wall of the Western Ghauts; and although the higher and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> clouds make their way into the plains, and occasion frequent, and sometimes heavy showers, which refresh the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> and the ground, yet they are seldom of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. Occasional showers, however, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at other seasons, and preserve the verdure of the fields throughout the year. The country of Mysore, from its elevation and its temperate climate, not only produces all the other grains and vegetables of other parts of India, but also many of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It appears to have been formerly in a much higher state of cultivation than at present; but it was nearly ruined, partly by the invasion of armies, partly by the rigorous administration of Hyder, and still more by that of his son Tippoo. It is now rapidly recovering from its depopulation under the sway of the British. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">Rice</a> is cultivated on the higher and lower grounds; and the cultivation is much aided by means of reservoirs and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, whence the farmers irrigate their fields and gardens. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> also produces the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> clayey lands are best adapted. The crop of raggy, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of coarse grain which supplies all the lower classes with their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> food, is the most important of any raised on the dry field. Wheat is cultivated in gardens, or in the rich soil of the beds of the tanks, which have been exhausted for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a>. It is only a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, however, that is raised. The Ricinus communis is found here, and produces abundance of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> and a variety of other purposes. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BETEL">betel</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> tree thrives on the low grounds, where it can obtain a supply of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and the poppy is cultivated, both for making opium, and on account of the seed, which is much used in the sweet cakes that are eaten by the higher ranks of the natives. The cocoa-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> palm begins to produce in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> when it is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight years old. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> is here in a very backward state, and the implements used are very imperfect. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> has neither coulter nor mould-board to divide and turn over the soil, and it seldom penetrates more than three inches deep. The fields are in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> very imperfectly cleared; and after six or eight ploughings in all directions, numerous small bushes remain as erect as before the labour commenced. Considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is, however, paid to the manuring of the soil; every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> collecting a heap from the dung and litter of his cattle, intermixed with the ashes and soil of their houses. The cattle reared are cows, buffaloes, sheep, and the long-legged goat; the native breed of horses here, as in most parts of India, is a small, ill-shaped, vicious pony. Above the Ghauts, asses are much used as beasts of burden. The breed is small, and no pains are taken to improve it. Swine were formerly very common in Mysore, but they were banished by Tippoo from the vicinity of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. There are three varieties of sheep—tawny, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and black. Common <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is found in abundance in many places, and is extracted for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> or manufacturing purposes. Carbonate of soda is also found amongst the Chitradroog Hills, mixed with common salt. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>-ore abounds in different parts, though it is worked in a very slovenly manner. At the iron-works near Chinnarayana Durga, the smelters procure from the one about 47 per cent. of malleable iron, which is, however, very impure. The principal rivers, which have been already enumerated, are all inconsiderable, with the exception of the Cauvery, as long as they continue within the limits of this province. There are many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tanks and reservoirs in the higher grounds throughout Mysore, but there are no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The water in these tanks is always sweet, and preferred on this account to that of wells, which is very frequently brackish. Upon the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Tippoo <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> in 1799, the territories of the fallen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> were divided, and the portion now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the name of Mysore was allotted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TITULAR">titular</a> rajah of the same name, the representative of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>. MYSTERIES (Greek Μυστήρια, a word ultimately derivable from the root MU, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> produced with closed lips) were ceremonies in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> religions, conducted secretly, and only in the presence of such as had undergone <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of initiation. The ultimate origin of such ceremonies is doubtless to be sought for in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> itself, and the feelings of awe and reverence with which its objects are regarded. For to such feelings is directly traceable whatever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> sacerdotal exclusiveness or legislative <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> may be supposed to have had in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> and preservation. Mystery, in one form or another, is inherent in religion, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> never disappear from it. Mysterious ceremonies, doctrines, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are co-ordinate developments of the same <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> feelings. The origin and significance of the ancient mysteries have been the subject of much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> and discussion. On these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> some observations will be subjoined to the following succinct account of the most celebrated of these institutions: 1. The Mysteries of Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>.—These two deities, like the reigning deities in all mythologies, are preceded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a> by others. A satisfactory explanation of this fact has not yet been reached; it was formerly the main support of the Euhemeristic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, and has been plausibly explained by that of successive worships, a theory which has also been applied to the explanation of many of the peculiar features of the myths themselves. It is certain, at all events, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, that the revolutions in her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> were accompanied by extensive changes in her religious systems, and by the displacement or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of the ancient and local deities in a more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a>, and the growth of new myths, in which, doubtless, the historical events attending these changes have been partially reflected. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> states, and his statement is confirmed by the monuments, that the Egyptian gods formed three orders (ii. 145). These three orders are successive dynasties of gods whose reign preceded that of mortal sovereigns. Of these three, the most recent is that of Osiris, whose son <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HORUS">Horus</a> is the last reigning god. (Bunsen, Egypt's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> in Uni. History, vol. i., p. 357.) These two deities alone, Osiris and Isis, were worshipped over the whole of Egypt, and their mythical history formed the subject of the mysteries. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> actual events, as we have supposed, are partially reflected in the story, the whole has been thrown into the prehistoric and dateless periods of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, and has been so interwoven with the ideal and purely symbolic, that the elements are not now distinguishable. Osiris, sovereign of Lower Egypt, is, with Isis, his sister-spouse, the originator of agriculture and the arts of peace and civilization. The cultivation of grain and of the vine, settled <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, letters, music, and the fine arts, are owing to him. He sets out on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of conquest and civilization, leaving the government in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Isis, against whom Typhon, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and implacable enemy of Osiris, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> in his absence, but is defeated, and affects reconciliation. Osiris visits Ethiopia, India, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and introduces a new order of things. On his return to Egypt, he is surprised by Typhon at a peaceful banquet, and put into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, which is committed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Isis, learning this, searches for his body, and is guided to Biblos in Phenicia. Her adventures here present a remarkable similarity to those of Demeter at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>; she becomes nurse in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to the son of Astarte, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of Biblos. At length she declares herself, gains possession of the coffin, and returns with it to Egypt, where she conceals herself with it. It is discovered by Typhon, who cuts in pieces the body of Osiris, and scatters it over the country. Isis again sets out in quest of the body, and succeeds in finding all the pieces but one, which she replaces with an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> phallus, and interts the body at Pousiri. According to other legends, she consigns each piece to a separate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, so that it is impossible afterwards to dishonour them. Horus defeats Typhon and makes him prisoner, but Isis sets him at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and banishes him. Of the ceremonies to which this myth corresponds our information is vague and imperfect. They seem to have been six in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and celebrated at different periods of the year. 1. The Aphaimnion, or disappearance of Osiris, on the 17th of Athyr (13th Nov.) 2. The Zetesis, or search for Osiris, about the winter solstice. In this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, the sacred cow, symbol of Isis, was led seven times round the temple. (Plut., De Is. et Osir. 52.) 3. The finding of Osiris in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. 5. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of Osiris. And 6. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the entrance of Osiris into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a> and Philae, supposed tombs of Osiris, were celebrated mystic rites, of which we have no certain information. These ceremonies throw considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> upon the meaning of the legend. Osiris was the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, life-giving power; hence the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the Nile, &c., and hence his symbol, the bull; Isis, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>, life-receiving power; hence Egypt, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, vegetation, &c., and hence her symbol, the cow. The life-giving power suffers in the course of the year a temporary death, but is restored to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> again in the vernal season. The Egyptian mysteries of Isis are to be distinguished from those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> Isis, established at Corinth, and afterwards so notorious at Rome. We have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of these mysteries, doubtless embellished by the author's fancy, in the Metamorphoses of Apuleius (lib. xi.) The festival was preceded by purification in the sea before sunrise, and at sunrise a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> was formed, in which the sacred coffin and image of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> was borne by a train of priests to the shore, when a curiously-adorned vessel was consecrated. The ceremonies of initiation were practised by night. The neophyte, after various lustrations and instructions, was led into the presence of the goddess, and there heard and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> what he dared not reveal. The discourse put by Apuleius in the mouth of Isis is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the inscription of Sais,—"I am all that has been, is, and will be." The advantages Mysteries. to be derived from initiation were, length of life, the protection of the goddess, and a happy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> in the next world. The worship of maritime Isis seems to have been introduced into Rome about the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the empire, and was for a long time held in contempt and detestation. This feeling doubtless facilitated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> of these mysteries into what they became under the later emperors,—scenes of debauchery, and all kinds of wickedness.
